README.md.overview: The README is the human-facing front door of the Return App: it says what the product is (a return-scanning app for VB Exports that loads marketplace return reports as lookup data and records physical arrivals in the permanent return scan register), how to install and start it, how to create the first users, and what each web page and client does. It is the first stop of the guided tour (step 1) and hands agents off to AGENTS.md for the binding rules. Its status lines are dated snapshots, so treat version numbers here as a point-in-time summary rather than the source of truth.

sections.title: Title and dated status
sections.explanation: An HTML comment records when the file was last updated, then the opening paragraph defines the core domain: marketplace return reports (Myntra VB/EJ, Flipkart, Meesho, Amazon, Ajio) become per-account lookup data, and a scan writes the permanent register record. The bold status line summarises test counts, the production URL and the Android and desktop versions. Notice that these numbers drift: the README still names Android tag `v1.0.63` while AGENTS.md's newer Current state names a later tag, so cross-check versions against AGENTS.md and the release manifest before relying on them.

sections.title: Agent pointer and quick start
sections.explanation: Agents are sent straight to AGENTS.md and the handoff notes. The quick start is deliberately short: `npm install`, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, set `DATABASE_URL` with `sslmode=verify-full` so the database certificate is checked, then `npm run dev` (or `RUN.bat` on Windows). The listed addresses (`/`, `/scan`, `/register`, `/claims`, `/uploads`, `/admin`) and the `/api/health` check on port 3001 match the routes and the health handler you will see in `server/index.ts`.

sections.title: Creating users from the CLI
sections.explanation: The app ships with no users or sample data, so the first administrator is created with `npm run user:create`. The password is read from the `NEW_USER_PASSWORD` environment variable rather than a command-line flag, which keeps it out of shell history and output. The section also explains the access model in plain terms: `Admin` is the only role with special meaning here, and other users see either their assigned accounts or every account when they have the all-marketplaces flag, which is exactly what `users.has_all_marketplaces` and `user_marketplaces` encode in the schema.

sections.title: The six web console pages
sections.explanation: Each bullet describes one page of the React console: Overview, Scan returns, Return register, Claims, Data uploads and Admin. Several project rules surface here in user language: figures are counted only from accounts the user can see (account scope), safe retries on scan save (idempotency), every ticket change is kept (append-only history), and previous lookup rows are kept as history when a new report is activated (activation, not replacement).

sections.title: Android and desktop clients
sections.explanation: This section introduces the two non-web clients that call the same API: the Kotlin Android scanner (CameraX scanning, evidence capture, in-app updates) and the Windows desktop app with its automation engine. The desktop bullets compress many architecture decisions into one list: the bundled React renderer at `returnapp://desktop`, panel-wise filing across six supplier panels, the 4 GB / 2-core hardware budget, process-tree termination, streamed evidence downloads, and the engine's fail-closed `ENGINE_TOKEN` rule for remote binds. Later tour steps (10, 12-14) show each of these in code.

sections.title: Example, CLI jobs and testing
sections.explanation: A worked example walks through activating a Flipkart report on the Data uploads page. The command-line jobs (`npm run sync:oms`) and the three verification commands (`typecheck`, `build`, `test`) are listed next. The note about `TEST_DATABASE_URL` matters: database-backed tests are reported as skipped without it, and the project treats a skipped check as not passed.

sections.title: Documentation index
sections.explanation: The closing list links every deeper document: the agent handoff, getting started, configuration, architecture, the register specification and the API reference. It restates that `CLAUDE.md` is intentionally absent and must not be invented, which is a recurring project rule. It also notes there is no license file in the repository.

AGENTS.md.overview: AGENTS.md is the mandatory starting point for any contributor, human or AI. It explains which tooling to install first, summarises what the project is and its current state, fixes the reading order for the rest of the docs, and lists the numbered rules that the code is built to uphold (account scope on every data route, activation instead of replacement, additive-only schema, verified database TLS, no secrets, and the desktop/engine rules). Tour step 1 pairs it with the README; later steps show these rules enforced in `server/db.ts`, `server/http.ts`, `server/auth.ts` and the engine code.

sections.title: Purpose of the file
sections.explanation: Two sentences set the contract: read this file and then the listed documents, in order, before changing any code. Everything that follows is written as an instruction set rather than a description, which is why later sections use imperative language and numbered rules.

sections.title: Required skills before work
sections.explanation: This block requires three helper tools on every task: graphify (a code knowledge graph queried before grep or file reads), ponytail (a smallest-change review discipline) and Understand-Anything (architecture and onboarding views whose graph lives in `.ua/`). It gives the exact check and install commands for PowerShell, and warns never to create a `CLAUDE.md`, because graphify would write there and hide AGENTS.md from Claude Code. The final paragraph makes clear that these tools never override the project rules: account scope, validation, audit history, security, `SYN-` test data and hardware limits all stay.

sections.title: What the project is
sections.explanation: A compact definition of the domain and the stack: Express 4 and PostgreSQL on the server, React 19 with Vite on the client, strict TypeScript, and `node:test` run through `tsx`. It also notes that the project runs on Windows with PowerShell as the primary shell, which explains the Windows-specific details elsewhere (for example `taskkill /T /F`).

sections.title: Current state snapshot
sections.explanation: A dated, bullet-by-bullet snapshot of what is deployed and verified: test counts, production health, the Android and desktop versions, recent desktop changes up to 1.3.6 (including the per-cycle watchdogs), the shared `DateField` rule for date inputs, the product master reset, and how claim follow-ups work (only Meesho implements `checkClaimStatus()`). Read it as the most recent status summary; it is newer than the README's status line, so prefer it when the two disagree.

sections.title: Required reading order
sections.explanation: A numbered path through the documentation: the handoff invariants, register status, audit matrix, ARCHITECTURE.md, API.md and REGISTER.md. Item 2 stresses that a missing `CLAUDE.md` is not permission to change the rules here, which guards against an agent treating an absent file as a blank slate.

sections.title: Core data and register rules
sections.explanation: Rules 1 to 11 are the invariants the server code is built around. Rule 1 (account scope bound as a SQL parameter) is implemented through `scopeFor`/`accountCondition` and the `scopeOf(req)` helper; rule 2 is `requireAdmin` in `server/http.ts`; rules 3 and 6 (activation, additive schema, never bump `SCHEMA_VERSION`) are enforced in `server/db.ts` and the schema files; rule 7 is the TLS logic in `connectionSettingsFor`. Rule 11, report only what you ran, governs how agents describe verification.

sections.title: Mobile, desktop and engine rules
sections.explanation: Rules 12 to 21 cover the other clients: APK release manifests must match published releases, the desktop must fit a 4 GB / 2-core budget and kill whole browser process trees, the engine owns the only filing and follow-up loops (kept apart by `poll-guard.ts`), a non-loopback engine bind needs an `ENGINE_TOKEN` of at least 24 characters, CORS is an exact allowlist, the preload bridge and its types change together, and every desktop change bumps the version. Rule 21 makes the skills-first workflow binding while keeping it subordinate to rules 1 to 20.

sections.title: Verification and desktop commands
sections.explanation: The three standard checks (`npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, `npm test`) are listed with the caveat that database tests skip without a `TEST_DATABASE_URL` whose name contains `test`. The note that `typecheck` spans four TypeScript projects explains the long `typecheck` script in package.json. Desktop and engine commands (renderer build/dev, `desktop:dist`, `engine`, `engine:docker`) follow.

sections.title: Graph, roles and handback
sections.explanation: The closing sections explain the role agents in `.claude/agents/` (a role gives instructions, not access), require a dated entry in the handoff session log when work ends, and include a tool-managed graphify block. That generated block tells agents to query the graph before reading raw files and to run `graphify update .` after code changes.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.overview: ARCHITECTURE.md is the system map used by tour step 2: one Express/PostgreSQL API serving the React web console, the Kotlin Android scanner and the Electron desktop claim bot. It describes the request path (session user, account scope, Admin check, error mapping), the main data flows (startup, sign-in, upload, scan, register, tickets, OMSGuru sync), and tables mapping modules and schema files to their responsibilities. Its header says it was last updated 2026-10-10, so some details (for example how the client authenticates, or the mention of `CLAUDE.md`) lag behind the code and AGENTS.md.

sections.title: System overview
sections.explanation: The opening describes the two main parts (Express API in `server/`, React SPA in `src/`), the inputs (report files, scanner input, the OMSGuru API) and the outputs (JSON, CSV/Excel downloads, database rows). The key sentence is that account limits are applied in SQL through `server/access.ts`, not in the UI. It also notes that the desktop app holds the only continuous claim-filing worker, while OMSGuru sync and reports are scripts.

sections.title: Component diagram
sections.explanation: A Mermaid graph shows how the route modules fan out to pure rule modules (`upload-policy.ts`, `register-rules.ts`, `marketplace-rules.ts`) and database services, all converging on `db.ts` and PostgreSQL. The split between 'pure' and 'database' modules is the functional-core / imperative-shell pattern you will see in later tour steps. The trailing paragraph explains the dev setup: Vite on 5173 proxies `/api` to the API on `PORT` (3001 by default), and production serves the built `dist/` folder from `server/index.ts`.

sections.title: Request path
sections.explanation: Four steps trace every data request: `requireUser` loads the session and computes the scope with `scopeFor`, `requireAdmin` gates configuration routes, services build SQL with `accountCondition` (or `FALSE` for no accounts), and `ServiceError` becomes an HTTP status through `sendError`. Note that step 1 says requireUser reads 'the bearer token'; the current `extractSessionToken` in `server/auth.ts` also accepts the HttpOnly session cookie. The caveat that services default to all accounts when no scope is passed is important: it exists for tests and scripts, so every route must pass the signed-in scope.

sections.title: Startup and sign-in flows
sections.explanation: Startup listens first, then `initDatabase()` runs `SELECT 1`, applies the ordered schema files in one transaction and adds the six marketplace channels; until that succeeds, database routes answer 503. Sign-in finds the user by email or alias, checks the password with bcrypt, creates a session with absolute and idle expiry, and is rate-limited by login and IP. These are exactly the paths implemented in `server/db.ts`, `server/index.ts`, `server/auth.ts` and `server/rate-limit.ts`.

sections.title: Upload, scan and register flows
sections.explanation: These subsections describe the business workflows in order: preview and activation of a return report (staged in memory, committed under an account advisory lock, old rows superseded not deleted), scanner-list validation, AWB lookup with a `decideLookup` outcome of found/duplicate/choose/not_found, idempotent scan save with a scan key and AWB advisory lock, register queries with bound filters and a fixed sort list, ticket status changes with history, Admin configuration that switches rather than deletes, and the OMSGuru sync. Each flow names its route, its service function and the transaction boundary, which makes this the best index for tour steps 6 and 7.

sections.title: Server module and schema tables
sections.explanation: A table lists each server module, its kind (Routes, Pure, Database, Infrastructure) and its main exports, followed by a table of schema files and when they run. Use it to locate code quickly, for example `http.ts` exports `userOf`, `scopeOf`, `actorOf`, `requireAdmin` and `sendError`. The schema table lists only some of the files that `SCHEMA_FILES` in `server/db.ts` applies, so treat that array as the authoritative list.

sections.title: Client module table
sections.explanation: The React client is mapped file by file: `App.tsx` for session and page address, `routes.ts` for path mapping, `api.ts` for the fetch wrapper and `ApiError`, `workspace.tsx` for shared context, and one file per page under `src/pages/`. The description of `api.ts` as adding a bearer token reflects an older design; tour step 8 notes that the client now sends HttpOnly cookie credentials.

sections.title: Android and desktop architecture
sections.explanation: The Android section summarises scanning, claim evidence capture limits, resumable uploads through the server (never directly to Firebase) and in-app updates. The desktop section explains the one-engine design: `desktop-agent/` owns the claim worker and the much slower follow-up worker, which never overlap because both drive the same supplier profile. It also covers the engine bind policy (loopback means no token, any other bind requires `ENGINE_TOKEN`), `AGENT_DATA_DIR`, low-spec hardware tuning, streamed evidence downloads and the NSIS installer with its scheduled task.

sections.title: Directory structure
sections.explanation: An annotated tree of the repository, from `desktop/` and `desktop-agent/` through `server/` and `src/` to `docs/`. It is useful for orientation, but note one stale entry: it lists `CLAUDE.md` as holding project rules, while AGENTS.md states that file is intentionally absent.

sections.title: Design notes
sections.explanation: A list of deliberate decisions and their consequences: the server binds `0.0.0.0`, CORS uses an allowlist plus CSRF origin/referer checks, sessions are SHA-256-hashed device-token rows, staged uploads live in memory and are lost on restart, lookup data is activated rather than replaced, scans keep their own snapshot, and database TLS verification cannot be turned off. The unused snapshot tables are kept so existing databases lose no rows.

package.json.overview: package.json ties the whole repository together as a single private ESM project (`"type": "module"`) that builds four things: the Vite web client, the esbuild-bundled Express API, the Electron desktop shell with its own Vite renderer, and the headless automation engine. Tour step 2 points here because the scripts reveal the architecture: a concurrent Vite + `tsx watch` dev loop, an esbuild server bundle, a four-project typecheck and an NSIS installer build. The `version` field doubles as the desktop release number that CI requires to be bumped.

sections.title: Package identity
sections.explanation: The package is private, ESM (`"type": "module"`) and versioned `1.3.6`. That version is not cosmetic: AGENTS.md rule 20 requires every desktop change to bump it so the in-app updater sees a new release. `main` points at the bundled Electron entry `desktop/dist/main.cjs`, which is CommonJS even though the rest of the project is ESM.

sections.title: Web and API dev/build scripts
sections.explanation: `dev` uses `concurrently` to run Vite and `tsx watch server/index.ts` side by side, so the client and API reload independently. `build` runs `vite build` for the client and then esbuild bundles `server/index.ts` into `server/dist.js` with `--packages=external`, meaning npm dependencies are not inlined and must be installed at runtime. That is why the production Docker image keeps production dependencies.

sections.title: Desktop and engine scripts
sections.explanation: The desktop pipeline builds the renderer with its own Vite config, bundles `desktop/main.ts` to CommonJS for Node 20 with `electron` and `ws` kept external, then packages with electron-builder (`desktop:dist` makes the NSIS installer). The engine runs directly through `tsx desktop-agent/src/desktop-app-server.ts`, with `--no-window` for headless mode and a Docker Compose variant. `start` runs the bundled API with a 384 MB V8 heap limit.

sections.title: Typecheck and test runner
sections.explanation: `typecheck` runs `tsc --noEmit` against four tsconfig projects (web, server, desktop + engine, desktop renderer), so a change that passes only one project is not fully verified. `test` uses Node's built-in test runner with `--import tsx` to execute TypeScript directly, with `--test-concurrency=1` so database-backed tests do not race. The test files are listed explicitly, so a new test file must be added here to run.

sections.title: Operational CLI scripts
sections.explanation: Each script runs a file in `server/scripts/` through `tsx`: creating users, loading the product master, inspecting spreadsheet layouts, syncing the OMSGuru catalog and daily data, generating return reports, and syncing Shopify, VMS catalog, payment amounts and return reasons. These are the hand-run jobs the README and ARCHITECTURE.md refer to.

sections.title: Runtime and dev dependencies
sections.explanation: Runtime dependencies show the server stack: Express 4, `pg`, `bcryptjs` for password hashes, `multer` for uploads, `ws` for the live socket, `xlsx` for spreadsheets, `@sentry/node` for error reporting, and AI SDK packages. React and `tsx` are runtime dependencies too. Dev dependencies hold the build tools (Vite, Tailwind, TypeScript, Electron, electron-builder) and the test helpers (`@testing-library/react`, `happy-dom`).

sections.title: electron-builder configuration
sections.explanation: The `build` block configures the Windows installer: app ID, output folder, and an explicit `files` allowlist that ships only the bundled main process, the renderer build, the preload script and public assets while excluding `tsx` and esbuild. The NSIS options make a per-machine, non-one-click installer with desktop and Start Menu shortcuts, and `include` pulls in `build/installer.nsh`, which ARCHITECTURE.md says registers the `ReturnAppClaimBot` scheduled task.

server/schema.sql.overview: schema.sql is the first of the ordered, additive schema files that `server/db.ts` applies on every start (tour step 3). It defines the base relational model: marketplaces (the root of per-account scope), users and their account assignments, the legacy sessions table, upload batches, expected returns and their items, receipt scans, claim tickets, sub-issue options and evidence counts. It also keeps a set of snapshot tables that the app no longer reads or writes, purely so existing databases do not lose rows.

sections.title: Header and access rule
sections.explanation: The header comments document the model's key conventions: `users.has_all_marketplaces = true` means no `user_marketplaces` rows, and all dashboard figures are computed from scans rather than seeded. It also lists the snapshot tables that are no longer used. Note that the first lines still describe initDatabase dropping prototype tables; the current `server/db.ts` has no drop path and refuses any schema file containing `DROP TABLE`, so that comment predates the present behaviour.

sections.title: Marketplaces and users
sections.explanation: `marketplaces` is the account table every scoped query ultimately filters on. `users` stores the free-text `role`, the bcrypt `password_hash`, an optional unique `login_alias`, and the `has_all_marketplaces` flag that the access rules read. `user_marketplaces` is a plain join table with a composite primary key, so assigning an account twice is impossible. Every statement uses `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which is what makes the file safe to run on every start.

sections.title: Sessions, couriers and SKUs
sections.explanation: `sessions` is the original token table keyed by the raw token; the newer hashed `user_sessions` table lives in schema-register.sql, and `server/auth.ts` falls back to this legacy table only when a token is not found there. `couriers` and `skus` are early reference tables used by the original expected-return model; `brand_badge` defaults to an empty string so the scan screen can hide an absent badge.

sections.title: Uploads and expected returns
sections.explanation: `upload_batches` records each imported file per marketplace. `expected_returns` is the lookup row a scan matches against, tied to a marketplace and optionally to its batch (`ON DELETE SET NULL`, so removing a batch row would not cascade into lookup data). `tracking_id` is declared `UNIQUE` here, but schema-import.sql later drops that constraint and replaces it with a per-account partial unique index for active rows. `expected_return_items` holds the lines of each return.

sections.title: Scans, tickets and evidence
sections.explanation: `receipt_scans` is the scan event, one per expected return, with CHECK constraints on `outcome` and `status`. `claim_tickets`, `missing_component_options` (the sub-issue list) and `evidence_events` (photo count and video flag) hang off a scan. Later files extend these tables with snapshot columns, scan items, issues and ticket history rather than altering their original definitions.

sections.title: Unused snapshot tables
sections.explanation: Ten tables (daily stats, reason stats, marketplace issue stats, SKU risk, claim stats, headline, report periods, scan shift, UI settings) were pre-computed dashboard snapshots. Each is marked as no longer read or written; figures are now computed from scans on each request. They are kept because the project's additive-schema rule forbids dropping tables, and the header says dropping them needs the user's approval.

sections.title: Migrations marker and indexes
sections.explanation: `schema_migrations` stores the `SCHEMA_VERSION` marker that `applySchema` inserts once. The indexes support the hot paths: sessions by user, scans by time, items in order, and case-insensitive unique email and login alias (the alias index is partial, applying only when an alias is set). `COMMENT ON` statements write the access rule and the snapshot-table status into the database catalog itself, so they are visible to anyone inspecting the schema directly.

server/schema-import.sql.overview: schema-import.sql is the second schema file applied by `server/db.ts` (tour step 3). It turns the base model into the return scan register: lookup activation states (staging, active, superseded), per-account AWB uniqueness, lookup line provenance, multi-ticket scans, configurable issue categories, scan items and issues with snapshot columns, an append-only ticket history and the register audit log. It also defines the product master and OMSGuru tables. Every statement is guarded (`IF NOT EXISTS`, `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, catalog checks), so it is safe to re-run on every start.

sections.title: Header and extra lookup columns
sections.explanation: The header states the file's contract: additive, safe to re-run, never rewrites scan history, and `SCHEMA_VERSION` is intentionally not bumped because a bump once meant dropping every app table. The first statements add an alternate tracking ID, a return reason and channel line identifiers with `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, plus an index on the alternate tracking ID because scans match either AWB.

sections.title: Lookup activation states
sections.explanation: This is the heart of the 'activation, not replacement' rule. `lookup_status` moves a row from `staging` to `active` to `superseded`, and superseded rows are kept because scans refer to them. Since PostgreSQL has no `ADD CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS`, a `DO $$ ... $$` block checks `pg_constraint` first. The global unique constraint on `tracking_id` is dropped and replaced by a partial unique index on `(marketplace_id, tracking_id) WHERE lookup_status = 'active'`, so Myntra VB and Myntra EJ can hold the same AWB and old superseded copies never collide.

sections.title: Lookup line provenance
sections.explanation: Lookup lines can now repeat a product within one return, so the old one-line-per-SKU unique constraint is dropped. `product_sku_source` records whether the product SKU came from the VB EXPORT product master, the OMSGuru master or stayed unresolved, enforced by a guarded CHECK constraint. `marketplace_sku_identifier` stores an FNSKU, ASIN or FSN only when the file carries one.

sections.title: Multi-ticket claim rules
sections.explanation: A scan can now open several tickets (one per issue), so the one-ticket-per-scan unique constraint is removed and replaced by a normal index. New columns track rejection reason, creator and timestamps. The status and rejection-reason CHECK constraints are added `NOT VALID`, a PostgreSQL option that enforces the rule for new and changed rows without rejecting older data already in the table.

sections.title: Issue categories and sub-issues
sections.explanation: `receipt_issue_categories` holds fixed codes (validated by a regex CHECK) with switches an Admin can change. It is seeded with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so Admin edits survive restarts. The `UPDATE` that clears `requires_ticket` for three categories is a deliberate exception: it runs on every start, so re-enabling that switch in Admin lasts only until the next restart, as the comment warns. Sub-issues reuse `missing_component_options` with a new `category_code` foreign key.

sections.title: Scan snapshots, items and issues
sections.explanation: Snapshot columns on `receipt_scans` copy the AWB, order and marketplace at scan time, so a scan stays correct after its lookup row is superseded. `client_scan_key` has a partial unique index, which is how a retried save returns the first result instead of creating a duplicate. `receipt_scan_items` holds exactly one verified row per expected line (`CHECK (verified)` and a quantity range check), and `receipt_scan_issues` records issues per line; both use `ON DELETE RESTRICT` so scan history cannot be cascaded away.

sections.title: Ticket history and audit log
sections.explanation: `claim_ticket_history` is append-only: every status change adds a row, and `ON DELETE RESTRICT` prevents removing a ticket that has history. `register_audit_log` records who did what to which entity, with a `jsonb` details column. The comment that details never hold passwords, tokens or connection strings is a rule the application code must follow when it writes audit rows.

sections.title: Product master and catalog tables
sections.explanation: `product_master` maps a marketplace listing SKU to the VB EXPORT master SKU, with an image URL column added afterwards via `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` so older databases get it too. `cancelled_returns` keeps orders cancelled before dispatch (no AWB, never scanned) for reporting. `sku_catalog` stores OMSGuru listing titles and images keyed by a normalized SKU.

sections.title: OMS snapshots, raw rows, invoices
sections.explanation: `oms_order_snapshots` caches OMSGuru order lookups with buyer fields removed from `raw_json`. `upload_rows` keeps every column of every uploaded row, valid or not, as `jsonb` keyed by normalized header names, so a renamed header in a later file maps to the same key. `oms_invoices` stores dispatched shipments pulled one IST day at a time, keyed by a composite `oms_key`.

sections.title: OMSGuru sync runs, listings, SKUs
sections.explanation: `oms_sync_runs` logs each sync step so a failed or throttled run is visible and can be re-run; `new_rows` was added later with `ALTER TABLE`. `oms_listings` and `oms_skus` hold the OMSGuru channel listings and master SKUs, each keeping the full `payload` so fields the code does not use yet are not lost. Indexes cover the join keys the catalog and master-bridge code use.

server/schema-register.sql.overview: schema-register.sql is the third schema file in `SCHEMA_FILES` (tour step 3). It adds the Phase 1 return register details: upload row classification, seeded logistics partners with courier aliases and verified tracking hosts, tracking and partner evidence on lookup rows, display identifiers on lookup lines, match evidence and snapshots on scans, performance indexes, and the persistent `user_sessions` table that `server/auth.ts` uses. It also seeds system settings for email reports, session timeouts and OMSGuru daily inventory updates. Like the other schema files it is additive and idempotent.

sections.title: Header and upload classification
sections.explanation: The header restates the rules: every statement is `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` or `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and old rows keep their values with new columns taking defaults. The first `ALTER TABLE` statements record the detected file format and the scannable, pending and rejected counts on each batch, plus warnings, duplicate kind, fingerprint and status on each raw row. These are the numbers the upload preview and Admin accounts page display.

sections.title: Logistics partners and seeds
sections.explanation: Three tables model partners, their courier-name aliases (optionally per marketplace) and their tracking hosts, each with an `active` flag so they are switched off instead of deleted. The unique index on `(alias_key, COALESCE(marketplace_id, 0))` treats a NULL marketplace as a real value so a global alias cannot be duplicated. Seeds join a `VALUES` list to partner names and use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. The comment notes an unverified Amazon carrier is deliberately not seeded and that hosts must agree with the link rules in `marketplace-rules.ts`.

sections.title: Lookup row tracking evidence
sections.explanation: The comment block is a data dictionary for new `expected_returns` columns: the resolved AWB versus the AWB exactly as the file wrote it, the carrier link and the AWB read from it, how the AWB was validated, and how the partner was detected and with what confidence. Each enumerated column gets a CHECK constraint added only if missing and marked `NOT VALID`, so older rows are not rejected. Keeping both raw and resolved values makes every lookup decision auditable.

sections.title: Lookup line display identifiers
sections.explanation: `display_order_item_id` separates what the register shows from a real channel order line, because Ajio and Amazon files supply a return order number or shipment ID instead. The header explains the fallback: the register reads `display_order_item_id` first and falls back to `order_line_id` for older rows. `sales_amount` is reserved for a future integration and nothing writes it yet.

sections.title: Scan match evidence
sections.explanation: Scans now record which stored field matched, which leg (return or forward) the AWB belongs to, the AWB as scanned, the source batch, and partner and validation snapshots. One detail breaks the usual pattern: `receipt_scans_matched_field_check` is dropped and re-added on every start (to allow the newer `order_number` value), while the other constraint is only added when missing. Both are `NOT VALID`, so existing rows are not re-checked.

sections.title: Scan items and claim amount
sections.explanation: Scanned items gain the same identifier, raw return type and source-row columns as lookup lines, so each scan item carries its own copy of the values at scan time. `claim_tickets.claim_amount` is added as a reserved column that stays NULL until a claims integration writes it.

sections.title: Performance indexes
sections.explanation: Partial indexes target the lookup hot path: alternate AWB and order number lookups only over `active` rows, and display or shipment ID lookups only where the value is non-empty. Indexing only the rows that are actually queried keeps the indexes small even though superseded history accumulates. Additional indexes speed up per-user scan history and audit log queries.

sections.title: Persistent device sessions
sections.explanation: `user_sessions` stores only `token_hash`, never the raw token, along with device metadata, a remember flag, absolute (`expires_at`) and idle (`idle_expires_at`) expiry, and revocation fields. The lookup index on `token_hash` is partial (`WHERE revoked_at IS NULL`), so validating an active session stays fast. This is the table `createDeviceSession` and `validateSessionToken` in `server/auth.ts` read and write.

sections.title: Report runs and system settings
sections.explanation: `scheduled_report_runs` uses a unique `period_key` so each report period is sent at most once, which makes the 60-second scheduler in `server/index.ts` idempotent. `app_system_settings` is a key/`jsonb` store seeded with `reports_config` and `session_config`; the session defaults (30 days remembered, 7 idle days, 24 hours standard, 4 idle hours) match `DEFAULT_SESSION_CONFIG` in `server/auth.ts`. A `can_receive_reports` flag is added to users.

sections.title: OMSGuru daily inventory updates
sections.explanation: `omsguru_daily_inventory_updates` stores each generated inventory CSV with its storage location and email/WhatsApp delivery status. The WhatsApp columns appear both in the `CREATE TABLE` and as separate `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` statements, so databases created before they existed also get them. An `UPDATE` migrates an old 19:45 schedule to 23:00 only when the old value is still present, and the Iron Send category is seeded again with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for safety.

server/db.ts.overview: server/db.ts is the database foundation and, according to the tour, the most depended-upon module in the graph (step 3). It turns `DATABASE_URL` into a pg connection with TLS certificate verification that cannot be disabled, owns the shared connection pool, and applies the ordered list of additive schema files in one guarded transaction at startup. A safety check refuses to apply any schema file that contains `DROP TABLE`, `TRUNCATE` or `DELETE FROM`, which enforces the project's additive-schema rule in code.

sections.title: Imports and schema version
sections.explanation: The module resolves the project root from `import.meta.url` (the ESM replacement for `__dirname`) so it can read the `.sql` files beside it. `SCHEMA_VERSION` stays at 1; the comment explains that bumping it no longer triggers a destructive rebuild, and AGENTS.md rule 6 forbids bumping it at all.

sections.title: Ordered schema file list
sections.explanation: `SCHEMA_FILES` is the authoritative, ordered list of schema files applied on every start, with a comment per file explaining its purpose. Order matters because later files alter tables created by earlier ones (schema-import.sql alters tables from schema.sql, and so on). `as const` makes the array a readonly tuple of literal strings. A new schema change goes into one of these files or into a new file appended here in the order it must run.

sections.title: History tables and safety guard
sections.explanation: `HISTORY_TABLES` documents the tables whose rows must never be destroyed (scans, items, issues, tickets, uploads, audit log, claims, automation jobs and follow-ups); it is declared for review purposes and not referenced elsewhere in the module. The actual guard, `assertSchemaFilesSafe`, is broader: it rejects any schema file that matches `DROP TABLE`, `TRUNCATE` or `DELETE FROM` anywhere, while `DROP CONSTRAINT` remains allowed for replacing old unique constraints with partial indexes. Because it runs before the apply, a destructive edit fails startup instead of reaching the database.

sections.title: TLS connection settings
sections.explanation: `connectionSettingsFor` parses the URL, strips `sslmode` and `sslrootcert` so pg cannot apply its own interpretation, and returns an explicit `ssl` object. Local hosts default to no TLS, remote hosts default to TLS, every TLS mode uses `rejectUnauthorized: true`, and `sslmode=no-verify` throws. A private CA can come from an environment variable, a CA file path or the URL's `sslrootcert`. Error messages deliberately never include the URL, so credentials cannot leak into logs; the `env` parameter makes the function easy to unit test.

sections.title: Shared and test pools
sections.explanation: `getPool` lazily creates one module-level `Pool` (max 10, min 2 connections, 8-second connect timeout) and reuses it for the life of the process. The `error` listener matters: without it, an idle client dropped by the server would emit an unhandled error and could crash Node. `openPool` creates a separate pool for the same database, which tests use to prove data survives a reconnect.

sections.title: Transactional schema apply
sections.explanation: `applySchema` checks file safety, opens a transaction, sets `lock_timeout = '15s'` so startup fails fast instead of hanging behind a long-held lock, runs each file in order, and records the schema version once. Any error rolls the whole apply back, so a half-applied schema never persists, and `finally` always releases the client. Because every statement in the files is idempotent, this same path works on an empty database and a populated one.

sections.title: Database initialization
sections.explanation: `initDatabase` returns a typed result instead of throwing when `DATABASE_URL` is missing, so the API can still start and answer 503 with a helpful message. Otherwise it checks connectivity with `SELECT 1`, applies the schema and adds the marketplace reference rows via `ensureReferenceData`. The `as const` on `ok` gives callers a discriminated union to branch on.

server/index.ts.overview: server/index.ts is the API's entry point and the root of its dependency tree (tour step 4). It loads configuration, initializes Sentry, builds the Express app with CORS, security headers, JSON parsing and a CSRF origin check, defines `requireUser` (which validates the session and attaches the account scope), handles sign-in and session routes, mounts every feature route module, hosts the Admin pages, serves the built web client, and starts the database, the live WebSocket and the background schedulers. It also handles graceful shutdown.

sections.title: Imports, env and Sentry
sections.explanation: The import list is effectively a table of contents for the server: auth, dashboard, db, http helpers, every `mount*Routes` module, schedulers, the rate limiters and the live socket. `dotenv` loads the project `.env` relative to the resolved root rather than the working directory. Sentry is initialized with an environment, a release name and a lower trace sample rate in production; note that a fallback DSN is hard-coded when `SENTRY_DSN` is unset, so error reports are sent even without configuration.

sections.title: User row and userSelect
sections.explanation: `UserRow` and `SessionRequest` type the signed-in user, and `userSelect` is one reusable SQL column list shared by login, `requireUser`, the WebSocket upgrade and Admin user lists. It computes derived values with correlated subqueries: the user's marketplace IDs as an integer array, the last session time across both session tables, today's scan count in Indian Standard Time, and an 'All marketplaces' or comma-joined assignment label. `password_hash` is selected for sign-in checks, but `publicUser` later picks only safe fields for the browser.

sections.title: Middleware stack and CSRF
sections.explanation: `trust proxy` makes `req.ip` and `req.secure` honour the reverse proxy. CORS uses an allowlist (local dev ports, the production domain, plus `CORS_ORIGIN`) with `credentials: true` so session cookies flow. A small middleware sets security headers, `express.json` caps bodies at 2 MB, and a CSRF guard rejects POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE whose `Origin` (or, failing that, `Referer`) is not on the allowlist. Requests with neither header pass, which keeps non-browser clients such as the Android app working.

sections.title: requireUser and auth helpers
sections.explanation: `scopeOfRow` converts a user row into an `AccountScope` via `scopeFor` from `access.ts`. `requireUser` is the central middleware: it answers 503 until the database is ready, extracts the token from a Bearer header or cookie, validates it, then attaches `req.user` (row plus scope) and session metadata before calling `next()`. Later handlers and the `http.ts` helpers read these values without repeating authentication. `authenticateUpgrade` repeats the same check for the `/api/live` WebSocket handshake, and `auditAdminChange` writes Admin changes to the audit log.

sections.title: Public and health routes
sections.explanation: These routes run without a session: a Brandfetch logo proxy that keeps the client ID on the server and only forwards image responses, the catalog image route (still gated on database readiness), `/api/health` which reports the connected database name or 503, a Sentry test route, and the mobile release manifest and APK download used by the Android in-app updater.

sections.title: Sign-in and session routes
sections.explanation: Login checks the IP limiter and the per-email limiter before touching the database, looks the user up by email or alias, and compares the password with bcrypt. A failure records both limiters and an audit row and returns the same generic 'Incorrect email or password' either way, so the response does not reveal which accounts exist. On success it rejects disabled accounts, resets both limiters, creates a device session, sets the HttpOnly cookie and also returns the token in JSON for clients such as Android. A dev-only route sets a cookie from a query token outside production; `/api/auth/me` and `/api/auth/logout` round out the flow, with logout revoking both the hashed and legacy session.

sections.title: Dashboard and feature modules
sections.explanation: The overview and claims figures are computed with the caller's `scope`, so a user only ever sees counts for their own accounts. Everything else is delegated: each `mount*Routes(app, requireUser)` call registers a feature module (uploads, scanner lists, register, product master, Shopify, OMSGuru, payments, return reasons, Iron Send, claim automation, claims, return tracking). Passing `requireUser` in keeps each module thin while ensuring it uses the same authentication and scope.

sections.title: Admin users and sub-issues
sections.explanation: Every route here chains `requireUser, requireAdmin`. User creation validates name, email and a 10-character minimum password, normalizes the role to a known value, hashes with bcrypt and inserts the user and marketplace assignments in a transaction. Notice that `auditAdminChange` uses the shared pool rather than the transaction client, so its audit insert is not part of that transaction. Disabling a user or resetting a password revokes all their sessions, and an Admin cannot disable their own account. Sub-issue options are never deleted: the DELETE route sets `active = false` so past scans keep their labels.

sections.title: Admin accounts, sessions, system
sections.explanation: The accounts route computes per-marketplace status (active lookup count and the latest batch's status and exception counts) and maps it to a label and tone for the UI. Session routes list active devices (flagging the current one by token hash), revoke a single session or all of a user's sessions, and read or update the timeout config. Report routes manage the email schedule and send tests, and `/api/admin/system` assembles a status summary of the database, product master, sessions, reports, OMSGuru and payment sync. Note that the OMSGuru item calls `getOmsguruConfig` four times instead of reusing one result.

sections.title: Static files, errors, startup
sections.explanation: When the built client exists, hashed `/assets` get a one-year immutable cache, HTML is served with no-cache headers, and a catch-all returns `index.html` for client-side routes while letting `/api` paths fall through. Sentry's Express handler is registered before the final error handler, which maps oversized uploads to 400 and hides internal messages in production. The server starts listening before `initDatabase()` completes, so `/api/health` can report 503 during startup; on success it attaches the live WebSocket and starts the 60-second scheduler and the optional Shopify sync. SIGTERM, SIGINT and uncaught exceptions trigger a graceful shutdown that clears timers, closes the socket server and drains the pools.

server/http.ts.overview: server/http.ts is a small helper module that keeps route handlers thin (tour step 4). It reads the user, account scope and audit actor that `requireUser` attached to the request, provides `requireAdmin` and `requireSupervisorOrAdmin` middleware, and maps a `ServiceError` (or any error object with a numeric status) to an HTTP JSON response. Route modules import these helpers instead of re-implementing authentication or error handling.

sections.title: Contract and imports
sections.explanation: The header comment states the ordering contract: `requireUser` in `server/index.ts` must run before any helper here, because it is what sets `req.user` with the scope from `scopeFor()`. Imports are type-only for Express and pull role checks from `access.ts` and `ServiceError` from `register-service.ts`.

sections.title: Request user accessors
sections.explanation: `SessionUser` describes what `requireUser` attaches, and `AuthedRequest` widens Express's `Request` type with it. `userOf` throws a clear developer error if a route forgot to put `requireUser` first, instead of silently treating the caller as anonymous. `scopeOf` returns the account scope that every service call must receive (project rule 1), and `actorOf` returns the `{ id, name }` shape used for audit records.

sections.title: Role guard middleware
sections.explanation: `requireAdmin` and `requireSupervisorOrAdmin` are standard Express middleware: they either send a 403 JSON error and return, or call `next()`. Role comparison is delegated to `access.ts` so the rule (free-text roles compared case-insensitively) lives in one place. Chaining `requireUser, requireAdmin` on a route is how project rule 2 (Admin routes check the Admin role) is enforced.

sections.title: Error to HTTP mapping
sections.explanation: `sendError` gives route modules one consistent error shape: a `ServiceError` becomes its own status with `error`, `details` and any `extra` fields. A second branch duck-types any object carrying a numeric `status`, clamping it to the 400-599 range and defaulting `details` to an empty array. Anything else is passed to `next(error)`, which reaches the global handler in `server/index.ts` and becomes a 500.

server/rate-limit.ts.overview: server/rate-limit.ts provides an in-memory limiter used to protect sign-in against brute-force attempts (tour step 4). A `RateLimiter` counts failed attempts per key within a time window and locks the key for a fixed period once a threshold is reached. Two shared instances are exported: one keyed by login email and a looser one keyed by client IP, both used by the login route in `server/index.ts`. State lives in process memory, so it resets on restart and is not shared across multiple server instances.

sections.title: Attempt record and options
sections.explanation: Each key maps to an `AttemptRecord` holding the failure count, the time of the first failure in the current window, and a `lockedUntil` timestamp. The constructor takes optional `maxAttempts`, `windowMs` and `lockoutMs`, defaulting to 5 attempts, a 5-minute window and a 5-minute lockout. Storing the state in a private `Map` keeps the class self-contained and easy to test.

sections.title: Checking for a lockout
sections.explanation: `isLocked` reports whether a key is currently locked and how many seconds remain, rounded up with `Math.ceil` so the user never sees zero while still locked. If the window has expired, it deletes the record, which doubles as lazy cleanup of the map. The injectable `now` parameter defaults to `Date.now()` and lets tests control time instead of waiting.

sections.title: Recording failures and resets
sections.explanation: `recordFailure` starts a fresh window when no record exists or the old window has expired; otherwise it increments the count and sets `lockedUntil` once the threshold is reached. The login route calls `reset` after a successful sign-in, so earlier failures do not count against a user who eventually typed the right password. `clear` empties the whole map, which is mainly useful in tests.

sections.title: Shared login and IP limiters
sections.explanation: `loginRateLimiter` allows 5 failures per account in 5 minutes, and `ipRateLimiter` allows 25 per IP, so one office network with several staff is not locked out by a single mistyped password while a single attacker still hits a ceiling. Both lock for 5 minutes. Exporting module-level singletons means every request in the process shares the same counters.

server/auth.ts.overview: server/auth.ts implements persistent device sessions (tour step 5). It generates 32-byte random tokens, stores only their SHA-256 hashes in `user_sessions`, sets an HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie, and accepts the token from either an `Authorization: Bearer` header or the cookie. Validation enforces revocation, disabled accounts, absolute expiry and idle expiry with sliding renewal, and falls back to the legacy `sessions` table so older sessions keep working during upgrades. It also provides Admin-facing session listing, revocation and timeout configuration, all written to the audit log.

sections.title: Design notes and session types
sections.explanation: The header lists the design decisions: high-entropy tokens, hash-only storage, cookie or Bearer transport, configurable absolute and idle timeouts, instant revocation and a legacy fallback. `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`, `SessionConfig` and `DEFAULT_SESSION_CONFIG` (30 days remembered, 7 idle days, 24 hours standard, 4 idle hours) match the `session_config` seed in schema-register.sql. `DeviceSession` is the shape returned to the Admin sessions page. The `scopeFor` import is not used in this file; account scope is computed in `server/index.ts`.

sections.title: Token and cookie helpers
sections.explanation: `generateToken` uses `crypto.randomBytes(32)` for 256 bits of entropy, and `hashToken` produces the SHA-256 hex digest that is the only form stored in the database. Since the token is already high-entropy random data, a fast unsalted hash is enough here, unlike passwords, which use bcrypt. `parseDeviceName` turns a User-Agent into a friendly label such as 'Chrome on Windows PC', and `parseCookies` is a minimal cookie parser that URL-decodes values.

sections.title: Session timeout configuration
sections.explanation: `getSessionConfig` reads `session_config` from `app_system_settings` and clamps each value to a safe range (for example remembered sessions between 1 and 60 days). If the table does not exist yet it returns the defaults instead of failing. `updateSessionConfig` merges a partial update over the current values, clamps again, upserts with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, and writes an audit row naming the Admin who changed it.

sections.title: Creating a device session
sections.explanation: `createDeviceSession` picks the absolute and idle durations based on whether the user chose 'remember this device', computes both expiry timestamps, truncates the User-Agent and IP to bounded lengths, and inserts a `user_sessions` row containing only the token hash. It returns the raw token once so the caller can set the cookie and return it in JSON. `maxAgeSeconds` is derived from the absolute duration so the cookie and the server-side row expire together.

sections.title: Cookies and token extraction
sections.explanation: `setSessionCookie` builds the `Set-Cookie` header by hand with `HttpOnly` (JavaScript cannot read it) and `SameSite=Lax` (sent on top-level navigation but not on most cross-site requests), and adds `Secure` behind HTTPS, behind a proxy that reports HTTPS, or in production. `clearSessionCookie` expires it immediately. `extractSessionToken` checks the Bearer header first, which suits the Android app, then the session cookie, then a legacy `return_token` cookie.

sections.title: Validating a session token
sections.explanation: `validateSessionToken` rejects very short tokens, hashes the token and looks it up in `user_sessions` joined to the user, using the caller-supplied `userSelectQuery` so index.ts controls which user columns come back. It returns null for a revoked session, a disabled user, or an expired absolute or idle deadline. When more than 5 minutes have passed since the last activity, it extends the idle deadline in a fire-and-forget update, which keeps request latency low and limits write traffic. If the token is not found there, it falls back to the legacy `sessions` table, which compares the raw token because those older rows were never hashed.

sections.title: Revoking sessions
sections.explanation: `revokeSessionById` sets `revoked_at` and `revoked_by` only on a still-active row and writes an audit entry only when something actually changed. `revokeAllSessionsForUser` revokes every active session for a user, also deletes their legacy `sessions` rows (ignoring errors if that table is unavailable), and audits the count. Revocation is a soft update on `user_sessions`, so the record of the device and who revoked it is kept.

sections.title: Listing active sessions
sections.explanation: `listActiveSessions` returns up to 100 unrevoked, unexpired sessions, optionally for one user, newest activity first. The user filter is added as a bound parameter rather than string-concatenated, and `isCurrent` is computed by comparing token hashes so the raw token is never needed. Any query error returns an empty list, which keeps the Admin page usable even if the sessions table is missing.

server/access.ts.overview: The pure account-scope module that every data route depends on. It turns a signed-in user's role, `has_all_marketplaces` flag and assigned marketplace ids into an `AccountScope`, and it builds the SQL fragments that bind that scope as a query parameter. Nothing here touches the database, which is why so many modules import it and why it can be tested directly. Tour step 5 presents it as the code behind the project's first rule: account scope on every data route.

sections.title: The account rule, in prose
sections.explanation: The header comment is the specification: an Admin sees everything, any other user sees everything only when `users.has_all_marketplaces` is true, and otherwise only the accounts in `user_marketplaces`. It also fixes the HTTP contract. A named account outside scope is a **403**, while a single return, scan or ticket outside scope is a **404**, so the response never confirms that the record exists. The scope is read once per request in `server/index.ts`, and this file only applies it.

sections.title: Scope type and constants
sections.explanation: `AccountScope` is a discriminated union: `{ all: true }` or `{ all: false; marketplaceIds }`. Callers must check `scope.all` before they can read the id list, so the compiler stops code from treating an unrestricted scope as an empty list. `ALL_ACCOUNTS` is a shared constant, and `NO_ACCESS_MESSAGE` is the one refusal text that the routes and `upload-policy.ts` reuse.

sections.title: Role predicates
sections.explanation: Each role check trims and lower-cases the role string, so `Admin`, `admin ` and `ADMIN` all match. Wrapping the value in `String(role || "")` keeps a null or undefined role from throwing; it just fails the check. The `Inward` role has a comment of its own because it is an operational role for Iron Send, not a scanner role. `isSupervisorOrAdminRole` combines two roles for routes that allow either one.

sections.title: Building and testing a scope
sections.explanation: `scopeFor` returns `ALL_ACCOUNTS` for an Admin or an all-marketplaces user. For anyone else it de-duplicates the assigned ids, drops anything that is not a positive integer and sorts the rest, so the result is the same whatever order the database returned. `allowsAccount` is the in-memory check that routes use before acting on one named account, for example the marketplace selected on an upload.

sections.title: SQL condition builders
sections.explanation: `accountCondition` adds the scope to a query without ever putting ids into the SQL text. It pushes the id array onto the caller's `params` and returns `column = ANY($n::integer[])`, using the new parameter's position. For an unrestricted scope it returns `TRUE`, and for a user with no assignment it returns `FALSE`, so that user gets zero rows instead of an error. `accountListParam` supports the other query style, `($n::integer[] IS NULL OR ...)`, where `null` means every account. `register-service.ts` uses that style in its lookup SQL.

sections.title: Fail-closed fallback scope
sections.explanation: `NO_ACCOUNTS` is the scope to use when a caller has none, such as a script or a test. It is the narrowest possible scope, so a missing scope can only hide data and never widens access. Compare the register service, whose functions default to `ALL_ACCOUNTS` for older tests. `docs/REGISTER.md` lists that default as a known limit.

server/upload-policy.ts.overview: Pure activation policy for an uploaded return file. It counts what a parsed file contains (scannable, pending, rejected, duplicate, cancelled and tracking-related rows), lists the hard blockers that stop activation, and lists the confirmations the user must give before a partial activation. `upload-routes.ts` calls the same functions twice, at preview and again at import, so the server never trusts the preview. This is the "blockers and confirmations" part of tour step 6.

sections.title: Purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The header states the contract. A file activates only when `activationBlockers` returns nothing and the user has accepted everything in `confirmationsNeeded`. Error rows and pending rows stay in upload history without discarding the safe rows in the same file. The module imports `isScannableRow` and `rowStatus` from `sheets.ts`, so row classification is defined in one place only.

sections.title: PreviewCounts shape
sections.explanation: `PreviewCounts` is the full set of figures the upload screen shows. The comments set out the distinctions that matter: `validRows` (structurally readable) differs from `scannableRows` (has a trustworthy AWB and a positive quantity), and `exactDuplicateRows` (identical rows, not counted) differs from `repeatedRows` (same AWB/SKU/line with different details, kept). The tracking fields (`trackingCorrectedRows`, `trackingKeptRows`, `trackingUncheckedRows`) correspond to the `TrackingValidation` outcomes in `marketplace-rules.ts`.

sections.title: Counting a parsed file
sections.explanation: `countPreview` makes one pass over the rows and increments every counter that applies, so one row can count in several categories. Some counts come from structured fields (`row.valid`, `duplicateKind`, `trackingValidation`). Others are found by matching regexes against the human-readable `pendingReasons` and `warnings` strings that `sheets.ts` writes. The regex approach is fragile: if the wording of a message in `sheets.ts` changes, these counts can quietly drift unless the two files are updated together.

sections.title: Hard activation blockers
sections.explanation: Blockers are the reasons no confirmation can override: no access to the account, a fatal parse error, an empty file, or a file with zero scannable rows. Row-level errors are deliberately left off this list, because a mostly-good file should still activate its safe rows. The routes pass `accountAllowed: true` after checking scope themselves, but the parameter keeps this rule testable without HTTP.

sections.title: Required confirmations
sections.explanation: Confirmations are soft gates that need an explicit `confirm: true`. There are three: rows excluded from active lookup (errors, pending, cancelled and duplicates added together), identifiers that Excel stored as numbers, and Meesho rows where the tracking link disagrees with the file's AWB. Each message is written for the person at the screen and says what happens next, for example that the file's AWB is used.

sections.title: Final activation gate
sections.explanation: `canActivate` requires both no blockers and at least one scannable row. The second check repeats part of `activationBlockers` on purpose, as defence in depth, so a caller that builds its own blocker list still cannot activate an empty set.

server/upload-routes.ts.overview: Express routes for the lookup-data upload workflow: upload history, the blank CSV template, `POST /api/uploads/preview` (parse, check and stage in memory) and `POST /api/uploads/import` (re-check and activate). The routes stay thin by delegating parsing to `sheets.ts`, policy to `upload-policy.ts` and the transactional commit to `lookup-import.ts`. They enforce account scope, ownership of a preview, a 15-minute expiry and single use. In tour step 6 this file connects the browser to the import pipeline.

sections.title: Contract and imports
sections.explanation: The header gives the central rule: preview changes no lookup data, and import re-checks everything (owner, age, scope, blockers, confirmations) because "the preview is never trusted on its own". It also says the staged entry is removed before the commit starts, so the same preview can never be activated twice. If that commit then fails, the user has to upload the file again.

sections.title: Limits and exception mapping
sections.explanation: `PREVIEW_TTL_MS` (15 minutes), `SAMPLE_LIMIT` and `WARNING_LIMIT` keep previews short-lived and responses small. `previewException` turns a non-scannable `ParsedRow` into the structure the exception table shows. Its status is checked in a fixed order: duplicate, then cancelled, then pending (valid but not scannable), then rejected. `sourceTrackingId` and `shipmentId` fall back to raw columns (`reverse_leg_tracking_id`, `return_awb_no`, `shipment_id`) so the user sees what the file actually said.

sections.title: In-memory staging and file intake
sections.explanation: A staged upload holds the parsed rows, the counts and the product-SKU and image maps found at preview time, keyed by a random UUID in a module-level `Map`. `forgetExpired` evicts old entries lazily whenever a new preview arrives. Because staging lives in process memory, a server restart (or a second instance) loses every pending preview, which is acceptable here because the user just uploads again. `multer.memoryStorage()` with a 25 MB cap means files never touch disk.

sections.title: Naming accounts without leaking
sections.explanation: `accountIdOf` looks up a marketplace id by name. `describeAccounts` builds the refusal text for a file that contains rows for other accounts, and it names an account only when the user's scope allows it. Any other account is shown only as "another account". This is the 404-style non-disclosure rule from `access.ts`, applied to an error message.

sections.title: Warning and partner summaries
sections.explanation: `warningSamples` lists each distinct warning text only once, up to the limit, and can add one summary line for unmapped listing SKUs. Note that the preview route passes an empty `unmapped` array, so that line is never produced there (unmapped SKUs are reported separately under `productMapping`). `partnerSummary` counts valid rows per detected logistics partner and falls back to `UNKNOWN_PARTNER_LABEL` rather than guessing.

sections.title: History and template routes
sections.explanation: `GET /api/uploads` lists the latest 200 batches for the accounts the user can see, using `accountCondition` over `b.marketplace_id` so the scope is a bound parameter. `GET /api/uploads/template` returns `templateCsv()`, which contains only a header row, so an unchanged template cannot import a made-up return.

sections.title: Preview: parse, check, stage
sections.explanation: Preview checks its inputs in order: a file is present, a marketplace is chosen, that marketplace exists, and the user's scope allows it (403 otherwise). It then parses the grid and inspects the header layout. A file with valid rows for a different account is refused before anything is staged, which enforces one account per file. It computes the counts, product-SKU mapping, blockers and confirmations, and stages the file only when it is not fatal. The response also returns the current active row count, the header diagnostics, sample errors, tracking corrections, partner counts and a message saying that activation replaces the account's lookup data but never the register.

sections.title: Import: re-validate and commit
sections.explanation: Import refuses an unknown or foreign `uploadId`, an expired preview, or an account now out of scope, then re-runs `activationBlockers` (409) and requires `confirm: true` when confirmations exist. It can stream progress as Server-Sent Events, in which case the default pause between batches is 1000 ms (0 otherwise). The staged entry is deleted *before* `commitLookupUpload` runs, which is the single-use guarantee. After a commit it publishes an `upload.activated` live event. The catch block handles errors that happen after streaming headers were already sent by writing an SSE `error` frame instead of calling `next`.

server/sheets.ts.overview: The spreadsheet parser behind every lookup-data upload and the product-master import. It reads CSV (with its own RFC 4180 reader) or the first XLSX sheet, finds the header row by name, and maps each record into a `ParsedRow` using a per-marketplace mapper (Myntra, Flipkart, Meesho, Ajio, Amazon, or generic). Its core rule is that an identifier whose digits might have been lost to Excel is never repaired or guessed. It is left blank, marked pending or rejected. Tour step 6 describes it as the place where strict identifier rules are applied before anything reaches the database.

sections.title: Imports and cancellation constants
sections.explanation: The parser takes header lists from `import-profiles.ts` and the pure normalizers from `marketplace-rules.ts`, so this file only maps data. `CANCELLED_RETURN_TYPE` and `CANCELLED_REASON` encode a project rule: a Myntra row with no tracking number but an order line was cancelled before dispatch, so it is recorded as a Courier Return that can never be scanned. The misspelling "Dispached" is the stored value and should not be corrected casually.

sections.title: ParsedRow and identifier kinds
sections.explanation: `ParsedRow` is the central record type of the import pipeline. The comments explain the meaning of each field: `trackingId` is the lookup key (blank when untrusted), `orderLineId` holds only *real* order lines, and `displayOrderItemId` with `displayIdentifierKind` keeps the Ajio return order number and the Amazon shipment id apart from real order lines. The marketplace SKU identifier kinds (FSN, ASIN, JioCode, Myntra SKU code) are also never mixed. The optional fields added with the marketplace layouts (fingerprint, CSV vs. link AWB, validation outcome) record how each value was decided, so it can be audited later.

sections.title: Result types and grid model
sections.explanation: `ParseResult.fatal` rejects the whole file before any row is saved. The product-master types (`MasterRow`, `MasterParseResult`, `MasterPreview`) report conflicts and invalid images instead of fixing them silently. The `Grid` type stores, beside each row's text cells, a `suspect` set: the column indexes whose XLSX cell was a number too long or too fractional to trust as an identifier. CSV cells are always text, so CSV suspect sets are always empty.

sections.title: Reading CSV and XLSX safely
sections.explanation: `GENERIC` lists the header aliases used for marketplaces that have no profile. `isUntrustedNumber` flags non-integers and values of 1e15 or more, because Excel keeps only 15 significant digits. `cellText` writes whole numbers through `BigInt` so they never appear in scientific notation, and `cleanId` strips the `="..."` and apostrophe wrappers that exports use to keep leading zeros. The hand-written `parseCsv` keeps every field as text and handles quoted commas and newlines. `readGrid` reads XLSX with `raw: true` so it sees stored values rather than display text, and records suspect columns before converting cells to strings.

sections.title: Locating headers and building fields
sections.explanation: `locateHeader` scores the first 40 non-blank rows by how many required headers each contains (headers are compared after `normalizeHeader`, never by column letter). It returns the best row together with the names still missing. `readPreamble` collects key/value lines above the header, such as Meesho's Supplier ID. `toFields` builds one `Map` per record in two passes: exact headers first, then aliases only where the canonical field is empty. It attaches suspect columns through a `WeakMap`, so that metadata goes away with the record and adds no fields to it. `pick`, `firstHeader` and `pickFirst` are small lookup helpers built on that map.

sections.title: Identifier, quantity and status rules
sections.explanation: `readId` applies the no-guessing rule. A lookup key in scientific notation, or stored as an untrusted number, becomes a pending reason when the caller passes a pending list (and an error for older layouts). A non-key identifier is blanked with a warning. `parseQuantity` accepts only whole numbers of 1 or more, and it can treat zero as pending, which Ajio uses. `rowStatus` defines the five states (rejected, cancelled, duplicate, scannable, pending), and `isScannableRow` is the single test that both `upload-policy.ts` and `lookup-import.ts` rely on. The remaining helpers cover money parsing, row fingerprinting (SHA-256 over sorted keys), and dropping rows that have no identifying data at all.

sections.title: Row scaffold and generic mapper
sections.explanation: `baseRow` gives every field a neutral value so each mapper sets only what its layout provides. `finish` derives `valid`/`error` from the error list, keeps `csvTrackingId`, and de-duplicates pending reasons. `genericRow` handles marketplaces with no profile through the `GENERIC` aliases. A blank tracking id makes the row pending rather than rejected, while a missing SKU or a bad quantity is a hard error. Descriptive fields stay empty when the file does not supply them; the app never invents text.

sections.title: Myntra, Flipkart and Meesho mappers
sections.explanation: `myntraRow` uses the return AWB, or the forward AWB only when the return AWB is blank, and keeps the other as `altTrackingId`. A row with both AWBs blank and an order line present becomes the cancelled-before-dispatch case. `flipkartRow` joins the reason and sub-reason, made readable by `humanize`, and records the FSN as the marketplace SKU identifier. `meeshoRow` is the strictest. It decides the AWB with `resolveTrackingId` against the tracking link, treats a blank or scientific AWB as a hard *error* (not pending), and rejects a number-stored AWB unless a verified link confirms its digits. It joins SKU and variation with `skuWithVariation`.

sections.title: Ajio and Amazon mappers, dispatch
sections.explanation: `ajioRow` uses Return AWB No as the key, stores RETURN ORDER NUMBER as a display identifier of its own kind with an empty `orderLineId`, and treats a zero quantity as pending. `amazonRow` uses only the Reverse Leg Tracking ID. When it is blank the row is pending, and the forward leg is never used in its place; the forward AWB and RMA id are kept for audit, and the Shipment ID becomes the display Order Item ID. Both read the return type from a list of candidate headers via `pickFirst`. `mapRow` dispatches on the profile id and falls back to `genericRow`.

sections.title: Repeats, seller guard and entry points
sections.explanation: `flagRepeats` classifies repeats within a file but never merges or sums them. A row with an identical fingerprint is marked `exact_import_row` and not counted again. The same AWB/SKU/line with different details, or a second return event id, is kept and flagged. `sellerProblem` compares the seller id in a column or the preamble with the expected id for the chosen account, and rejects the whole file on a mismatch before any row is saved. `parseSpreadsheet` is the main entry point (grid, profile, header, seller guard, map, flag). `inspectLayout` locates the header the same way for diagnostics and stores nothing.

server/marketplace-rules.ts.overview: Pure marketplace rules with no database access: header normalization, product-master scope ranking, return-type mapping, SKU and variation joining, placeholder master SKUs, verified carrier tracking links, the Meesho AWB decision, and logistics-partner detection from carrier aliases. `sheets.ts`, `lookup-import.ts` and the register service all call these functions, and they are tested without a database. In tour step 6 this is the home of return-type mapping, AWB repair and carrier detection.

sections.title: Normalization and scope ranking
sections.explanation: `own` reads only a table's own properties, so a header such as `constructor` can never match an inherited key. `normalizeHeader` strips a BOM and folds spaces and hyphens into underscores, so `Return AWB No` and `return-awb-no` compare equal. `aliasKey` keeps only letters and digits for comparing carrier names. `marketplaceRank` scores how well a product-master scope fits an account: 3 for an exact match, 2 when one name contains the other as whole words, 1 for `all`/blank, and 0 for a different account. Rank 0 is what stops one account from using another account's mapping.

sections.title: Return-type mapping
sections.explanation: Each marketplace has its own code table (for example Ajio `rvp`/`rto`/`repl`, Amazon `customer_return`/`undelivered`), and the comments note which sample file confirmed each one. Unknown marketplaces fall back to a generic table. `normalizeReturnType` never maps an unknown code silently. It returns the text as written with `known: false`, and `returnTypeWarning` turns that into a row warning, so a new code from a marketplace is noticed instead of being mislabelled.

sections.title: SKU variation and listing keys
sections.explanation: `skuWithVariation` appends a size with `_` unless the SKU already ends with that size as a separate token. A regex built from the escaped size and anchored after a separator prevents false matches such as treating the `M` at the end of `XM` as a size. `parentListingSku` drops a short trailing article suffix (for example `_A`) but never a real size token from `SIZE_TOKENS`. `listingSkuCandidates` returns the exact, space-less and parent forms, in priority order, for the master lookup in `lookup-import.ts`.

sections.title: Placeholder masters and scope labels
sections.explanation: Placeholder or parking codes such as `B16`, `KD2`, `D6`, `D12`, `INACTIVE*` and `N/A` must never overwrite or shadow a real product SKU. The same rule exists twice, as a JS set plus regex (`isPlaceholderMasterSku`) and as a PostgreSQL POSIX regex string for SQL-side filtering, so the two definitions have to be kept in sync by hand. `normalizeMasterMarketplace` folds channel labels into the lowercase scopes stored in `product_master`, treating blank and `global` as `all`.

sections.title: Verified tracking-link parsing
sections.explanation: `LINK_RULES` is an allowlist. Each rule names one host, its carrier, whether rounding correction is allowed, and how to read the AWB from the path or query. Only Delhivery numeric AWBs are eligible for rounding correction; the alphanumeric carriers (Shadowfax, Valmo, PocketShip, Xpress Bees) are only compared. `parseTrackingLink` accepts only `https:` links on an allowlisted host, and returns `none`, `invalid`, `unverified` or `ok`. A link on any other host is never used to change an AWB.

sections.title: Excel digit-loss arithmetic
sections.explanation: These helpers model how Excel damages long numbers. `roundToFifteenDigits` uses `BigInt` to round a 16-digit value at its last digit, and `truncateToFifteenDigits` zero-fills everything past the 15th digit. `matchesScientificAwb` checks whether a scientific-notation string could be a given full AWB, by digit count and prefix or a relative-error tolerance. `resolveTrackingId` does not call it, and in this codebase it appears only in this file.

sections.title: The Meesho AWB decision
sections.explanation: `resolveTrackingId` returns a `TrackingDecision` that always keeps the CSV value as written. A blank AWB is never filled from a link, and a scientific-notation AWB is `damaged_awb` straight away. A missing, unreadable or unverified link leaves the CSV value in place, with a warning. An exact match is `match`. Only when a rounding-eligible link's numeric AWB truncates or rounds to the 16+ digit CSV value is the link AWB used (`mismatch_resolved`). Any other difference is `mismatch_kept` and needs a person to check. The doc comment mentions scientific-notation matching, but the code returns `damaged_awb` for scientific values before it reads the link.

sections.title: Logistics partner detection
sections.explanation: `PartnerIndex` holds database aliases keyed `"<marketplace or *>|<aliasKey>"`. `aliasHit` tries an exact marketplace-scoped alias, then an exact global one, then the longest stored alias stem (at least 6 characters) that the carrier text starts with. Scoped matches win ties, so `delhiveryexpress` resolves to Delhivery. `detectPartner` returns a verified match or the `Unknown / Pending Verification` fallback, with a warning telling an admin to add the alias. The `_trackingUrl` parameter is unused, which matches the comment that a tracking link does not name the partner.

server/lookup-import.ts.overview: The database side of lookup-data import. It resolves each listing SKU to a product SKU (the VB EXPORT product master first, then a single unambiguous OMSGuru master code), attaches catalog titles and images, and commits one validated upload in a single transaction. The commit stages new rows, supersedes the account's previously active rows (kept because scans refer to them) and activates the new ones. Rows are never merged by AWB. In tour step 6 this is the final step of the upload workflow, called from `upload-routes.ts`.

sections.title: Contract and mapping types
