sections.explanation: The header sets three rules: a failed upload rolls back completely, superseded rows are kept, and each non-duplicate row becomes its own expected line with its own quantity. `ProductMapping` carries everything the preview computes (counts, unmapped SKUs, an image per listing, the source per listing, and a partner decision per row) so the import can reuse it unchanged. `identifierFor` reads the marketplace SKU identifier set by the row mapper and never looks up a header by name.

sections.title: Ranked product-master lookup
sections.explanation: `masterSkusForListings` collects every candidate key (exact, space-less, parent) in compact form and fetches all matching `product_master` rows in one `ANY($1)` query. For each requested pair it scores every row as candidate position x 10 plus `marketplaceRank`, minus 1000 for a placeholder master. That makes exact beat space-less, space-less beat parent, account-specific beat `all`, and any real SKU beat a placeholder. When the best row is still a placeholder, it looks for a real "donor" row with deterministic tie-breaks. Placeholder results are never returned.

sections.title: Resolving product SKUs for a file
sections.explanation: `resolveProductSkus` first runs `applyPartners` so the preview can show partner warnings, then resolves each distinct listing. A product-master hit is used first. An OMSGuru code is used only when exactly one code matches; several codes leave the listing `unresolved` rather than picking one. Rows are changed in place: `row.sku` becomes the master SKU, and `productName` takes the `sku_catalog` title. The product master's own image link overrides the catalog image for the same listing.

sections.title: OMSGuru master codes
sections.explanation: The SQL narrows candidates by upper-cased, trimmed channel SKU. The final comparison in JS uses `normalizeSkuKey`, the same key every other join uses, so the database filter and the matching rule stay consistent. Each listing maps to the set of distinct non-empty `sku_code` values, and the caller decides what to do when there is more than one.

sections.title: Commit types and chunk sizes
sections.explanation: `ImportProgressEvent` defines the SSE progress payload (phase, batch index, percent, message) that `upload-routes.ts` streams. `LookupCommitInput` takes *every* parsed row, valid or not, because all of them are written to `upload_rows`. `ImportItem` is one expected line with its full provenance (source line number, fingerprint, return event, shipment id). `ROW_CHUNK` and `CANCEL_CHUNK` limit the size of the multi-row INSERT statements.

sections.title: Grouping scannable rows by AWB
sections.explanation: `groupReturns` creates one group per tracking id, and the group's first row supplies the expected-return header fields. Every scannable row becomes a separate item. Quantities are never summed, so two lines of the same SKU stay two lines with their own order line, return event and source line. Non-scannable rows are skipped here; they exist only in `upload_rows`.

sections.title: Raw row history insert
sections.explanation: `insertUploadRows` writes every row in chunks of 400 as one parameterized multi-row INSERT. `$1` and `$2` (batch and marketplace) are shared, and each row's 12 values are numbered from a running offset. It stores the row status, the error, the warnings, the duplicate kind, the fingerprint and the redacted raw columns as JSON, so the full report can be checked later.

sections.title: Staging lookup rows
sections.explanation: `stageGroups` upserts the courier, inserts one `expected_returns` row per AWB with `lookup_status = 'staging'` and all the tracking and partner evidence, then upserts each SKU and inserts its `expected_return_items` line. The SKU upsert keeps the existing `image_url` when the new value is empty. Batching is cosmetic and for pacing only: at each batch boundary it can emit progress and sleep `pauseMs`, but everything stays inside one transaction, so batches do not commit separately. It inserts row by row, which is simple but makes several round trips per item on large files.

sections.title: Replacing cancelled rows
sections.explanation: Cancelled-before-dispatch rows are not scans, so the account's `cancelled_returns` set is deleted and re-inserted in full, inside the same transaction. `ON CONFLICT (marketplace_id, order_line_id) DO NOTHING` absorbs duplicate order lines within the file. This is the one place in the import that deletes rows. Lookup rows, by contrast, are superseded, not deleted.

sections.title: The single-transaction commit
sections.explanation: `commitLookupUpload` refuses a file with no scannable rows, opens a transaction, and sets a `lock_timeout` that grows with the row count and pause length. It takes a per-account `pg_advisory_xact_lock` so two uploads for one account cannot interleave. It then writes the batch, raw rows, staged groups and cancelled rows, and records unmapped listings. The switch-over is two UPDATEs: previously `active` rows become `superseded`, and this batch's `staging` rows become `active`. Older batches are labelled `Replaced` and a `lookup.activate` audit row is written. Any error triggers `ROLLBACK`, so the previous active data is never left missing.

server/register-rules.ts.overview: Pure rules for the return scan register, with no database access: tracking and ticket normalization, the Meesho flyer rules, matched-field and leg detection, the four-way lookup decision, full scan-submission validation, ticket status changes, register row mapping and the CSV/XLSX column sets. `register-service.ts` loads reference rows and applies these rules inside transactions, and the client mirrors several of them. Tour step 7 describes it as the rules layer of the register.

sections.title: Constants and tracking normalization
sections.explanation: `TICKET_STATUSES` is a `const` tuple, so the `TicketStatus` type comes from the same list that validation uses. `isValidClientKey` limits the browser-made idempotency key to 8-100 safe characters. `normalizeTracking` upper-cases and trims, refuses scientific notation, and strips barcode prefixes (`#`, `ORDER:`, `ORD#`). It also rewrites an Amazon order id, with or without hyphens, into the canonical `408-1234567-1234567` form, so a scanned order barcode can match.

sections.title: Meesho flyer evidence rules
sections.explanation: A flyer id is claim evidence captured only for Meesho returns that have a real issue. `normalizeFlyer` applies the tracking-style rules plus length bounds. `flyerErrorFor` sets the policy. Outside Meesho issue returns (including Iron Send-only and clear scans), any flyer data is refused. On a Meesho issue return the user must explicitly choose `scanned` (with a valid id that differs from the return AWB) or `unavailable` (with no id). An empty decision is refused, so a missing flyer is recorded as unavailable and never left blank by default.

sections.title: SKU display and matched leg
sections.explanation: `productSkuFor` hides an unresolved product SKU so the scanner sees a gap instead of a guess, and `productSkuSourceFor` labels lines saved before sources were recorded as `unrecorded`. `matchedFieldFor` records which stored identifier the scanned value matched: the primary AWB (with its leg from `trackingSource`), the alternate AWB (forward leg), or an order or item id. Order-id matching ignores hyphens and spaces, but only when the cleaned value has at least 8 characters, so short inputs cannot match loosely. The label maps translate these codes for exports.

sections.title: Lookup decision
sections.explanation: `decideLookup` returns one of four outcomes. No entries gives `none`, more than one gives `choose`, and a single entry is `duplicate` when it was already received or has no active shipment, otherwise `single`. Several matches are never resolved automatically, because the same AWB can exist in two accounts. An entry with `shipmentId: null` represents an earlier scan in an account whose lookup row has since been superseded, so it can never be received twice.

sections.title: Submission and category types
sections.explanation: `CategoryRule` holds the flags that shape validation: clear, missing, ticket required, sub-issue allowed or required, active, and the optional `isOperational`. `countsAsReturnIssue` treats an unknown category as an issue, so a misconfigured category is never hidden from issue figures, while operational categories such as Iron Send are excluded. `ScanSubmission` is the typed body that `register-routes.ts` builds, including the scanned AWB and the flyer fields.

sections.title: Validating a scan submission
sections.explanation: `validateScanSubmission` collects *all* errors instead of stopping at the first, so the screen can list every problem. Every expected item must be listed exactly once, belong to the return and be physically verified, with a received quantity from 0 to the expected quantity. Each issue must use an active, non-clear category with a valid quantity, respect the sub-issue and ticket requirements, and use a ticket code that is unique within the submission. Two balance checks finish the job: missing-item issue units must equal the units not received, and other issues cannot exceed the units received. An issue with a duplicate ticket is kept out of that coverage math on purpose.

sections.title: Status, labels and ticket changes
sections.explanation: `scanStatusFor` derives the stored scan status: Clear with no issue, Raised when a ticket exists, otherwise Draft. `describeIssues` builds the short `issue_label` text, such as `Missing product (Belt) x2`. `ticketStatusError` allows any move between valid statuses (there is no transition map, as `docs/REGISTER.md` notes) but refuses a no-op change, an over-long reason, or a rejection without a reason.

sections.title: Register row mapping
sections.explanation: `RawRegisterRow` matches the columns of the register UNION query. Fields after `line_no` are optional so rows from older queries still map. `mapRegisterRow` drops `no_issue` entries, moves operational (Iron Send) entries out of the issue list into `ironSendQty`, and builds a ticket object only when a ticket id exists. `amount` and `claimAmount` are reserved and stay null until a verified source exists (sales amount is passed through when present). Fallbacks such as `UNKNOWN_PARTNER_LABEL` and `not_applicable` keep every field filled.

sections.title: Export column sets
sections.explanation: There are three nested column sets: the 19 approved columns (the default export, in mapping order), the extended set (adds received quantity, scanner, source and matched tracking), and the operational set (adds traceability: file, link and scanned AWBs, source file and batch, raw return type, Iron Send quantity, flyer). Each set extends the previous one by spreading it, so the shared columns always come first in the same order. `headersFor` chooses the set by mode.

sections.title: Records and CSV injection guard
sections.explanation: `registerRecords` builds cell arrays in exactly the order `headersFor` returns, and both the CSV and the XLSX export use it, so the two formats cannot disagree. Multi-issue cells are de-duplicated and joined with `; `. `csvCell` guards against spreadsheet formula injection by prefixing an apostrophe to any value that starts with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab or CR, then quotes and escapes it. `register-routes.ts` applies the same guard to XLSX cells.

server/register-service.ts.overview: The transactional service layer of the return scan register. It applies the pure rules from `register-rules.ts` to PostgreSQL. It handles account-scoped AWB lookup against active lookup rows, idempotent scan recording (client scan key, a per-AWB advisory lock and unique indexes as the backstop), issue correction from the scan bench, ticket status changes with history, issue-category administration, and the paginated register and its export. Every function takes the pool and the caller's `AccountScope`. Tour step 7 describes it as the place where the rules become transactions.

sections.title: Imports, errors and helpers
sections.explanation: The header summarizes the guarantees: one transaction per write, an injectable pool for tests, a client key that makes saves idempotent, AWB advisory locks with unique indexes as the final guard, and scope applied to every read and write. `ServiceError` carries an HTTP status plus optional `details` (the validation list) and `extra` (for example the time and scanner of an earlier scan), which `sendError` in the routes turns into a response. `withClient` makes sure the pooled client is released, and `writeAudit` writes JSON details to `register_audit_log`.

sections.title: Accounts and shift figures
sections.explanation: `accessibleAccounts` lists the accounts allowed by the scope, in display order. `shiftCounts` counts today's scans in IST (`Asia/Kolkata`) as total, clear and issue, and sums the open Iron Send units, all under the account condition. Iron Send returns therefore count as correct, not as issues. `presentShift` formats the figures and reports accuracy as the clear rate. `workspaceUi` returns the header date and the claims badge, which counts tickets not yet Approved or Rejected within the scope.

sections.title: Issue-category reference and admin
sections.explanation: `loadCategoryRules` and `loadSubIssueRules` read the reference tables that validation needs. `scanSession` sends the scan screen the shift, the accounts, and only the *active* categories and sub-issues. `updateCategory` can change only `active` and `requiresTicket` (via `COALESCE`, so an omitted field stays unchanged). The rule flags that shape validation are fixed in code. `createCategory` derives a lowercase underscore code from the label when none is given, refuses duplicates with 409, adds the category at the end of the sort order, and audits it.

sections.title: Lookup types and match SQL
sections.explanation: `LookupResponse` matches the four lookup outcomes. `ACTIVE_MATCH_SQL` searches only `active` lookup rows by primary or alternate AWB, order number (hyphen- and space-insensitive when at least 8 characters), forward AWB, return event, or item-level order line, display id or shipment id. It filters by optional account name, optional shipment id and `$4`, the account list, where null means all. `SCAN_MATCH_SQL` uses the same matching against existing scans so duplicates are found even after the lookup row was superseded. `ITEMS_SQL` and `SHIPMENT_HEADER_SQL` load the details, and `displayItemOf` falls back to the order line for older rows.

sections.title: Shipment detail and lookup
sections.explanation: `loadShipmentDetail` builds the scan-bench view. Items with a blank or placeholder product SKU, or one ending in certain suffixes, are looked up again in `product_master` on the fly, and missing images are filled from it. It also computes which stored identifier matched. `lookupShipment` normalizes the input and refuses a named account outside scope with 403. It then merges active matches with prior scans and adds a `shipmentId: null` entry for each account that already received the AWB but no longer holds it as active, before calling `decideLookup`. Unmatched lookups and duplicate attempts are audited when an actor is given.

sections.title: Receipts, replay and issue labels
sections.explanation: `ScanReceipt` is what a save returns: the scan's own snapshot fields, counts, flyer, refreshed shift and claims badge, plus `replayed`. `findScanByKey` and `marketplaceOfScan` support idempotent replay, including refusing a replayed key whose scan lies outside the caller's scope. `loadReceipt` reads the *snapshot* columns (with fallbacks to the lookup row) and excludes operational categories from the issue count. `issueLabelParts` names only real issues when there are any, so an Iron Send on the same parcel does not change the issue label.

sections.title: Recording a scan
sections.explanation: `recordScan` first replays a known client key. Inside the transaction it checks scope (404) and active status, takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock` on `awb:<account>:<tracking>`, then checks the key again, because a concurrent save may have just won. It locks the lookup row `FOR UPDATE`, refuses an AWB already received in that account (409, with time and scanner), validates the submission, checks that ticket codes are new and applies the flyer rule. It then inserts the scan with every snapshot field, the items, the issues and their `Raised` tickets with first history rows, the Iron Send records, the evidence counts and an audit row. The catch block turns unique-violation races on the client-key index into a replay. One thing to notice: the return-tracking sync is wrapped in a JS try/catch but runs on the same transaction without a savepoint, so a SQL error there would still abort the PostgreSQL transaction.

sections.title: Correcting a scan's issues
sections.explanation: `correctScanIssue` lets the employee who saved a scan change its issues from the bench; any other user gets a 404. It audits the previous issues and tickets as `scan.issues_replaced` first, then deletes the previous ticket history, tickets and issue rows and writes the new ones. The comment above the function says issues are "only added", but the body replaces them, and the audit snapshot is what keeps the old state on record. With no issues submitted, the scan reverts to Clear with full quantities and no flyer. Otherwise the submission is re-validated, the flyer rule is applied and the scan's outcome, label and status are recalculated. Iron Send records are re-synced in both branches.

sections.title: Ticket status and history
sections.explanation: `ticketAccount` resolves a ticket's account through its scan, so both ticket functions can report an out-of-scope ticket as 404. `updateTicketStatus` locks the ticket row, applies `ticketStatusError`, stores the rejection reason only when the new status is Rejected, adds a `claim_ticket_history` row (which keeps the reason for every change) and audits the change. `ticketHistory` returns the history in chronological order with the name of whoever made each change.

sections.title: Register query, list and export
sections.explanation: `REGISTER_UNION_SQL` returns one row per verified scan item from snapshot columns, plus a `legacy` branch for older scans without item rows that reads the lookup row instead. Both branches have the same column order, as `UNION ALL` requires, and they compute `issue_codes` so that Iron Send-only lines also match `no_issue`. `buildRegisterWhere` always adds the scope first, so filters can only narrow results, and binds every filter value. `sortClauseFor` places only allowlisted column expressions in the SQL text. `listRegister` limits page size to 200, `exportRegisterRows` refuses rather than truncates beyond 50,000 rows, and both overlay real master SKUs onto placeholder product SKUs. `registerOptions` builds scoped filter lists.

server/register-routes.ts.overview: The HTTP layer of the return scan register: account list, scan lookup/complete/correct, scan session, the register list and CSV/XLSX export, ticket status and history, and Admin-only configuration of issue categories and logistics partners (with their aliases and tracking hosts). Every route parses and checks input, passes the signed-in user's scope to `register-service.ts`, and maps a `ServiceError` to its status through `sendError`. In tour step 7 this is where the register is exposed over HTTP, bound to the scope from step 5.

sections.title: Purpose and imports
sections.explanation: The header states the layering. Routes pass the scope down so the restriction is applied in SQL, configuration needs `requireAdmin`, and a `ServiceError` becomes its HTTP status with message and details. The imports show that partner, alias and host writes come from `admin-config.ts`, while register logic comes from the service and rules modules. `COLUMN_MODES` lists the accepted export column sets.

sections.title: Input parsers and validators
sections.explanation: `filtersFrom` checks every query value before it can reach SQL. Ids must be positive integers, dates must be `YYYY-MM-DD`, the ticket status must be in `TICKET_STATUSES`, and free-text filters are length-limited. `submissionFrom` turns an untrusted JSON body into a `ScanSubmission`. Missing values become values the rules will reject (for example `NaN` ids), so validation stays in one place. It also upper-cases and limits the flyer id. `columnModeFrom` refuses unknown modes, and `safeCell` applies the same formula-injection guard to XLSX that `registerCsv` applies to CSV.

sections.title: Switching a tracking host
sections.explanation: `setDomainActive` is the one partner operation written in this file rather than in `admin-config.ts`. It runs a small transaction that flips `logistics_partner_domains.active`, returns 404 for an unknown id, and writes a `partner.host` audit row. It follows the project rule that a host is switched off, never deleted, and every change is audited.

sections.title: Accounts and scanning routes
sections.explanation: `GET /api/accounts` fills the account selectors on the scan and upload screens. `POST /api/scan/lookup` validates an optional `shipmentId` (sent back after a `choose` result) and passes the actor, so unmatched and duplicate lookups are audited. `POST /api/scan/complete` sends the receipt first and then publishes a `scan.saved` live event only when the save was not a replay, so retries do not trigger duplicate notifications. `POST /api/scan/correct` publishes `scan.corrected`, and `GET /api/scan/session` loads the bench's reference data.

sections.title: Register list and export
sections.explanation: `GET /api/register` passes page, page size, filters, sort and scope to `listRegister`, and the service limits and allowlists those values. `GET /api/register/export` accepts `format=csv|xlsx` and `columns=approved|extended|operational`, and builds both formats from `headersFor` and `registerRecords`, so they match the screen column for column. The XLSX branch builds a workbook in memory with SheetJS and sends it as a buffer. `GET /api/register/options` returns the scoped filter lists.

sections.title: Ticket routes
sections.explanation: Both ticket routes validate the numeric id before calling the service, which applies scope and returns 404 for tickets outside it. A successful status change publishes a `ticket.updated` live event with a null marketplace id, so the event itself does not reveal which account the ticket belongs to.

sections.title: Issue-category administration
sections.explanation: Every category route is gated by `requireUser` and `requireAdmin`. The PATCH copies only boolean `active` and `requiresTicket` fields from the body and refuses an empty change, which matches the service rule that the validation-shaping flags are fixed. The POST creates a category (the code is optional and derived from the label) and returns 201.

sections.title: Logistics partner administration
sections.explanation: Partners, their courier-name aliases (optionally limited to one marketplace) and their tracking hosts can be listed, added, and switched on or off, but never deleted. Each mutating route validates the id, requires a boolean `active` for toggles, and passes the actor so the change is audited. These aliases are what `detectPartner` in `marketplace-rules.ts` matches carrier text against at upload time.

docs/REGISTER.md.overview: The specification of the return scan register: the 19 approved columns and the two larger export sets, the data model and its additive schema changes, the per-marketplace layouts and values, return-type and Meesho tracking-link rules, repeat classification, partner detection, lookup activation, lookup ambiguity, scan recording, account access, issue and ticket rules, concurrency, verification and known limits. Tour step 7 points to it as the document that defines the register's columns and its rules for activation, concurrency and idempotency. In a few places it has fallen behind the code.

sections.title: Purpose and status
sections.explanation: The opening paragraph sets the main split of the project: marketplace files are *lookup data* (what is expected) and scans are the *permanent record* (what arrived). It notes that the register reuses existing tables with additive schema files. The status line cites test counts and refers to the agent handoff note for live verification.

sections.title: Register columns and export sets
sections.explanation: The table gives each of the 19 approved columns and its source. Notable points: Order Item ID can be a real order line or a display identifier with its own kind, and Amount and Claim Amount are reserved and left empty. The extended (23) and operational (37) sets correspond to `REGISTER_CSV_HEADERS` and `REGISTER_OPERATIONAL_HEADERS` in `register-rules.ts`. The section admits that the approved mapping CSV was never found, so the column list comes from the specification and still needs checking.

sections.title: Data model
sections.explanation: This table lists each table's role and what changed: `lookup_status` with the staging, active and superseded states, the tracking evidence columns on `expected_returns`, the snapshot columns on `receipt_scans`, and the reference tables for partners, categories and sub-issues. The closing paragraph restates the schema invariant: only `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, NOT VALID constraints, new tables or indexes and idempotent inserts, and `SCHEMA_VERSION` is never bumped because a bump drops the app tables.

sections.title: Layouts, return types, Meesho links
sections.explanation: This section explains which column each marketplace layout supplies for every register value, the return-type mapping table that `normalizeReturnType` implements, and the Meesho AWB decision (blank and damaged AWBs are refused, and only an exact 15-digit rounding against a Delhivery link resolves to the link value). It lists three verified link forms. The code's `LINK_RULES` now also allows `tracker.shadowfax.in`, the Shipsy (Valmo), Valmo (PocketShip) and Xpress Bees hosts, so the list here is incomplete.

sections.title: Repeated rows and partners
sections.explanation: The repeat rules match `flagRepeats` in `sheets.ts`: exact duplicates are kept but not counted, while same-line differences and second return events are kept and flagged, and nothing is summed. The partner section describes a three-step order that includes matching the tracking-link host. The current `detectPartner` implementation matches carrier aliases only and ignores its tracking URL parameter, so step 2 does not apply in code.

sections.title: Lookup data and activation
sections.explanation: This is the specification for `upload-routes.ts` and `commitLookupUpload`. Preview stages and changes nothing, and activation re-checks every blocker on the server. Partial activation needs `confirm: true`, but a confirmation never overrides a fatal or no-scannable blocker. The transaction is ordered: raw rows, partner decisions, staged scannable rows, cancelled rows replaced, old active rows superseded, new rows activated. An advisory lock per account and the single-use staged file prevent interleaving and double activation.

sections.title: Lookup ambiguity and scan recording
sections.explanation: The four lookup outcomes (`found`, `duplicate`, `choose`, `not_found`) match `decideLookup`. `not_found` deliberately covers AWBs that exist only in accounts the user cannot see. The eight steps of `recordScan` are listed in order: replay, scope and active check, advisory lock, already-received check, full validation, new tickets, matched-field comparison, inserts. The paragraph about snapshots explains why a later upload cannot change a recorded scan.

sections.title: Access, issues, tickets, SKUs
sections.explanation: The account-access rules repeat `access.ts`: Admin, all-marketplaces, assigned accounts, 403 for a named account and 404 for a single record. The issue-rule table shows the seeded categories, and the text states the coverage invariants that `validateScanSubmission` enforces. Tickets use a five-state status with no transition map and full history, which the doc separates from the 14-state claims lifecycle. Product SKU resolution follows the order product master, then a single unambiguous OMSGuru code, otherwise unresolved.

sections.title: Legacy, API, admin, concurrency
sections.explanation: Legacy scans appear as one row per shipment line with no received quantity, which is the `legacy` branch of `REGISTER_UNION_SQL`. The API notes describe the register filters, the export formats and column sets, the 50,000-row refusal and the formula guard. Admin can only add and switch off reference data, never delete it. The concurrency list names the safeguards: the client scan key, the per-AWB advisory lock, the row lock, and the unique indexes `receipt_scans_client_scan_key_uidx` and `receipt_scans_expected_return_id_key` as the backstop.

sections.title: Verification and known limits
sections.explanation: This section lists each test file and what it covers. The database suites need a `TEST_DATABASE_URL` whose database name contains `test`, and they create only `SYN-` data. The rule that a skipped check has not passed is stated explicitly. Known limits include the 50,000-row export cap, scope parameters that still default to all accounts for older tests, the missing ticket transition map, and a script that does not yet filter on `lookup_status`.

src/App.tsx.overview: The root component of the React 19 web console. It handles only session state and page routing. It checks the cookie session through `/api/auth/me`, shows a boot screen, a connection-error screen or the login page, picks the page from the URL path with the History API, sends scanners to `/scan`, and provides the shared workspace context to every page. The pages themselves live in `src/pages/`. Tour step 8 introduces it as the entry point of the console.

sections.title: Imports and page titles
sections.explanation: The imports show how the shell is put together: `api`/`ApiError` for HTTP, `isAdminUser` for the client-side admin check, `pageFromPath`/`PAGE_PATH` for URL routing, the `Sidebar`/`Header` shell, one component per page, and `WorkspaceContext`. `PAGE_TITLES` is typed as `Record<Page, string>`, so adding a new `Page` value without a title is a compile error.

sections.title: State and URL navigation
sections.explanation: The initial page comes from `window.location.pathname` through a lazy `useState` initializer. `openPage` pushes a history entry only when the path actually changes, and a `popstate` listener (removed on unmount) keeps the page in step with the back and forward buttons. This gives client-side routing without a router library. The header date and claims badge stay empty until the server provides them, as the comment says.

sections.title: Session check and recovery
sections.explanation: `checkSession` calls `/api/auth/me`, which relies on the HttpOnly cookie, and loads the user, claims badge and header date. A scanner who lands on `/` or `/dashboard` is redirected to `/scan` with `replaceState`, so the back button does not return them to the dashboard. The error handling separates two cases. A 401 means signed out, so the user is cleared. Any other failure (network or 503) only sets a connection message and deliberately keeps an existing signed-in user.

sections.title: Logout
sections.explanation: Logout posts to `/api/auth/logout` but ignores network errors, so local state is always cleared even when the server cannot be reached. It then resets to the dashboard and pushes `/`. Ending the server session depends on that POST succeeding; the local reset only stops showing the workspace.

sections.title: Boot, error and login gates
sections.explanation: Three early returns run in order: a logo-only boot screen while the session check is running, a full connection-error card with a retry button when there is no user and the service cannot be reached, and the `Login` page when signed out. `Login`'s `onLogin` callback sets the same state as `checkSession`, including the scanner redirect, so a fresh sign-in and a restored session end up in the same place.

sections.title: Workspace provider and page switch
sections.explanation: The `WorkspaceValue` object (user, badge, header date, `openPage`, `setClaimsBadge`) is provided to the whole shell, so pages read it with `useWorkspace()` instead of receiving props. A non-blocking banner with a Reconnect button appears for connection errors while signed in. Pages are rendered conditionally, one `&&` per page, which mounts only the active page and remounts it on every switch. The Admin page is also guarded on the client with `isAdminUser`, but that only hides the screen. The server's `requireAdmin` is the real enforcement.

src/workspace.tsx.overview: A small module that defines the React context shared by every page of the signed-in console: the session user, the claims badge, the header date and the navigation callbacks. `App.tsx` provides the value and pages read it with the `useWorkspace()` hook. Tour step 8 mentions it as the workspace context that `App.tsx` passes to every page.

sections.title: WorkspaceValue type
sections.explanation: `WorkspaceValue` is the contract between the shell and the pages. It contains read-only session data (`user`, `claimsBadge`, `headerDate`) and two callbacks: `openPage` for navigation, which updates the URL, and `setClaimsBadge`, so a page such as Claims can refresh the sidebar badge after a change without a full session reload.

sections.title: Context and guarded hook
sections.explanation: The context is created with a `null` default instead of a fake value. `useWorkspace()` throws `Workspace missing` when it is used outside the provider. That turns a wiring mistake into an immediate, obvious error, and it lets every caller treat the returned value as non-null without checking for it.

src/routes.ts.overview: Maps each web console page to its own URL path and back. App.tsx uses `pageFromPath` to choose the page to render from the browser's path, so a refresh stays on the same tab. It is the smallest piece of the React console covered in tour step 8, and it depends only on the `Page` union in types.ts.

sections.title: Page-to-path table
sections.explanation: `PAGE_PATH` is typed as `Record<Page, string>`, so TypeScript requires an entry for every member of the `Page` union in types.ts: adding a page without a path is a compile error. The internal page key and the URL do not always match. The `reports` page, for example, lives at `/register`. The dashboard owns the root path `/`.

sections.title: Resolving a path to a page
sections.explanation: `pageFromPath` strips one trailing slash (but never shortens `/` to an empty string) and then looks the path up in the table in reverse. Unknown paths fall back to `dashboard` instead of throwing, so an old bookmark still lands on a valid page. Nothing role-specific lives here. The tour notes that App.tsx adds role defaults on top, such as sending scanners to `/scan`.

src/api.ts.overview: The web console's only HTTP helper. Every page calls `api<T>()` to talk to the Express server. Requests rely on the HttpOnly session cookie instead of a token held in JavaScript, and failures surface as a typed `ApiError` that carries the server's message, rule details and full response body. A second helper, `downloadFile`, saves exports to the user's disk. Tour step 8 introduces it as the small fetch wrapper the whole client is built on.

sections.title: Typed ApiError
sections.explanation: `ApiError` extends `Error` with the HTTP `status`, a `details` array for validation failures that break several rules, and the raw response `body`. Keeping the body lets callers read extra fields. ScanReturns.tsx, for example, reads `err.body.time` and `err.body.scannedBy` from a 409 to explain who already received a parcel. Because it is a real class, callers can test `instanceof ApiError` and then check `status`.

sections.title: Legacy token purge
sections.explanation: This top-level block runs once, when the module is first imported, and deletes a `return_token` key from `localStorage` that an older login scheme left behind. The comment links it to a rule that credentials never live in localStorage: the session now exists only in an HttpOnly cookie that scripts cannot read. The try/catch and the `typeof window` guard keep the import safe outside a browser, for example in tests.

sections.title: The api() fetch wrapper
sections.explanation: The wrapper sets `Content-Type: application/json` only when three things hold: there is a body, the body is not `FormData` (the browser must write its own multipart boundary), and the caller did not set the header. `credentials: "include"` sends the session cookie. Because it comes before `...options`, a caller can override it. The response is parsed as JSON only when the server says it is JSON, and a parse failure becomes `null` instead of an exception. A non-2xx response throws `ApiError` with the server's `error` text, or a generic message that includes the status code.

sections.title: File downloads
sections.explanation: `downloadFile` fetches with the same cookie credentials, turns the response into a Blob, clicks a temporary download link that points at an object URL, and then revokes the URL. When an error response has a JSON body, its message is used. Exports therefore stay behind the same session check as every other route, and no public download link is ever created.

src/types.ts.overview: The TypeScript types the web console shares across its pages. They mirror the JSON the server returns for sessions, scans, the register, uploads, the product master, Iron Send, analytics, claims, automation and return tracking, so a page and the route it calls agree on field names at compile time. Tour step 8 notes that this file keeps the client in step with the API from steps 4 to 7. The file holds only type declarations, except for two lookup tables for claim statuses.

sections.title: Pages, icons and session
sections.explanation: `Page` is the union that routes.ts maps to URLs. `IconName` lists every icon the shared `Icon` component can draw, so a misspelled icon name fails to compile. `SessionUser` is the signed-in user record the console works with, and it carries ready-to-show strings such as `scansToday`. The comment on `AccountOption` restates a core rule: lists of accounts always come from `/api/accounts` for the current user, never from a hard-coded list of marketplaces.

sections.title: Dashboard and shift figures
sections.explanation: These types serve the dashboard and the scan bench sidebar: recent-scan rows, stat tiles, throughput per operator and per marketplace, and the `ShiftCard` on the scan page. Several analytics types keep the server's snake_case column names (`operator_id`, `items_qty`), which shows the rows pass from SQL to the client unchanged. `IssueCategory` carries the flags behind the scan bench rules (`isClear`, `isMissing`, `requiresTicket`, and the sub-issue flags). The optional `isOperational` flag marks Iron Send, which is recorded but kept out of issue figures, claims and OMSGuru.

sections.title: Scan lookup and receipt contract
sections.explanation: `LookupResponse` is a discriminated union on `status` with four values: `found`, `duplicate`, `choose` and `not_found`. ScanReturns.tsx switches on exactly these values. `LookupShipment` keeps every tracking field (from the file, from a tracking URL, alternate and forward) plus the field and leg that the scanned AWB matched, because the scan saves that evidence. `ScanReceipt.replayed` tells the client that an idempotent retry returned an earlier save instead of creating a new one.

sections.title: Iron Send tracking
sections.explanation: Records, batches and summary counters for the Iron Send workflow (`server/iron.ts`), in which units go out for ironing and come back. States are string unions (`pending`, `partial`, `overdue`, and so on), so a typo in a filter fails to compile. As its inline comment says, `IronBatch.location` separates pieces sent to an outside khaata on a challan from pieces ironed in-house at the return desk.

sections.title: Return analytics report
sections.explanation: `AnalyticsReport` is the payload behind Register > Return Analytics. It holds totals, a comparison with the previous period, and breakdowns by day, week, marketplace, SKU, size, issue category and reason. The breakdown rows reuse `AnalyticsCounts` through intersection types (`AnalyticsCounts & {...}`), so every breakdown carries the same core counters. `StructuredInsight` adds insight cards with a category and a severity next to the plain `insights` strings.

sections.title: Register rows and options
sections.explanation: `RegisterRow` is one verified item of a scan, or one legacy line. Its comment says the first fields are the 19 approved register columns, followed by service and traceability columns. Each issue carries its optional `RegisterTicket`, and the Iron Send quantity and the Meesho flyer ID are optional fields on the row. `RegisterPage` wraps the rows with paging and sort state, and `RegisterOptions` fills the filter dropdowns with data from the server.

sections.title: Uploads and product master
sections.explanation: These types cover the upload workflow from tour step 6: history rows, the detailed `UploadCounts`, the `UploadPreview` with its `blockers`, `confirmations` and `canActivate` flag, exceptions per row, and the final `UploadImportResult` with counts of activated, superseded, pending and rejected rows. `ScannerListPreview` covers matching an uploaded list of scanned values against expected returns. The product-master types describe the staged import that the client works through in batches of 500 rows. Comments note that SKU conflicts are reported, never guessed.

sections.title: Claim records and status labels
sections.explanation: `ClaimStatus` lists the 14 lifecycle states that also appear in `CLAIM_STATUSES` in server/claims-service.ts. `CLAIM_STATUS_LABELS` and `CLAIM_STATUS_TONES` are the only runtime values in the file. Typing them as `Record<ClaimStatus, string>` forces a label and a colour tone for every status. `ClaimDetail` extends `ClaimRow` with media, status history and the evidence-completeness result. The Meesho types describe that marketplace's issue options and prefilled claim draft.

sections.title: Automation agents and claim lookup
sections.explanation: These types serve the desktop claim automation in tour steps 11 and 12: registered agents with heartbeat and authorization state, queued jobs with stage, attempts and logs, and supplier credentials. `MarketplaceCredential` exposes only `usernameMasked` and no password, so the client type has no field that could hold a secret. `ClaimReturnLookup` gathers everything needed to start a claim for a return: items, missing-item amounts, deadline fields, any existing claim, templates and standard reasons.

sections.title: Return tracking and claim eligibility
sections.explanation: These shapes serve the return-tracking view (`server/return-tracking.ts`), which compares marketplace return records with physical scans. `ClaimEligibilityStatus` encodes the aging buckets (eligible, expiring soon, expired, delayed RTS) that decide whether a claim can still be filed. The `physical*` fields link a portal record to its receipt scan, and `isFalseDelivery` flags a mismatch between a marketplace delivery claim and what arrived. The summary counts these discrepancies.

src/pages/ScanReturns.tsx.overview: The browser's warehouse scan bench, and the largest page in the web console. It turns a barcode scan into an AWB lookup within the user's accounts. Single-item returns auto-save as normal returns, and multi-item or multi-quantity parcels open a verification modal. Staff can record issues (categories, sub-issues, tickets, Iron Send, the Meesho flyer ID), and every result comes with an audio and visual verdict. The page repeats the server's validation rules for instant feedback but leaves the final decision to the server. It also listens to live changes, so saves on other benches update the shift figures. Tour step 9 covers it together with the live sync modules.

sections.title: Imports and display helpers
sections.explanation: Catalog images are never loaded straight from a marketplace. `catalogImageSrc` sends any absolute http(s) URL through the server's `/api/catalog-image` proxy and drops anything else. The label maps only name results the server already decided, such as which tracking field and leg matched; the client never decides the match itself. `IssueForm` and `LineForm` keep form values as strings, and `received` starts empty so nothing is assumed until staff type a number. `sizeFromSku` reuses the server's garment-size tokens to show a size chip.

sections.title: Feedback, chip order and themes
sections.explanation: `ScanFeedback` drives the large result banner, which must be readable from across the bench. Issue chips get short bench labels (`CHIP_LABEL`) and an adaptive order. `orderedCategories` always puts the clear category first, then sorts by a usage score (fixed baselines plus counts this workstation keeps in `localStorage`), then by a fixed rank. Every `localStorage` call sits in a try/catch, so blocked storage only loses the personal ordering. `CATEGORY_THEMES` gives each issue code its own colours, with a neutral fallback for unknown codes.

sections.title: Client-side rules, chimes and states
sections.explanation: `linePlan` repeats the server's rules for each line so problems show while staff type. The received quantity must be a whole number from 0 to the expected quantity, and the physical check must be ticked. Missing-item issues must cover exactly the missing units, and other issues cannot exceed the units received. As the comment says, the server still decides on save. `playScanChime` makes short tones with the Web Audio API, with distinct patterns for success, issue, Iron Send and error, and ignores audio failures. `ScannerState` names the bench's states: READY, LOOKUP, VERIFYING, SAVING, SAVED, and the error, duplicate and choose-account states.

sections.title: Bench state, focus and live sync
sections.explanation: The component keeps many values in both state and refs (`scannerStateRef`, `scanQueueRef`, `flyerAwaitingRef`). The global key and focus handlers are registered once, and refs let them read current values instead of stale closures. `transitionTo` changes the bench state and puts focus back in the scan box, except in VERIFYING and SAVING, so typing in the modal is never interrupted. On mount the page loads the shift, issue categories and sub-issues from `/api/scan/session`, and the user's accounts from `/api/accounts`. `useLiveChanges` refreshes the shift figures when data changes elsewhere, and it warns when another device has just saved the parcel on screen. A pointer-up handler and a once-a-second focus check return focus to the scan input, so a hardware scanner never types into nothing.

sections.title: Unboxing evidence camera
sections.explanation: Recording each unboxing with a webcam is optional, behind a toggle saved in `localStorage`. `startEvidenceRecording` uses `MediaRecorder` with one-second chunks, and it reads refs instead of React state so it always sees the current recorder. `stopEvidenceRecording` returns a Promise that resolves from the recorder's `onstop`, so a save can wait for the last chunk and know whether a video exists. Only the photo count and a has-video flag go out with the scan. The video itself stays on this workstation as an object URL.

sections.title: Save payloads and outcomes
sections.explanation: The Meesho flyer rule lives here. `needsFlyerFor` is true only for a Meesho shipment with at least one non-operational issue, so clear scans and Iron Send never ask for a flyer. `bodyFor` builds the exact JSON sent to `/api/scan/complete` and `/api/scan/correct`, including the `clientScanKey` idempotency key and the scanned AWB. `showSaved` and `showProblem` turn a receipt or a failure into a toast and update the session counters. A success toast disappears after 3.5 seconds; duplicate and error messages stay until the next scan. `handleAlreadyReceived` treats a 409 saying the return has already been received as a duplicate scan, because the lookup was stale: another bench saved the parcel first.

sections.title: Auto-save, issues and flyer
sections.explanation: `autoSave` posts a normal return as soon as a single-item return matches. It retries once, after 600 ms, and only for network errors or 5xx responses. The running save's promise is kept in `saveFlight`, so the next lookup or issue correction waits for it. If staff tap an issue chip while that save is running, the lines waiting in `pendingLines` are sent through `/api/scan/correct` right afterwards. `recordIssue` and `submitFlyer` handle the Meesho flyer step: the next barcode, or the unavailable link, completes the save. A flyer value equal to the return label's AWB is rejected.

sections.title: Lookup and barcode capture
sections.explanation: `runLookup` posts to `/api/scan/lookup` and branches on the four `LookupResponse` statuses. A single-unit return auto-saves with no popup, a multi-SKU or multi-quantity return opens the verification modal, a duplicate or not-found result shows a banner, and `choose` asks staff to pick an account. Each matched return gets a fresh `crypto.randomUUID()` as its idempotency key. `handleBarcodeScan` buffers up to 10 barcodes while a parcel is in progress, so fast scanning never loses a parcel. A global keydown listener detects hardware-scanner input outside any text field, meaning keys that arrive less than 80 ms apart. Another listener makes Enter retry a failed save or clear a duplicate.

sections.title: Line edits and manual save
sections.explanation: `chooseReport` applies one issue chip to the whole expected quantity of an item (received becomes 0 for missing-item categories) and saves the correction straight away. `plans`, `problems` and `canSave` are recomputed from `linePlan` on every render, so the Save button and its tooltip always show the first unmet rule. `save` serves the verification modal. It waits for the flyer when one is needed, stops the evidence recording, posts the payload, records chip usage, and moves on to the next buffered barcode. `retrySave` retries on the path that failed and resends the last flyer decision. In the modal, Escape cancels and Enter saves.

sections.title: Rendered bench and modals
sections.explanation: The JSX lays out the scan form: an account select with Auto detect, the scan input, and sound, focus and fullscreen controls. Below it come the toast and error banners, the account-choice panel, and the result card with the match evidence, item switcher, catalog image and issue chips. The side column shows today's shift card, the session counters and the evidence camera. The multi-item verification `Modal` repeats the flyer panel and saves on Enter. Duplicate and not-found panels are drawn from `response.status`, and button `title` attributes say why a control is disabled. This follows the project rule that every control either works or explains why not.

src/live.tsx.overview: The client half of live sync. A single module-level store per browser tab keeps a WebSocket open to `/api/live` and falls back to polling `/api/sync/state` every 3.5 seconds. Both channels report the same sync cursor, the newest audit-log id. Pages subscribe through `useSyncState` and `useLiveChanges`. When the cursor moves they reload their data through the normal scoped API, so the content of a message is never applied directly. `LiveSyncBadge` shows the connection mode. Tour step 9 pairs this file with server/live.ts.

sections.title: Contract, types and module state
sections.explanation: The header comment states the design: the push channel only signals that data changed, and pages reload through the normal API, so nothing is applied twice and the account rule always holds. `SyncMode` has the four values shown in the badge. State lives in module-level variables instead of React state, so every component in a tab shares one connection, and `Set`s of listeners pass state and change notices on to subscribers. `reconnectDelay` starts at 2 seconds and is capped at `MAX_RECONNECT_MS` (30 seconds).

sections.title: Cursor bookkeeping
sections.explanation: `setState` replaces the state object instead of mutating it and notifies subscribers, which is what `useSyncExternalStore` needs to detect a change. `noteCursor` keeps the highest cursor seen so far. A pushed change is passed on as it arrived. A cursor learned from a poll or a tick produces a synthetic `resync` change only when it moves past an earlier non-zero cursor, so the first cursor a tab sees is stored without triggering a reload.

sections.title: Polling fallback
sections.explanation: `pollOnce` asks `/api/sync/state` for the cursor through the shared `api()` wrapper, so polling uses the same cookie session. It sets the mode to `polling` on success and `offline` on failure, but never overrides `live`, because a working socket is the stronger signal. The null checks on `pollTimer` make `startPolling` and `stopPolling` safe to call repeatedly.

sections.title: WebSocket with backoff
sections.explanation: `connect` picks `ws:` or `wss:` to match the page's protocol and connects to the same host, so the session cookie goes along with the upgrade request. When the socket opens, the backoff resets and polling stops. Messages are parsed defensively: bad JSON is ignored, `change` messages carry the kind, account and ids, and any other message (`hello`, `tick`) only updates the cursor. When the socket closes, the tab falls back to polling at once and schedules a reconnect. The delay doubles each time, up to 30 seconds. `onerror` only closes the socket, so all recovery happens in the close handler.

sections.title: Lazy start and wake-up checks
sections.explanation: `ensureStarted` runs once per tab, when the first subscriber arrives, so a page that never uses live sync never opens a socket. When a tab becomes visible again it polls at once instead of waiting for the next interval. When the browser comes back online it also polls, and it reconnects the socket if none is open. `subscribeState` returns an unsubscribe function, as `useSyncExternalStore` requires.

sections.title: React hooks
sections.explanation: `useSyncState` exposes the store through React's `useSyncExternalStore`, which keeps every component that reads it consistent during a render. `useLiveChanges` keeps the latest callback in a ref, so callers do not have to memoize it. It debounces a burst of changes into one reload, 400 ms by default. The `maxWaitMs` cap (at least 3 seconds) guarantees a refresh on a busy floor where saves arrive every few seconds, which would otherwise keep resetting a plain debounce so it never fired.

sections.title: Synced-time label
sections.explanation: `syncedLabel` turns the last sync time into relative text (just now, seconds, minutes) and switches to an IST clock time after an hour. It uses an `Intl.DateTimeFormat` fixed to `Asia/Kolkata`, so the label does not depend on the PC's locale. `useNow` re-renders on an interval, so relative labels keep updating instead of freezing.

sections.title: LiveSyncBadge component
sections.explanation: A small status pill that reads `useSyncState` and re-renders every second. `MODE_TEXT` holds the short label and `MODE_TITLE` the tooltip; the offline tooltip tells staff that scans are not lost and the screen retries on its own. The `status` role makes the pill an accessible live region. The `compact` prop hides the time text, and the scan bench uses it that way.

server/live.ts.overview: The server half of live sync, used by both the web console and the Android app. It attaches a WebSocket endpoint at `/api/live` to the HTTP server, checks the session on each upgrade with the same rule as the API, and pushes small change notices filtered by account scope. The newest `register_audit_log` id serves as the sync cursor, and polling clients read the same cursor from `GET /api/sync/state`. Tour step 9 describes this module as the piece that keeps every open screen current.

sections.title: Protocol notes
sections.explanation: The header documents the whole design. Every change that other screens must see writes an audit row in the same transaction, so the newest audit id also works as a sync cursor: two clients with the same cursor have seen the same data. Clients get a `change` message right away and a `tick` every 15 seconds. They never apply a change from the message itself. They reload through the normal scoped routes, which keeps the account rule in force and makes duplicate messages harmless.

sections.title: Types and client registry
sections.explanation: `ChangeKind` lists the published events: scans saved or corrected, tickets, upload activation, Iron Send events and claim updates. Each connected socket is stored as a `LiveClient` with the user's `AccountScope` and an `alive` flag for the heartbeat. The caller passes in the `LiveAuthenticator`, so this module does not depend on auth.ts directly and can be tested with a fake authenticator.

sections.title: Cursor and visibility rule
sections.explanation: `currentCursor` reads `MAX(id)` from `register_audit_log`, or 0 when the table is empty. `changeVisibleTo` is the scope filter. A change reaches only clients whose scope includes its `marketplaceId`, checked with `allowsAccount` from access.ts. A change with no account, such as a setting, goes to everyone. This is how the project's account-scope rule extends to push messages.

sections.title: Publishing a change
sections.explanation: `send` checks that the socket is open and swallows send errors; the heartbeat cleans up broken sockets. Services call `publishChange` after a transaction commits, and it never throws. It returns at once when no client is connected. Otherwise it reads the fresh cursor and sends the payload only to clients allowed to see the change. A failed push does no lasting harm, because clients notice the new cursor on the next tick or poll.

sections.title: Authenticated upgrade
sections.explanation: The `WebSocketServer` runs in `noServer` mode with a 4 KB `maxPayload`, because clients only listen. On every HTTP `upgrade` event the path must be exactly `/api/live`; any other path gets its socket destroyed. The injected authenticator checks the session: the cookie for the browser, the Authorization header for the Android app. A failed check gets a raw `401` response, and an error inside the authenticator gets a `503`. Accepted clients are registered, any incoming message or pong marks them alive, and each one immediately receives a `hello` with the current cursor.

sections.title: Heartbeat and ticks
sections.explanation: Every 15 seconds the loop terminates clients that did not answer the previous ping, marks the rest as not alive, and pings them again. This is the standard `ws` heartbeat pattern for dropping dead connections, for example behind a proxy. The loop then broadcasts a `tick` with the current cursor, so a client that missed a `change` still catches up. Any earlier timer is cleared first, so calling `attachLiveServer` twice does not leave two loops running.

sections.title: Shutdown
sections.explanation: `closeLiveServer` stops the tick timer, terminates every socket and empties the registry, for a clean shutdown or a test teardown.

android/app/src/main/java/shop/youthnic/.overview: The Android `Application` subclass for the native scanner. Android creates it once per process, before any activity, and it builds the app-wide singletons every screen uses: the session store, the API client, the sound manager and the image cache. It also creates the update notification channel and schedules the periodic update check. Tour step 10 starts here.

sections.title: Package and imports
sections.explanation: The imports show how the app is organized: data services (`ApiClient`, `SessionManager`, `ImageCache`) live in `data`, the updater in `update`, and audio in `util`. No UI classes are imported, because this class only wires services together.

sections.title: App-wide services
sections.explanation: Each service is a `lateinit var` with a `private set`, so other classes can read it but only this class can assign it. `lateinit` is safe here because `onCreate` runs before any activity can read these fields. Activities reach the services by casting, for example `(application as ReturnScanApp).apiClient` in ScannerActivity.

sections.title: Startup wiring
sections.explanation: The order matters: `SessionManager` is created first because `ApiClient` and `SoundManager` both take it as a constructor argument. `AppUpdater.ensureChannel` creates the notification channel that update notices need on Android 8 and later. `scheduleBackgroundCheck` queues a WorkManager job, so a phone learns about a new APK even when nobody opens the scanner.

sections.title: Global instance
sections.explanation: The companion `instance` lets code that has no `Context` reach the application. It is set at the very start of `onCreate` and has a private setter. It is a convenient service locator, but it also makes these services global state for the whole process.

android/app/src/main/java/shop/youthnic/.overview: The core of the Android scanner: a full-screen activity that runs a continuous CameraX preview with ML Kit barcode analysis. It looks each AWB up in the chosen account, opens a verification bottom sheet, saves the scan, and confirms the verdict with a sound cue, an optional screen flash and a last-scan banner. It also shows the live sync status, today's shift figures and an update banner, and it pauses the camera when the phone is idle to save battery. Tour step 10 describes it together with its activity_scanner.xml layout.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The imports list the building blocks. CameraX supplies `Preview`, `ImageAnalysis` and `ProcessCameraProvider`, with `Camera2Interop` for low-level focus control. ML Kit does the barcode scanning and coroutines run the network calls. Project classes such as `BarcodeRules`, `DuplicateGuard`, `LiveSync`, `ScanSignals` and `AppUpdater` do the rest. `ActivityScannerBinding` is the View Binding class generated from activity_scanner.xml.

sections.title: Activity state and permission launcher
sections.explanation: The account to scan arrives through intent extras. `DuplicateGuard` ignores the same code for 8 seconds and any code for 1.5 seconds after a scan, so a barcode left in view is not looked up again and again. `isRequestInFlight` (an `AtomicBoolean`) and `openDialogs` (an `AtomicInteger`) are the two gates that pause analysis while a lookup runs or a dialog is open. They are atomic because the analyzer runs on a background executor. `savedSheet` is compared by identity, so a late reply can only close its own sheet. Refusing the camera permission does not close the scanner, because manual AWB entry still works.

sections.title: Lifecycle and UI wiring
sections.explanation: `onCreate` reads the extras, builds the flash overlay, the UI and the barcode client, loads session data, and creates `LiveSync`, whose callbacks refresh the shift and update the connection pill. The tones are prepared after the first frame, so the first verdict is not delayed. `onResume` restarts the camera (or shows the permission overlay), the idle watch, the update check, live sync and the clock ticker. `onPause` stops all of them and releases the camera. The whole paused overlay is clickable, not just its button, so a tap anywhere on it wakes the camera.

sections.title: Session data, sync pill and updates
sections.explanation: Session data holds the issue categories the verification sheet needs, plus today's figures. If the scanner opened offline, `ensureSessionData` loads it again at the first lookup. `refreshShift` runs on resume and whenever the live cursor moves. It keeps the existing issue rules and replaces only the figures, so an open sheet is not disturbed, and an expired session sends the user back to login. `renderConnection` colours the pill Live, Auto-sync or Offline and adds an IST time, and a once-a-second ticker keeps relative times from freezing. `checkForUpdates` shows a tappable banner when AppUpdater reports a newer APK.

sections.title: Camera permission overlays
sections.explanation: This part handles the runtime camera permission. When Android will no longer show its permission dialog (`CameraPermission.isBlocked`), the overlay's text and button switch to opening the app settings instead. The idle pause reuses the same overlay with different strings, so one place on screen always explains why the camera is not running.

sections.title: CameraX binding and ML Kit analysis
sections.explanation: The ML Kit client is limited to the 1D and 2D formats couriers use. As the comments explain, the analysis stream targets 1080p, above the 720p preview, because 1D barcodes need more horizontal pixels. Both streams force continuous autofocus through `Camera2Interop`, since the thin bars blur when focus locks at a fixed distance. `STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST` drops stale frames. `processImageProxy` limits analysis to one frame per `CameraTuning.ANALYZE_EVERY_MS`, skips frames while a dialog or request is active, and always closes the `ImageProxy` so CameraX can deliver the next frame. `onBarcodesDetected` normalizes the value, extracts the identifier, checks the duplicate guard and starts one lookup.

sections.title: Lookup and account choice
sections.explanation: `executeLookup` claims the in-flight flag with `compareAndSet`, so two detections cannot start two lookups. It calls `ApiClient.lookupAwb` and branches on the result. A found return opens the verification sheet after a CHECK cue. A duplicate or not-found result shows a banner and frees the scanner. A `choose` result lists the candidate accounts in a dialog with nothing pre-selected. `failLookup` removes the AWB from the duplicate guard, so the same parcel can be scanned again as soon as the problem is fixed.

sections.title: Verification sheet and commit
sections.explanation: Each sheet gets an idempotency key from `BarcodeRules.generateClientScanKey`. A second tap on Save after an error reuses the same key, so a retry can never save a return twice. Every way of leaving the sheet goes through one dismiss listener, which keeps the scanner from staying blocked after a swipe. A save reply is tied to the sheet that started it (`owner`), so a reply that arrives after a newer sheet opened never closes the wrong one. On success the shift count comes from the server's receipt and a replayed save is not counted twice. A recent-scan entry is recorded, and the camera resumes after 500 ms with no need for a scan-again button.

sections.title: Verdict signals and banners
sections.explanation: `signal` plays the cue through the shared `SoundManager` and flashes the screen if that setting is on. `flashScreen` animates the alpha of a full-window overlay about every 16 ms, using levels from `ScanSignals` and one colour per cue (OK, DUPLICATE, NOT_FOUND, CHECK, STOP). `showBanner` fills the last-scan card. Its KDoc explains that the status text is white on a bar of the verdict colour, because text in the verdict colour was invisible on a bar of the same colour.

sections.title: Controls, idle pause and navigation
sections.explanation: The manual-entry and recent-scans dialogs each increment `openDialogs` when shown and decrement it in a single dismiss listener, so analysis pauses exactly while a dialog is open. `startIdleWatch` checks every 5 seconds and unbinds the camera after `CameraTuning.IDLE_PAUSE_MS` without activity. `updateKeepScreenOn` keeps the screen on only while the camera runs, which saves battery on shared warehouse phones. `goToLogin` clears the session and starts a fresh task, and the companion object defines the intent extra keys that callers use to open this activity.

android/app/src/main/res/layout/activity.overview: The View-based layout behind ScannerActivity, inflated through View Binding as `ActivityScannerBinding`. From top to bottom it stacks a hidden update banner, a header with the account and sync status, a fixed-height camera area with overlays, a scrollable result area and a bottom action bar sized for thumbs. Tour step 10 presents it as the screen of the continuous CameraX scanner.

sections.title: Root and update banner
sections.explanation: A vertical `LinearLayout` fills the screen. `tvUpdateBanner` starts as `gone`. When AppUpdater finds a newer release, ScannerActivity shows the banner with the new version name and makes it open the update dialog when tapped.

sections.title: Header: account, sync and progress
sections.explanation: The header holds the back button, a colour strip (`viewChannelColor`) tinted with the marketplace colour, the active account name, and `tvConnectionStatus`, the pill that ScannerActivity restyles as Live, Auto-sync or Offline. Below it, `tvProgressScanned`, `tvProgressPending` and `progressBarScans` show today's figures. The `tools:text` values only fill the Android Studio preview and never reach the device.

sections.title: Camera preview and viewfinder
sections.explanation: The camera area is a black `FrameLayout` 240dp tall, so overlays can sit on top of the `PreviewView` that CameraX draws into. The viewfinder is a wide, short rectangle (260 x 96 dp) shaped for 1D courier barcodes rather than square QR codes. `tvScannerHint` shows status text such as lookup progress, and `progressSubmitting` spins while a lookup runs.

sections.title: Flash and verdict stamp overlays
sections.explanation: These overlays were meant for verdict feedback, and the comment lists the colour for each cue. In the current code, no Kotlin file under `android/app/src/main/java` refers to `viewScreenFlash` or `layoutSignalStamp`. ScannerActivity instead adds its own full-window flash view in `initFlashOverlay()`. Both views stay `gone` at runtime, and `tools:visibility` shows the stamp only in the editor preview.

sections.title: Idle and permission overlay
sections.explanation: `layoutCameraPaused` covers the camera with a dark translucent panel and is `clickable`, so a tap anywhere on it wakes the camera. ScannerActivity rewrites `tvCameraPausedTitle`, `tvCameraPausedSub` and `btnResumeCamera` for two cases: the idle pause, and a missing camera permission (with a link to settings when Android blocks the dialog).

sections.title: Last scan card
sections.explanation: The results area is a `ScrollView` with weight 1, so it fills all the space between the camera and the bottom bar. `cardScanBanner` is the last-scan card. `bannerLastVerdict` is its coloured header bar, holding `tvBannerStatus` and the relative time `tvLastVerdictTime`, and below it come the AWB, the order line and the details. The card starts hidden and appears after the first verdict.

sections.title: Idle state card and legend
sections.explanation: This card shows before any scan: a ready message and a legend of verdict colours (OK green, duplicate blue, not found purple). It uses the same colour resources as the flashes and banners, so staff learn one colour code. The legend labels are hard-coded strings, not string resources.

sections.title: Bottom action bar
sections.explanation: A 64dp bar with four equal actions (torch, manual entry, recent scans, settings) that share the `ScannerAction` and `ScannerActionLabel` styles. Each action is a `LinearLayout` with an id. ScannerActivity attaches click listeners to `btnTorch`, `btnManualEntry`, `btnRecentScans` and `btnSettings`, and it changes `tvTorchLabel` to show whether the torch is on or off.

android/app/src/main/java/shop/youthnic/.overview: The Android in-app updater. Its KDoc says it checks the server's release manifest (`GET /api/app/latest`) for a newer APK. It notifies once per version and shows an update dialog that cannot be dismissed when the version is required. It downloads the APK through `DownloadManager`, verifies the SHA-256 and passes the file to the system installer through a `FileProvider`. This is the phone side of the release flow; server/mobile-release.ts is the server side (tour step 10).

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: The imports show how the updater works: `DownloadManager` for the download, `NotificationCompat` for update notices, WorkManager for the periodic background check, `FileProvider` to share the APK with the installer, and `MessageDigest` for the SHA-256 check. `BuildConfig` supplies the installed version code to compare against.

sections.title: Constants and shared state
sections.explanation: `AppUpdater` is a Kotlin `object`, a singleton for the whole process. Shared preferences record which version was already announced and which download is in progress, so both survive an app restart. `available` and `lastCheckAt` are `@Volatile` because both the UI and the background check read them. `installedVersionCode` comes from `BuildConfig.VERSION_CODE`, which is why the version code the server reports must match the published APK.

sections.title: Checking for a release
sections.explanation: `check` runs at most once every 10 minutes unless `force` is true, and returns the cached answer in between. The network call runs on `Dispatchers.IO`. A release is kept only if `isNewerThan(installedVersionCode)` is true, and a newer release triggers a one-time notification. Failures come back as `Result.failure` instead of an exception, so a caller such as ScannerActivity can simply hide the banner.

sections.title: Notifications and background checks
sections.explanation: `ensureChannel` creates the update channel once, on Android 8 and later. `canNotify` respects the Android 13 notification permission and the user's notification setting. `notifyOnce` stores the announced version code so each version is announced only once, and tapping the notice opens the app's launch activity. `scheduleBackgroundCheck` queues a unique periodic WorkManager job that runs every 3 hours when the phone is online. Its `KEEP` policy leaves an existing schedule in place instead of resetting it on every app start.

sections.title: Update dialog
sections.explanation: `showUpdateDialog` builds a message with the new and installed version names, the download size and the release notes. When the installed version is below the release's minimum (`isRequiredFor`), the dialog uses the required title, has no Later button and cannot be cancelled. An optional update shows once per version unless `always` is set, which is the case when staff tap the scanner's update banner.

sections.title: Starting or resuming the download
sections.explanation: The APK is saved under a name that includes the version code, in the app's own external downloads folder. If a download for the same version is already recorded, it is reused: a finished file goes straight to verification, and a download still running reopens the progress dialog. Otherwise old downloads and leftover `return-scan-*.apk` files are removed before a new `DownloadManager` request is queued. Any failure, including a missing download service or a URL that is not http, falls back to opening the release page in a browser.

sections.title: Progress dialog polling
sections.explanation: `query` reads the status and byte counts for one download id and returns null on any error. `showProgress` opens a dialog with a progress bar and polls every 400 ms in the activity's `lifecycleScope`, so polling ends with the activity, and hiding the dialog cancels the job. When the download finishes or fails, the dismiss listener is cleared before the dialog is closed, so closing it from code does not cancel the job that is handling the result. The job then moves on to verification, or shows the retry dialog.

sections.title: Integrity check and install
sections.explanation: `verifyAndInstall` hashes the file on `Dispatchers.IO` in 64 KB chunks and compares the result with the manifest's `sha256`, ignoring case. On a mismatch it deletes the file, forgets the download id and reports a damaged download. One gotcha: a blank `sha256` in the manifest skips the comparison entirely. On Android 8 and later, `install` checks the permission to install unknown apps and keeps the file in `pendingInstall` while the user grants it. It then opens the installer with a `FileProvider` content URI (authority `<package>.updates`) on Android 7 and later, or a plain file URI on older versions.

sections.title: Permission settings, retry and fallback
sections.explanation: `openInstallPermission` opens this app's unknown-sources screen, falling back to the general security settings. `resumePendingInstall` lets an activity continue the install once the user comes back with the permission granted. `showFailed` offers Try again, Open in browser or Close, with different messages for a failed download and a damaged one. `openDownloadPage` opens the release page URL, or shows it in a toast if no browser can handle it.

server/mobile-release.ts.overview: Serves the Android release manifest and the APK download. `handleLatestRelease` and `handleApkDownload` are Express handlers, mounted elsewhere, that tell installed phones which version is current, with its SHA-256 and size, so AppUpdater can offer and verify the update. The newest Android tag is read from GitHub releases and cached for 10 minutes; `data/return-scan-release.json` and a bundled default serve as fallbacks. Together with the APK workflow, this is why the project rules require every scanning change to ship with a matching release entry (tour step 10).

sections.title: Release shape, default and cache
sections.explanation: `MobileReleaseInfo` is the manifest the phone reads: version code and name, minimum required version, SHA-256, size, notes and URLs. `RELEASE_FILE` points into the `data` folder one level above this module's folder, which is the project root. `DEFAULT_RELEASE` is the hard-coded floor (1.0.58, version code 10058), used when nothing newer is available; AGENTS.md notes that this fallback lags behind the latest published APK. `cachedRelease` and `lastFetchTime` keep the last GitHub answer for `GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_MS` (10 minutes).

sections.title: Reading the newest Android tag
sections.explanation: The repository publishes two release families, Android `v1.0.N` and desktop `desktop-v*`, so GitHub's latest-release alias could point at a desktop installer. Instead the function lists 30 recent releases, skips drafts and prereleases, and keeps the highest `v1.0.N`. The version code is `10000 + N`, which must match the code the APK workflow builds into the app. The SHA-256 comes from the APK asset's `digest`. One gotcha: when an asset has no digest, the code falls back to the bundled default's hash, which belongs to a different APK, so AppUpdater's integrity check would most likely reject the download as damaged. Any error returns null.

sections.title: Fallback manifest
sections.explanation: `getMobileReleaseInfo` returns the cached GitHub release when it is at least as new as the default. Otherwise it starts from `DEFAULT_RELEASE` and lays `data/return-scan-release.json` over it. It does this only when the file has no version code or one at least as new as the default, so a stale file can never push phones below the bundled floor. Read and parse errors silently keep the default.

sections.title: Manifest endpoint handler
