sections.explanation: `handleLatestRelease` refreshes the GitHub cache when it is empty or older than 10 minutes, and it accepts the GitHub answer only if that is not older than the default. Until a GitHub answer has been cached, every request tries GitHub again. The response is `available: true` plus the manifest. Fallback download and page URLs are built from `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`, so the links are correct behind a reverse proxy.

sections.title: APK download handler
sections.explanation: If a locally built APK exists in any of three known output paths, `handleApkDownload` serves it with the Android package MIME type, a file name that includes the version, and `no-cache`. Otherwise it redirects to GitHub. It builds the tag URL from the resolved version instead of using the latest-release alias, again because that alias may point at a desktop installer.

server/claims-service.ts.overview: The server's core claims logic: claim records tied to a scanned return, configurable evidence templates, the lifecycle state machine with its status history, and evidence media whose bytes live in Firebase Storage. Every read and write takes the caller's account scope, and a claim outside that scope is reported as not found, so its existence is not revealed. Changes are recorded in `claim_status_history` and in the shared `register_audit_log`. Tour step 11 starts here, before the automation queue turns claims into jobs.

sections.title: Header, statuses and limits
sections.explanation: The header comment sets the rules: scoped access, 404 for claims outside the scope, a history entry for every status change, and media served by the server with no public links. Its statement that all transitions are allowed is out of date: `CLAIM_TRANSITIONS`, further down, rejects any move it does not list. `CLAIM_STATUSES` is declared `as const`, and `ClaimStatus` is derived from that array, so the type and the list can never drift apart. The client repeats the same 14 values in src/types.ts. The `MAX_*` constants cap user-entered text, and `RETENTION_MONTHS` sets how long evidence is kept.

sections.title: Record types
sections.explanation: Server-side shapes for templates, template fields, media rows, status history, the claim row, the claim detail and the paged list result. They match the client types in src/types.ts field for field, which keeps the claims page and the API in step. `ClaimDetail` adds the computed `evidenceComplete` and `missingEvidence` fields to the stored row.

sections.title: Validation and the transition table
sections.explanation: The validators are pure functions that return an error string or null, so routes and tests can use them without a database. `CLAIM_TRANSITIONS` is the lifecycle state machine. For example, `paid` is final, `rejected` can only move to `reclaim` or `escalated`, and the failure states can return to `processing` for a retry. `evidenceContentError` checks magic bytes (JPEG, PNG, WebP, PDF, an MP4 `ftyp` box, the WebM header) instead of trusting the file name or MIME type, so a renamed file cannot pass as evidence.

sections.title: Audit helper and template reads
sections.explanation: `auditClaimChange` writes claim events to the same `register_audit_log` the register uses, so a claim change also moves the live sync cursor. `listClaimTemplates` returns global templates (`marketplace_id IS NULL`) plus the templates for accounts in scope, and `accountCondition` binds the account list as a query parameter. The fields are fetched in a second query with `ANY($1::integer[])` and grouped in a `Map`, which avoids one query per template. `getClaimTemplate` applies the same scope rule to a single template and reports a template outside the scope as not found.

sections.title: Template administration
sections.explanation: Create, update, add-field and deactivate-field each run in one transaction that also writes an audit row. They follow the BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK pattern and call `client.release()` in `finally`. `updateClaimTemplate` builds its `SET` clause from only the fields provided, with every value still passed as a parameter. Fields are never deleted, only marked inactive. These functions take an `Actor` but no scope, and the section comment says templates are Admin-managed, so the role check belongs in the route. After a change they re-read the template with an all-accounts scope (`{ all: true }`).

sections.title: Claims queue listing
sections.explanation: `listClaims` always starts its WHERE clause with the account-scope condition. It then adds optional filters: status (valid statuses only), account, a text search across reason, title, AWB and order number, and an IST date range checked with a regex. The page size is clamped: 25 by default, and at most `maxPageSize` or 100. The query prefers values snapshotted on the claim or the scan (`awb_snapshot`, `order_number_snapshot`) over live lookup data. It computes `days_remaining` against today's date in Asia/Kolkata and marks a claim overdue when that number is negative.

sections.title: Claim detail and scan search
sections.explanation: `getClaim` loads the claim within the caller's scope, or returns 404, and then fetches its media and status history together with `Promise.all`. Evidence completeness is worked out by counting active media per field key against the template's required fields and their `min_count`, which gives a readable list of missing evidence. `searchClaimScans` finds receipt scans by AWB, alternate AWB or order number (at least 3 characters, at most 20 results) and flags whether each already has a claim, which supports the one-claim-per-scan rule.

sections.title: Creating a claim
sections.explanation: Inside one transaction, `createClaim` loads the scanned return and checks its account with `allowsAccount`, answering 404 rather than 403 for a scan from another account. For Meesho, `prepareMeeshoClaim` supplies the issue code, sub-order, packet details and due date. A second claim for the same scan is refused with 409. A named template is checked against the marketplace, and the best active template is used instead if it does not fit. If none exists, a default template that requires product images and an unboxing video is created, so creating a claim is never blocked. The claim starts in `pending_evidence` with a first history row and an audit entry.

sections.title: Status changes
sections.explanation: `updateClaimStatus` runs in a transaction. It loads the claim within scope, rejects a change to the same status (400) and any transition the table does not allow (409), and requires complete evidence before `ready_for_claim`. The amount rules are strict: an approved amount only when approving, a paid amount and payout date only when marking a claim paid, and a paid claim needs both the amount and a payout reference. The evidence check calls `getClaim` with the connection pool, not the transaction's client. Every change adds a row to `claim_status_history` and to the audit log.

sections.title: Evidence media
sections.explanation: Media rows store only metadata: storage path, content hash, size, MIME type and a retention date 24 months ahead. The bytes live in Firebase Storage. `addClaimMedia` and `deactivateClaimMedia` move a claim between `pending_evidence` and `ready_for_claim` on their own as required evidence is added or removed, and each move gets a history entry. `prepareClaimMediaUpload` runs before an upload. It rejects fields that are not in the claim's template, and when the same content hash is already attached it returns that media id instead of uploading again. It also enforces the field's maximum count, size limit and MIME type family, and builds a cleaned-up storage path from the marketplace, order number, claim id, field key and hash.

server/claim-automation-service.ts.overview: The core of the claim automation queue on the server. It encrypts supplier portal credentials, registers and authenticates desktop automation agents, turns a claim into a queued job, leases jobs to agents inside transactions, accepts progress and completion reports under lease and authorization checks, and mirrors marketplace ticket IDs into the return scan register. It is the service behind the agent API in claim-automation-routes.ts and the heart of tour step 11; the automation engine from step 12 is the caller of its leasing and completion paths. The file also hosts the return lookup used when a claim is created from mobile or web.

sections.title: Imports, encryption and row types
sections.explanation: Supplier portal passwords are stored with AES-256-GCM. `encryptionKey()` derives a 32-byte key by SHA-256 hashing the `AUTOMATION_SECRET_KEY` environment variable and throws a 503 `ServiceError` when it is shorter than 32 characters. There is deliberately no fallback key in source, because a shared default would make every installation's ciphertext recoverable. `encryptSecret` uses a fresh 12-byte IV and stores `iv:tag:ciphertext` as hex, so the GCM auth tag travels with the data and any tampering fails decryption. `decryptSecret` swallows errors and returns an empty string, which callers treat as 'no credential' instead of crashing; `maskSecret` keeps only the first and last two characters for display. The two row types describe what the dashboard lists for agents and jobs.

sections.title: Agent registration and authentication
sections.explanation: `registerOrUpdateAgent` upserts by `agent_uuid` and stores only a SHA-256 hash of the agent's API key; if the desktop sent no key, a random 24-byte key is generated and returned once. Its route requires a signed-in Supervisor or Admin and records `registered_by_user_id`, and `scopeForAutomationAgent` later rebuilds an `AccountScope` from that enrolling user's role and marketplace assignments, so an agent can never see more accounts than the person who enrolled it (rule 1: account scope on every data route). `authenticateAutomationAgent` hashes the supplied key and compares it with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, substituting a zero buffer when the stored hash is missing or malformed so the comparison still runs in constant time. When a `jobId` is passed it also proves the job is assigned to this agent and answers 404 otherwise. `listAutomationAgents` derives 'offline' in SQL when the last heartbeat is older than 90 seconds instead of trusting the stored status.

sections.title: Marketplace credentials
sections.explanation: `listMarketplaceCredentials` is scope-bound through `accountCondition` (plus rows with no marketplace) and never returns secrets: the username is decrypted only so it can be masked. `getPortalLoginForSetup` is the one function that returns a decrypted username and password, matched case-insensitively by account or marketplace name, and its route is Admin-only. `saveMarketplaceCredential` finds an existing active row by marketplace or account name and builds the `UPDATE` dynamically, pushing each parameter together with its `$n` placeholder so the indices stay in step. Encrypted fields are written only when a new username or password is supplied, so saving other settings never wipes a stored secret. New rows default to `assisted` mode with approval before submit and auto-prepare on, and `defaultMarketplacePortalUrl` fills in a portal URL when none is given.

sections.title: Queueing and leasing jobs
sections.explanation: `createOrQueueAutomationJob` queues only Meesho claims (the one fully automatic panel) and returns the existing job id unless the latest job failed, so repeated calls do not stack duplicates. `pollNextAutomationJob` does all its work in one transaction. It first handles expired leases: a job that expired in `submitting` has an unknown external outcome (Meesho may already have accepted it), so it moves to `manual_intervention_required` and is never resubmitted automatically, while expired jobs in earlier stages go back to `queued` until `max_attempts` is reached and then fail. Each of these changes writes claim status history and an audit row. The lease query applies the M8 eligibility allowlist (only `ready_for_claim`, `processing`, `reclaim` or `escalated` claims), binds the agent's scope, and uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` so two agents never lease the same row. An `approved` job advances to `submitting` and anything else to `downloading_media`, with a 15-minute lease and an incremented attempt count.

sections.title: Execution bundle
sections.explanation: `getJobExecutionBundle` returns everything the desktop needs to file one claim: claim snapshots (sub-order, AWB, packet state, issue code, return type), the portal URL, decrypted credentials, and the active evidence files with size and content hash so the agent can verify its downloads. A `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` picks the job's own credential first and falls back to the marketplace's active credential when the job has none. It also returns the live `claimStatus`, which the engine re-reads just before Submit so a stale or already-resolved claim is not filed (the submit guard from tour step 13). The route that serves the bundle has already checked that the job belongs to the calling agent.

sections.title: Progress reporting
sections.explanation: `updateJobProgress` accepts only a fixed set of stages and refuses `submitting` outright with a 409: under the M9 fix that state is granted only by the queue lease, so a worker cannot authorize itself to submit by reporting it. With an `agentId`, the job row is locked and the update is accepted only from the agent holding a lease that has not expired. A reported `failed` with attempts remaining is stored as `queued` so the job retries, and the lease is refreshed for 15 minutes only while the job is in an active stage; `not_eligible` clears any stale marketplace claim id. The claim status follows the job stage (prepared becomes `waiting_for_approval`, manual and not-eligible become `manual_action_required`, failed becomes `failed`), with a history row and an audit entry written in the same transaction.

sections.title: Syncing tickets into the register
sections.explanation: This is how a marketplace ticket reaches the return scan register. `mapToReceiptIssueCategory` turns a claim reason or issue code into a register issue category by keyword, defaulting to wrong product. `syncClaimTicketToRegister` accepts either a pool or a transaction client so it can run inside `completeJobSubmission`'s transaction. It upserts the scan's `claim_tickets` row, appending a numeric suffix until the ticket code is unique, and writes `claim_ticket_history` naming both the old and the new code so a replaced ticket stays auditable. It then makes sure the scan is marked as an issue, creates a scan item from the expected return if none exists, and links a `receipt_scan_issues` row to the ticket, checking first whether the ticket is already linked elsewhere because a partial unique index allows only one issue per ticket.

sections.title: Completing a submission
sections.explanation: `completeJobSubmission` records a marketplace ticket exactly once. Replaying the same ticket on a completed job (a network retry) is a no-op, while a different ticket on a completed job, a not-eligible job, or a claim that already has a recorded outcome is rejected with 409; another job for the same claim completed with a different ticket also blocks the write. Unless `operatorOverride` is set, the M9 authorization checks run under the row lock: the caller must be the lease-holding agent, the lease must still be live, and on approval-required accounts the job must be in the backend-issued `submitting` stage, so a saved supplier login never authorizes submission. On success the job is marked completed, `createFollowUpForJob` arms ticket tracking, the claim moves to `submitted` with history and audit rows, and the ticket is synced into the register as Raised, all in one transaction.

sections.title: Approve, retry and list jobs
sections.explanation: `approveJobForSubmission` is the human gate on approval-required accounts. It refuses jobs that are finished, failed, ruled out or mid-flight (a worker actively preparing or submitting keeps its lease) and claims in states that cannot be submitted; otherwise it sets the job to `approved` and the claim to `processing`, so the next lease turns it into `submitting`. `retryAutomationJob` resets a job to `queued` with zero attempts, but never for a completed or submitting job or a claim with a recorded outcome, since that would file twice; operator-held claims go back to `ready_for_claim` so the re-queued job can actually lease. Both functions are scope-bound and lock the job row. `listAutomationJobs` builds a scoped, filtered, paginated listing and clamps the page size to 100 before interpolating it into the SQL.

sections.title: Return lookup for claims
sections.explanation: `lookupReturnForClaim` powers the claim form on mobile and web for both scanned and unscanned returns. One scope-bound query matches the input against many identifiers (tracking, alternate and forward tracking, return event, order number, flyer, scanned tracking and item-level IDs) case-insensitively, including a hyphen- and space-insensitive comparison for inputs of eight or more characters, and prefers rows that already have a scan. It then loads the items, collects missing-component lines and amounts from the scan's issues, and computes the claim deadline: Meesho uses `MEESHO_TAT_DAYS` and `meeshoClaimDueDate` from meesho-claims.ts, other marketplaces seven days inclusive. Finally it attaches the marketplace's templates and suggested claim reasons: Meesho codes are ordered so the detected issue comes first, with text from `meeshoClaimDescription`, and the other marketplaces get fixed text templates.

server/claim-automation-routes.ts.overview: Mounts the HTTP routes for claim automation: the unified claim creation used by the Android and web clients, the agent API the automation engine calls (registration, heartbeat, job polling, bundle, progress, completion, follow-up leasing and results), and the Supervisor/Admin operations for approving, retrying and manually resolving jobs and for managing supplier credentials. Handlers stay thin and delegate to claim-automation-service.ts and claim-follow-up-service.ts, using the helpers from server/http.ts described in tour step 4. It is the network face of tour step 11.

sections.title: Imports and request helpers
sections.explanation: The imports show the split of responsibility: business logic lives in claim-automation-service.ts and claim-follow-up-service.ts, while `scopeOf`, `actorOf`, `requireAdmin`, `requireSupervisorOrAdmin` and `sendError` come from server/http.ts. `text` trims string inputs and turns anything else into an empty string, and `positiveId` accepts only positive integers, so malformed IDs become `null` instead of reaching SQL. `agentCredentials` reads the agent's identity from the `X-Agent-UUID` and `X-Agent-Key` headers; the agent API authenticates with these instead of a user session.

sections.title: Return lookup route
sections.explanation: `mountClaimAutomationRoutes` receives the shared `requireUser` middleware from server/index.ts. The first route, `GET /api/claims/return-lookup`, accepts the search under several query names (`query`, `search`, `awb`, `orderId`), requires at least three characters, and passes the caller's scope to `lookupReturnForClaim`, so a user only finds returns in accounts they can see. A miss returns 404 with `found: false` rather than an empty object.

sections.title: Unified claim creation
sections.explanation: `POST /api/claims/unified-create` creates a claim in one call, which is what the Android client uses. Without a `receiptScanId` it resolves one, either from `expectedReturnId` or by looking up the AWB or sub-order. When the return was never scanned, it opens a transaction, checks the expected return against the caller's scope, and creates a Draft issue scan plus scan items copied from the expected return items, so the claim still hangs off the register. It reuses an existing claim for the scan or creates one, then updates the snapshot columns with `COALESCE(NULLIF(...))` so empty inputs never overwrite stored values. Queueing the automation job and syncing the ticket to the register are best-effort: failures are logged as warnings and the claim is still returned with 201.

sections.title: Agent registration
sections.explanation: `POST /api/automation/agent/register` is the only agent endpoint behind a user session: it needs a signed-in Supervisor or Admin. The engine calls it with the operator's bearer token, and `registeredByUserId` records that operator. Every later agent request is scoped through `scopeForAutomationAgent` from that user, so enrolment fixes which accounts the agent may work on.

sections.title: Agent heartbeat, polling and job reports
sections.explanation: These routes deliberately skip `requireUser` and call `authenticateAutomationAgent` with the header credentials instead. Job-specific routes pass the job id so the service also checks the job is assigned to this agent, and polling and job listing use the enrolling user's scope. Progress and completion pass the authenticated `agent.id` down, so the M9 lease-holder and submission-authorization checks happen inside the service under a row lock. After a successful state change the route calls `publishChange` with the claim's marketplace, so the live WebSocket from tour step 9 refreshes open screens filtered by account.

sections.title: Follow-up ticket routes
sections.explanation: `GET /api/automation/follow-ups/due` leases the next ticket check that is due for the agent, scoped like job polling, and answers `hasFollowUp: false` in the common case where nothing is due. `POST /api/automation/follow-ups/:id/result` records one check's outcome, and an unknown outcome string falls back to `error`. The service verifies that this agent holds the lease on the row, and the response includes `statusChanged` and the stop reason so the engine can decide whether its assistance pass is worth running.

sections.title: Supervisor and admin job operations
sections.explanation: The dashboard routes require a user session. Listing agents needs Supervisor or Admin; listing jobs and follow-ups is open to any signed-in user but bound to their scope. Approve and retry are Supervisor/Admin actions that pass the caller's scope and actor to the service and then publish a live change. `manual-resolve` lets an operator record a ticket they filed by hand: it requires a marketplace claim reference and calls `completeJobSubmission` with `operatorOverride: true`, which keeps operator-approved resolution separate from automated submission because no worker lease is involved.

sections.title: Credential routes
sections.explanation: `GET /api/automation/portal-login-secret` returns a decrypted supplier login and is restricted to Admins (rule 2), because it is the only route that exposes a stored password. `GET /api/automation/credentials` returns the scope-bound list with masked usernames only. `POST /api/admin/automation/credentials` saves a credential (Admin-only); approval-before-submit and auto-prepare stay on unless the body sets them to `false` explicitly. The function ends by mounting the AI memory routes from ai-memory-routes.ts on the same app.

server/claim-follow-up-service.ts.overview: Server-side ticket tracking for filed claims. When a filing job completes, this module creates one follow-up row per claim; the automation engine leases due rows, reads the ticket on the supplier portal, and reports back here, where the result is normalized, the claim status is advanced, and the next check is scheduled or the row is stopped. The cadence and terminal rules are pure functions (the header points to server/tests/claim-follow-up.test.ts), and nothing deletes a row: a stopped follow-up stays for history. This is the part of tour step 11 that schedules re-checks until a ticket is approved, rejected, paid or reconciled.

sections.title: Constants and outcomes
sections.explanation: The header states the design: create on completion, re-check on a cadence, stop on a terminal state, a missing status reader or an exhausted budget, and never delete. The constants set a 48-hour interval, a budget of 90 checks (about 180 days), a three-error streak limit and a 15-minute lease. `FOLLOW_UP_TERMINAL_STATUSES` lists the states with nothing left to chase, and `FOLLOW_UP_OUTCOMES` is the closed list of outcomes an agent may report; anything else is rejected with 400.

sections.title: Normalizing portal status text
sections.explanation: Supplier portals show free text, so `normalizeFollowUpStatus` maps it to one key with ordered regular expressions where the first match wins. Rejections and negative phrases come first, so 'not approved' or 'closed without approval' can never read as approval; final positive states follow; active states such as escalated, reopened and under review come last. Anything unmatched is `unknown`, which keeps the follow-up running: as the comment puts it, wrongly closing a live ticket loses it, while an extra check costs nothing.

sections.title: Terminal states and stop messages
sections.explanation: `isTerminalFollowUpStatus` checks a normalized key against the terminal list. `claimStatusForFollowUp` maps a ticket state to a claim lifecycle status, or `null` when the state should not change the claim (for example `submitted` or `unknown`); the comment notes it may only return statuses from `CLAIM_STATUSES` in claims-service.ts. `stopReasonMessage` turns a stop reason into the operator-facing sentence shown on the dashboard, such as asking for a manual check after repeated errors.

sections.title: Deciding the next step
sections.explanation: `decideFollowUpStep` is the pure core of the cadence. `not_supported` stops the row without counting a check, because a marketplace without a status reader cannot be chased; a new submission re-arms it once a reader exists. `login_required` is neither an error nor a spent check, so the row just waits for the next cadence. A `status_read` counts as a check and stops on a terminal state or when the budget runs out, while `not_found` and `error` count as both a check and an error and stop after three in a row. `nextCheckAtFrom` is a plain hours-ahead helper; note that `recordFollowUpResult` below schedules with `nextEligibleCheckAt` from nightly-window.ts instead.

sections.title: Row type and date helper
sections.explanation: `FollowUpRow` is the camelCase shape the web dashboard and the engine's follow-up table receive, combining the follow-up columns with the marketplace name, order number and claim status from joins. `iso` converts `pg` Date values to ISO strings and keeps nulls as null, so timestamps are serialized the same way everywhere.

sections.title: Creating or re-arming a follow-up
sections.explanation: `createFollowUpForJob` runs inside `completeJobSubmission`'s transaction on the same client, so a ticket and its tracking row commit together. It inserts from the job, claim and credential with the first check 48 hours out, and does nothing when the ticket reference is empty. The unique index on `claim_id` plus `ON CONFLICT (claim_id) DO UPDATE` gives one follow-up per claim: re-filing resets the counters, lease, stop reason and timer on the existing row instead of adding a second one.

sections.title: Leasing a due check
sections.explanation: `leaseNextDueFollowUp` mirrors job leasing but is simpler, because reading a ticket has no external side effect: expired leases go back to `scheduled` with a note in `last_error` instead of being escalated. It then selects the oldest active, scheduled, due row inside the agent's account scope with `FOR UPDATE OF f SKIP LOCKED`, so concurrent agents never take the same ticket, and marks it `leased` for 15 minutes. The result carries the portal URL and marketplace ticket ID the engine needs to open the panel.

sections.title: Recording a check result
sections.explanation: This function holds the trust boundary. It locks the row and requires the reporting agent to hold the lease. The server re-normalizes `statusText` itself and accepts the client's `normalizedStatus` hint only when it agrees, so a bare 'Resolved' or 'Closed' scraped from a portal can never approve or pay a claim on the agent's word. `decideFollowUpStep` then sets the counters, stop reason and next check (aligned into the nightly window by `nextEligibleCheckAt`), and a history entry is appended to the JSONB array. When the ticket maps to a claim status, the claim row is locked and updated only if the status changes: rejections append the reason to remarks (preferring a note that starts with 'Rejected:'), approvals and payments parse a rupee amount into `approved_amount`, and each real change writes `claim_status_history`. An audit row is always written, and the returned `statusChanged` compares the new reading with the previous one.

sections.title: Dashboard listing and summary
sections.explanation: `listFollowUps` binds the caller's scope through `accountCondition` and can filter to active rows or a ticket or order search. One query computes the dashboard counters with `COUNT(*) FILTER (...)`: active, due now, due within 24 hours, resolved, stopped for another reason, and rows with errors. The page query sorts active rows first by next check, uses `COUNT(*) OVER()` for the total, and clamps the page size to 200. Rows are mapped to `FollowUpRow` with explicit null handling for the optional ids.

server/schema-claim-automation.sql.overview: Additive schema for claim automation: supplier portal credentials, automation agents, the claim job queue, extra snapshot columns on claims, seeded portal URLs and evidence templates, and the follow-up table for ticket tracking. Every statement is idempotent (`IF NOT EXISTS`, `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) and nothing is dropped, following the project rule that schema changes only add and never bump `SCHEMA_VERSION`. It is the storage behind tour step 11 and sits beside the base schema files from step 3.

sections.title: Marketplace credentials table
sections.explanation: The header restates the migration contract: additive, safe to re-run, no version bump. `marketplace_credentials` stores one supplier login per account in `username_encrypted` and `password_encrypted` (filled by the AES-256-GCM helpers in claim-automation-service.ts), an `auth_state` JSONB slot, and the automation switches `automation_mode`, `require_approval_before_submit` and `auto_prepare`. The marketplace foreign key uses `ON DELETE SET NULL`, and a partial unique index allows only one active row per account name, so a retired credential can stay in the table while a new one is active.

sections.title: Automation agents table
sections.explanation: `claim_automation_agents` records each desktop or server engine: a unique `agent_uuid`, host and version details, the last heartbeat with current task info, and `api_key_hash`, so only a hash of the agent key is stored. `registered_by_user_id` links the agent to the operator who enrolled it, which is where its account scope comes from. Note the `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` after `CREATE TABLE`: databases created before that column existed get it on the next run, which is the standard additive pattern in this project.

sections.title: Claim job queue table
sections.explanation: `claim_automation_jobs` is the queue the engine leases from. Each job references its claim with `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, so a claim with automation history cannot be deleted, while the credential and agent links fall back to null. It tracks the stage, attempts against `max_attempts` (default 3), the marketplace ticket, a screenshot path, the manual-action reason, a JSONB log and `lease_expires_at`. The partial index on `(stage, created_at)` for `queued` and `approved` rows matches the oldest-first lease query, and the partial lease index keeps expired-lease recovery cheap.

sections.title: Claim snapshot columns
sections.explanation: Seven columns are added to the existing `claims` table with `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` and non-null defaults: customer name, total price, shipped date, SKU, claim content, manual notes and an evidence summary. These snapshots let a claim keep the values used for filing even if lookup data changes later, the same idea as a scan keeping its own snapshot (rule 3).

sections.title: Seeded portal credentials
sections.explanation: This inserts a placeholder credential row for each known marketplace with its supplier portal URL, `assisted` mode, approval before submit and auto-prepare on, and no username or password. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` has no conflict target, so it also covers the partial unique index on account name; once a row exists the insert is a no-op and never overwrites credentials an Admin has saved.

sections.title: Default claim templates and evidence fields
sections.explanation: Each marketplace gets a 'Standard Claim Template', and a `CROSS JOIN (VALUES ...)` expands a template into evidence field slots with labels, types, required flags, counts and size limits. Flipkart gets images only, with no unpacking video. Watch the mismatch between comment and code: the comment says Meesho gets images plus video, but the first field insert filters on Myntra VB, Myntra EJ and Ajio only, so this file creates Meesho and Amazon template rows without any field slots. `ON CONFLICT (template_id, field_key) DO NOTHING` keeps the inserts idempotent.

sections.title: Follow-up tracking table
sections.explanation: `claim_automation_follow_ups` backs ticket tracking. A row stores the marketplace ticket, stage, `is_active` with a `stop_reason`, the last status read, the next check time and 48-hour interval, a check count and error streak, a lease and agent, and a JSONB history. The unique index on `claim_id` enforces one follow-up per claim, which is what lets `createFollowUpForJob` use `ON CONFLICT (claim_id)`. The partial index on `next_check_at` for active rows serves the due-check lease query, and a partial lease index supports reclaiming expired leases.

desktop-agent/src/desktop-app-server.ts.overview: The automation engine: one long-running Node process that owns the only claim-filing loop and the only ticket follow-up loop (rule 14) and serves an HTTP API for the Electron renderer, the headless Linux dashboard and remote clients. The Electron shell embeds this module and drives it through exported functions such as `engineStart`, `enginePause` and `engineRunOnceNow`, while remote clients reach the same state over HTTP behind the CORS allowlist and the bearer-token gate. It ties together the pieces of tour step 12 (agent-client.ts for the backend, poll-guard.ts so the loops never overlap, cycle-watchdog.ts so a hung cycle heals itself, engine-config.ts for the bind policy) and hands each job to a marketplace automation from step 13.

sections.title: Imports, engine state and busy guards
sections.explanation: All engine state lives in module-level variables that the worker loops, the HTTP routes and the Electron shell read together, so they cannot disagree. The flags are documented carefully: `isCurrentlyProcessing` is set only after a job is leased, `pollInFlight` covers the whole filing cycle, `portalTestInFlight` covers a supplier login test, and `followUpInFlight` covers a ticket check. `cycleGeneration` is bumped at the start of every cycle so a body abandoned by the watchdog can tell it is stale and stop before writing anything. `logger.onLog` fans each log entry out to Server-Sent Events subscribers. `engineBusy` and `supplierProfileInUse` feed these flags to the pure rules in poll-guard.ts, and `ensureViewForManualShow` refuses (409) to create a supplier view while the worker owns the profile.

sections.title: The filing poll cycle
sections.explanation: `pollAndProcessJob` runs one filing cycle. It asks `shouldRunPollCycle` whether a cycle may start (a manual Poll Now bypasses only the paused check) and wraps the work in a `runCycle` closure raced against `POLL_CYCLE_TIMEOUT_MS` by `withCycleTimeout`. Inside, it leases a job, refuses panels held for an operator, fetches the bundle, streams evidence to disk, opens the supplier browser and gets the marketplace class from the registry. The action is `submit` only when the backend-issued lease stage is `submitting`, so a saved login never authorizes submission (M9), and before a submit, or a prepare on an auto-submit account, it re-fetches the bundle and runs `isSafeToSubmitBundle` (F4). Generation checks before each side effect make an abandoned body quit quietly. Results map to prepared (browser kept open for approval), completed (`completeJob`, then evidence cleanup), manual intervention (an operator task) or not eligible. On timeout the callback clears the flags and releases the tab, and `submissionOutcomeUnknown` turns a lost completion acknowledgement into manual review instead of a plain failure.

sections.title: Follow-up assistance pass
sections.explanation: The section opens with two scheduler counters used later (`schedulerStarted`, `idlePolls`) and the follow-up worker's bookkeeping. `runFollowUpAssist` runs after a ticket check has already been reported and is advisory only: it never changes the report and never acts on the portal. It refreshes the local cache of approved recovery procedures when stale, prefers an approved procedure matching the error signature, then tries AI Center routing, then a direct provider call whose proposal must pass `validateAiProposal`, and otherwise files an operator task. Every failure is caught and logged. One gotcha is visible in `ASSIST_SYSTEM_PROMPT`: the second line starts with `+` after a trailing `+`, so JavaScript applies unary plus to the second string and the prompt ends with `NaN` instead of the 'Never invent ticket IDs' sentence.

sections.title: The follow-up worker cycle
sections.explanation: `pollAndProcessFollowUp` checks one ticket. It runs only while the worker is running, the engine is idle and no login browser is held, and it skips outside the 01:00-02:00 IST window when nightly-only mode is on (`nightlyFollowUpOnly()`, the `FOLLOW_UP_NIGHTLY_ONLY` switch in AGENTS.md). It sets `followUpInFlight`, which blocks filing cycles until it finishes. Inside a `runCheck` closure raced against `FOLLOW_UP_CYCLE_TIMEOUT_MS`, it leases a due ticket, reports `login_required` when the panel has no saved session and `not_supported` for an unknown marketplace without opening a browser, and otherwise opens the panel profile and calls the class's `checkClaimStatus`. An empty status is reported as `not_found`; a read status goes up with its hint and note. On timeout or error the leased ticket is reported as `error` so the server reschedules it instead of waiting for the lease to expire. `scheduleNextFollowUp` keeps its own timer chain and lets it lapse when the worker pauses.

sections.title: Poll cadence and scheduler
sections.explanation: `pollDelayMs` polls faster after real work (half the interval, at least 5 seconds) and backs off to double and then triple the interval as the queue stays empty, keeping an idle PC within the low-spec CPU budget (rule 13). `scheduleNextPoll` keeps `pollTimer` non-null for the life of the chain so a resume cannot start a second chain, with `pollInFlight` as the second guard. `engineRunOnceNow` is Poll Now: while running it only nudges the chain, and while paused it queues one manual cycle on `manualRunChain` so back-to-back requests each get their own cycle and the pause holds. `startScheduler` starts the countdown and heartbeat intervals once, then the filing chain and the follow-up chain, whose first look-up runs about 10 seconds after start so overdue tickets are caught right after sign-in.

sections.title: Server-rendered dashboard HTML
sections.explanation: `getDashboardHtml` returns a complete single-page dashboard as one template string: sign-in, status and KPI cards, the panels and follow-up tables, the AI Center and AI memory views and a live log, with inline scripts that call the engine's own `/api/*` routes and refresh on intervals. The engine serves it at `GET /` for headless Linux deployments opened in a browser. The Windows desktop app never loads it; its window shows the bundled React renderer at `returnapp://desktop` instead (rule 17), so desktop UI changes belong in desktop/renderer, not here.

sections.title: Operator session and control surface
sections.explanation: Only an Admin or Supervisor may run the claim bot (`canRunClaimBot`). `readJson` caps request bodies at 20,000 characters and destroys the request beyond that. `portalBrowserSnapshot` returns the multi-tab supplier browser state while keeping the older top-level fields so legacy callers do not break. `beginClaimWork` registers the agent, marks AI Center tasks interrupted by a restart, and starts the scheduler, and `resumeClaimBotIfSignedIn` restarts the 24/7 bot at boot when a saved operator session exists. The exported control functions (`engineStatus`, `engineStart`, a no-op until someone is signed in, `enginePause`, `engineSetBackendUrl` and `engineBindInfo`) are what the Electron shell calls directly, reading the same variables as the HTTP routes.

sections.title: Server bootstrap, CORS and auth gates
sections.explanation: `startDesktopAppServer` installs crash guards before anything can throw and prunes the evidence cache once at startup. Each request gets CORS headers only for an origin allowed by `corsAllowedOrigin` (`returnapp://desktop`, the Vite dev origins outside production, and `ENGINE_CORS_ORIGINS`), and `OPTIONS` preflights to `/api/*` are answered with 204 before the token gate because a preflight carries no `Authorization` header (rule 18). `/api/health` is the only unauthenticated route and reports liveness only. Then comes the fail-closed gate: on a remote bind every other route needs a bearer token that `engineTokenMatches` compares in constant time (rule 15). The detailed `/api/v1/engine/info`, the dashboard at `/`, `/api/status`, and the operator session, login and logout routes follow; login signs out a user without the right role and returns 403, and logout pauses the worker.

sections.title: Feature routes
sections.explanation: Every remaining route checks `operatorSignedIn` first. Evidence routes stream files from the local cache after path validation and never call the backend, so they keep working offline. `/api/follow-ups` passes a failed backend read through as an error instead of an empty list. The scheduler routes accept an explicit `action=start|pause` so a stale menu label cannot flip the state the wrong way, and Poll Now never resumes a paused worker. Routes that would open a browser on a supplier profile respect the guards: a login test returns 409 while the engine is busy, sets `portalTestInFlight`, pauses the poller and restores it afterwards, and `run-one` refuses while the profile is in use. The `/api/portal-browser/*` routes manage the embedded supplier tabs (open, show, switch, close with the worker guard, detach, dock, focus). `test-claim` returns 404 in production, `/api/config` signs the operator out when the backend URL changes so the old token never reaches a new server, and `/api/logs/stream` serves Server-Sent Events. The server then listens on the resolved bind.

sections.title: Window spawner and entry point
sections.explanation: `launchAppWindow` opens the engine URL in a system Chromium-family browser in `--app` mode as a detached, unreferenced child process, and only logs a hint when no browser is found. `main` resolves the bind, starts the server, resumes the bot if an operator is already signed in, and opens the window only in local mode without `--no-window` or `HEADLESS=true`, so a server deployment never opens one. It uses `localEngineUrl(bind)` rather than a hardcoded 127.0.0.1 so an IPv6-only loopback bind still works. The final guard runs `main` only when this file is the process entry point, so the Electron shell can import the module without starting it twice.

desktop-agent/src/agent-client.ts.overview: The engine's HTTP client for the Return App server. `AgentBackendClient` registers the agent, sends heartbeats, leases claim jobs and follow-up ticket checks, fetches execution bundles, streams evidence files to disk with integrity checks, and reports progress, completion and follow-up results. It also carries a few dashboard reads made with the operator's bearer token. It is the part of tour step 12 that registers, sends heartbeats, leases work and streams evidence to disk, and the client side of the agent API in server/claim-automation-routes.ts.

sections.title: Wire types
sections.explanation: These types mirror the server's agent API: `JobPollResult` and `FollowUpPollResult` for leases, `FollowUpOutcome` and `FollowUpReport` matching the server's closed outcome list, and `JobExecutionBundle`, the claim payload returned by `getJobExecutionBundle` on the server, including credentials and evidence metadata with size and content hash. `FollowUpListResult` carries an explicit `ok` and `error`, so a failed read can never be shown as 'nothing is tracked'. The imports show the two kinds of auth: `operatorAuthorization()` for operator-signed requests and the saved agent config for agent requests.

sections.title: Registration
sections.explanation: The client keeps the agent key in memory and tracks `isRegistered`. `register` is the one agent call that uses the operator's bearer token, because the server requires a Supervisor or Admin session to enrol an agent. It sends the agent UUID, name, hostname, platform and version, then saves the key the server returns into the agent config so later calls authenticate with it. Any failure leaves `isRegistered` false and returns `false` instead of throwing, so callers simply try again later.

sections.title: Heartbeat and job polling
sections.explanation: Agent calls authenticate with the `X-Agent-UUID` and `X-Agent-Key` headers, and both methods register first when needed. A 401 or 404 response clears `isRegistered`, so the next call re-registers, which recovers automatically when the server no longer knows the agent or its key. Heartbeats fail silently on network jitter, and `pollJob` turns any failure into `{ hasJob: false }`, so a network problem looks like an empty queue to the worker loop instead of an exception.

sections.title: Follow-up polling and reporting
sections.explanation: `pollFollowUp` asks for the next due ticket check and, like `pollJob`, treats failure as 'nothing due'; most cycles return empty because the server only hands out a row when a check is due. `reportFollowUp` behaves differently: it throws on a non-OK response, so the engine knows the report did not land. It returns `statusChanged` from the server's answer, which the worker uses to skip the assistance pass when nothing changed.

sections.title: AI memory, tasks and ledgers
sections.explanation: These calls support the advisory AI features and all degrade gracefully. `getApprovedProcedures` returns `null` on failure so the caller keeps its local cache, and filters out malformed rows. `createOperatorTask` files a task the worker cannot finish alone and returns its id or `null`. `reportAgentRun` and `reportUsage` send ledger rows and only log on failure. None of them throws, because they run after the important report has already been sent.

sections.title: Bundles and evidence download
sections.explanation: `getExecutionBundle` fetches the job's claim payload and returns `null` on failure. `downloadEvidenceFiles` writes each file under `workDir/claim-<id>/` with a name built from the file id, field key and `path.basename` of the original name, which blocks path tricks in filenames. A file already present with the right size and SHA-256 hash is reused. Otherwise the response body is streamed with `pipeline` into a `.part` file (never buffered in memory, per rule 13), checked for size and hash, and renamed into place only after it verifies. If fewer files arrive than expected the method throws, so the claim is retried instead of filed with missing evidence.

sections.title: Evidence cleanup and pruning
sections.explanation: `cleanClaimEvidenceFiles` deletes a claim's downloaded evidence after the job settles but keeps the screenshots the job references, so operators can still inspect them. `pruneOldEvidenceFiles` removes any `claim-*` directory older than 24 hours by default, enforcing the 24-hour cache rule; the engine calls it once at startup. Both log and continue on errors instead of throwing.

sections.title: Progress, completion and connection test
sections.explanation: `updateProgress` and `completeJob` post to the job routes with agent headers and rethrow on failure. That matters for completion: the engine sets `submissionOutcomeUnknown` around `completeJob`, so a lost acknowledgement after the portal has issued a ticket becomes a manual check instead of a silent retry. `testConnection` pings the server's `/api/health` without credentials and reports status and latency, which lets a signed-out operator spot a wrong backend URL.

sections.title: Dashboard reads
sections.explanation: `getFollowUps` is an operator read, so it sends the operator's bearer token instead of the agent key. Every failure is reported as a failure with a status and message: no sign-in, a refused token (reported as 401 so the dashboard asks for a new sign-in), a server error mapped to 502, or an unreachable server mapped to 503. Returning an empty list instead would make the dashboard claim no tickets are tracked, which the comment compares to reporting an unrun check as passed. `getRecentJobs` reloads the agent key from config before each call and returns an empty page on failure.

desktop-agent/src/poll-guard.ts.overview: Pure decision functions that keep the engine's two worker loops and its browser-opening routes from colliding on the same supplier browser profile. They take plain state flags and return a boolean, so the rules can be unit-tested without a server or a browser; desktop-app-server.ts calls them with its live flags. This is the part of tour step 12 that keeps the loops from running at the same time, and it implements the rule that a follow-up check and a filing cycle block each other (rule 14).

sections.title: State shape
sections.explanation: The header records why these rules were pulled out: two review findings on PR #35, namely that a manual Poll Now must run one cycle even while paused, and that a route must notice a cycle in flight, not only a job being processed. `PollCycleState` names every condition that can own the supplier profile: the worker switch, a cycle in flight, a held login browser, a running login test and a running follow-up check, plus whether the request is a manual one-shot. The comments explain why each flag is separate; for example, a login test forces the worker off, so without its own flag a manual one-shot could slip past the paused check.

sections.title: shouldRunPollCycle
sections.explanation: A poll cycle may start only when nothing else owns the profile. The `manual` flag bypasses only the paused check; an overlapping cycle, a held login browser, a login test and a follow-up check still block it, because they all drive the same profile and debug port. Writing the rule as a series of early returns makes each condition easy to test on its own.

sections.title: engineBusy
sections.explanation: `engineBusy` is the test for routes that would start a browser on a supplier profile. `isCurrentlyProcessing` alone is not enough: it is set only after the lease returns, which leaves a window where the engine looks idle but is about to launch a browser. Adding `pollInFlight`, the login test flag and the follow-up flag closes that window. The optional flags go through `Boolean()` so missing values count as false.

sections.title: supplierProfileInUse
sections.explanation: This adds the third case: a browser left open by the manual-login flow. The poll cycle will not run while that browser is held, so a route that queues work for the profile, such as `run-one`, must refuse too; otherwise the claim would be accepted and then never picked up.

desktop-agent/src/cycle-watchdog.ts.overview: A small per-cycle watchdog for the engine's filing and follow-up loops, written after the 2026-11-17 incident in which a hung backend fetch during an internet outage left `pollInFlight` set and silenced both loops with no error logged. `withCycleTimeout` races a cycle against a hard ceiling so any hung await heals itself. It is the part of tour step 12 that keeps a hung network call from silencing the bot, and desktop-app-server.ts wraps both loops with it.

sections.title: Incident context
sections.explanation: The header explains the failure mode: every later poll and follow-up cycle is gated on in-flight flags, so one cycle that never returns stops everything quietly. The fix is to race each cycle against a timeout whose callback force-resets those flags, after which the loops resume at their normal cadence.

sections.title: Sentinel and ceilings
sections.explanation: `CYCLE_TIMEOUT` is a `unique symbol`, so no value a cycle returns can be mistaken for the timeout result, and TypeScript can narrow on it with a simple equality check. The ceilings are 20 minutes for a filing cycle (lease through browser teardown) and 8 minutes for a follow-up ticket check.

sections.title: withCycleTimeout
sections.explanation: The function wraps the cycle in a new promise guarded by a `settled` flag. If the timer fires first, `onTimeout` runs once, synchronously, before the sentinel resolves, and anything it throws is swallowed so the watchdog never throws into the worker loop. If the cycle settles first, the timer is cleared and its value or error passes through. A cycle that settles after the timeout is ignored, including a late rejection, so it cannot surface as an unhandled error. `timer.unref()` stops the watchdog timer from keeping the 24/7 process alive on its own. The cycle body itself is not cancelled, which is why the engine also checks `cycleGeneration` before any side effect.

desktop-agent/src/engine-config.ts.overview: The engine's bind and remote-access policy. It resolves host and port from the environment and fails closed: a loopback bind runs in local mode with no token, while any other bind requires an `ENGINE_TOKEN` of at least 24 characters or the engine refuses to start. It also provides constant-time token checks, bearer-header parsing and URL helpers used by the engine and the Electron shell. This is the part of tour step 12 that refuses a reachable bind without a strong token, implementing rule 15.

sections.title: Policy, defaults and types
sections.explanation: The header states the fail-closed rule for the three places the engine runs (a warehouse PC, a networked Linux server, a container) and promises that this module never logs the token or writes it to a config file. Defaults are host 127.0.0.1, port 3005 and a minimum token length of 24. `EngineBind` records the mode, whether the socket is reachable from outside, and the token, which stays empty in local mode.

sections.title: Resolving the bind
sections.explanation: `isLoopbackHost` recognises 127.0.0.1, ::1 and localhost after trimming and lowercasing. `parseEnginePort` falls back to the default when unset and throws on anything that is not an integer between 1 and 65535. `resolveEngineBind` reads `ENGINE_HOST`, `ENGINE_PORT` and `ENGINE_TOKEN` (taking the environment as a parameter so tests can pass their own) and throws a clear error when a non-loopback host is requested with a short or missing token. The process exits rather than expose the claim queue and supplier profiles anonymously, and the token is kept only in remote mode.

sections.title: Token checks
sections.explanation: `engineTokenMatches` treats an empty expected token as local mode and always matches. Otherwise it compares with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, after a length check because that function requires equal-length buffers, so response timing does not reveal how much of a guessed token was right. `bearerTokenFromHeader` accepts only an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header, case-insensitively; there is no query-string path for the token.

sections.title: Client URL helpers
sections.explanation: A bind host is not always an address a client can dial. `clientHostForBind` maps the wildcard binds 0.0.0.0 and :: to the matching loopback, since a URL like `http://0.0.0.0:3005/` is not routable. `localEngineUrl` wraps IPv6 literals in brackets, so an engine bound only to ::1 gets a working URL instead of one hardcoded to 127.0.0.1. `bareHostname` strips the brackets the WHATWG URL parser keeps on IPv6 hostnames.

sections.title: URL safety checks
sections.explanation: `isInsecureRemoteUrl` flags a plain `http:` URL to any non-loopback host: the engine token is a long-lived shared secret, so the shell refuses such a target instead of sending it in clear text, while plain http to loopback (a local engine or an SSH tunnel) is allowed. `isSameOrigin` compares parsed origins instead of string prefixes; the comment shows why, since `http://127.0.0.1:3005.evil.com/` and `http://127.0.0.1:30051/` both start with the expected origin text but are a different host or port. Both functions return `false` for URLs that do not parse.

desktop-agent/src/marketplaces/registry..overview: The factory that picks a marketplace automation class by name. Given a marketplace label, it returns the matching subclass of `BaseMarketplaceAutomation` (Meesho, Flipkart, Amazon, Myntra or Ajio), built with the browser, the job bundle, the evidence map and a work directory. The engine uses it for both filing and follow-up checks, which is how one interface serves every supplier panel in tour step 13.

sections.title: Supported marketplaces
sections.explanation: The registry imports the five concrete classes and the shared types. `SUPPORTED_MARKETPLACE_KEYS` is a readonly tuple, and `isMarketplaceSupported` lowercases the name and checks whether any key appears in it, so labels like 'Myntra VB' and 'Myntra EJ' both match 'myntra'. The follow-up worker calls it before opening a browser, so an unknown marketplace is reported as not supported without launching a window.

sections.title: getAutomationEngine factory
sections.explanation: The factory uses the same lowercase substring matching and builds the matching class with identical constructor arguments, which is what lets the engine call `execute()` or `checkClaimStatus()` without knowing which marketplace it has. An unknown marketplace throws with a message pointing to assisted manual filing; the follow-up worker catches that and reports `not_supported`.

desktop-agent/src/marketplaces/base-auto.overview: Defines the contract every supplier panel automation implements: the abstract `BaseMarketplaceAutomation` class, the result type for filing a claim, the result type for checking a ticket, and shared helpers for waiting on the page and for human-like typing, clicking and file uploads through the browser adapter. Subclasses such as meesho.ts supply the portal steps. It is the template-method half of tour step 13, with registry.ts as the factory half.

sections.title: Filing result type
sections.explanation: `MarketplaceAutomationResult` is what `execute()` returns. Its `stage` values line up with the job stages the server accepts: `prepared` (waiting for approval), `completed` with a `marketplaceClaimId`, `manual_intervention_required` with a reason, `not_eligible` when the marketplace refuses the order (the comment cites Meesho's packaging policy: the bot keeps it for manual review and moves on), and `failed`. A screenshot path can accompany any of them.

sections.title: Ticket check result type
sections.explanation: `ClaimStatusCheckResult` is a discriminated union on `supported`. `supported: false` carries only a reason and tells the server to stop chasing the ticket. `supported: true` carries the raw `statusText` exactly as the portal shows it, because the server does the authoritative normalization, plus an optional `normalizedStatus` hint, a screenshot path and a note.

sections.title: Abstract class and constructor
sections.explanation: Each subclass declares a `marketplaceName` and implements `execute('prepare' | 'submit')`. The constructor uses TypeScript parameter properties to store the browser, job bundle, evidence map and work directory as protected fields, and falls back to an empty map and the OS temp directory when callers pass nothing usable.

sections.title: Default checkClaimStatus
sections.explanation: The default implementation answers `supported: false` with a 'not implemented' reason. Combined with the server's rule that `not_supported` stops a follow-up, a marketplace without a status reader never has its portal opened every two days for nothing. Overriding this method in a subclass, as meesho.ts does, is all it takes to turn on ticket tracking for that marketplace.

sections.title: Waiting helpers
sections.explanation: `delay` defers to the browser adapter. `waitForSelector` polls `document.querySelector` every 500 ms until the element exists or the timeout (15 seconds by default) runs out, embedding the selector with `JSON.stringify` so quotes inside it cannot break the evaluated script. `waitForContent` waits until the page body has more than 40 characters of text, a cheap signal that a client-rendered portal page has loaded. Both return a boolean instead of throwing, so callers decide how to react.

sections.title: Human-like input helpers
sections.explanation: `humanType`, `humanClick` and `uploadFiles` log what they do (the character count, never the typed text) and delegate to the adapter's `humanType`, `humanClick` and `setFileInputFiles`. `typeText` and `clickElement` are void-returning aliases for subclasses that do not need the boolean result.

desktop-agent/src/marketplaces/meesho.ts.overview: The fully automatic Meesho supplier panel automation. `MeeshoAutomation.execute` signs in, opens Support, refuses to file a duplicate, navigates to the right Returns category, fills the Raise a Ticket form, uploads evidence with portal-acknowledgement checks, and either stops at `prepared` for approval or submits and captures the new ticket ID. `checkClaimStatus` reads a filed ticket from its per-ticket deep link with a deterministic classifier and falls back to the Support table. The pure parsing and validation helpers at the top are exported so fixtures can test them without a browser. This is the fully automatic implementation described in tour step 13.

sections.title: Portal category and packet mappings
sections.explanation: `MEESHO_PORTAL_ISSUE_LABELS` maps claim issue codes to the exact text of Meesho's Raise a Ticket categories, naming server/meesho-claims.ts as the authority. `resolveMeeshoIssueLabel` returns `null` for an unmapped code, and `resolveMeeshoPacketLabel` accepts only 'intact' or 'tampered'. Returning `null` instead of a default is deliberate: `execute` stops for human review rather than filing a wrong-return claim or guessing the parcel condition.

sections.title: Support-table parsers
sections.explanation: These pure functions work on table rows already read from the page as arrays of cell text. `findExistingTicketForOrder` collects 9- to 15-digit runs from the order references and reports a row as already filed only when it contains one of them and a different digit run, so order or AWB numbers are never mistaken for ticket IDs. `parseMeeshoTicketRow` finds a ticket's row and returns the other cells as status text, adding a hint only for clear paid, rejected or approved wording; a bare 'Resolved' row is left for the server to judge. `extractMeeshoResolution` pulls an approved rupee amount and a rejection reason out of free text with ordered regular expressions, keeping reasons between 6 and 499 characters.

sections.title: Ticket page classifier
sections.explanation: The per-ticket page classifier only reports status keys the server understands. There is no separate 'response needed' state: action-required wording maps to `under_review`, the server's own bucket for it, with the matched phrase kept in `statusText`. `TICKET_PAGE_STATUS_CLASSES` is checked in priority order with rejection first, and the comments say it was ported from the operator's legacy meesho_tracker.py. `classifyMeeshoTicketPageText` scans short chip-like lines (60 characters or fewer) before all lines, since status chips are more reliable than body text, and returns the matched line capped at 200 characters. `pickLongestTicketText` keeps the longest candidate text, capped at 8,000 characters.

sections.title: Upload rules and early blockers
sections.explanation: The comment block records a production incident: Meesho resets its file inputs after an upload, so `input.files.length` alone does not prove an upload worked, and an attachment counts only when the local file exists and the portal acknowledges it. `resolveMeeshoUploadField` maps an input id to an evidence field, and `checkMeeshoEvidenceFileLocal` checks the file exists, is not empty, is at most 50 MB and has an accepted extension. `validateMeeshoVideoForUpload` enforces the portal's .mp4-only, 23 MB video rule (with 512 KiB of tolerance for MB/MiB rounding) before any attempt. `detectMeeshoEarlyBlocker` matches visible portal messages such as 'ticket already exists' or 'not eligible' that mean the claim must not be filed.

sections.title: execute: guards, sign-in, duplicate check
sections.explanation: `execute` fails fast before touching the browser: without a verified category or a verified Intact/Tampered parcel state it returns `manual_intervention_required` with an explanation. It then signs in through `completePortalLogin`, taking a screenshot if that fails, extracts the seller slug from the panel URL and opens the Support page. It records the ticket IDs listed before filing, which is how a new ticket is recognised later, and uses `findExistingTicketForOrder` to refuse a second ticket for an order Meesho already shows (finding F7).

sections.title: execute: category navigation and form
sections.explanation: Before opening an issue page the code needs a verified return type: RTO or courier returns (every `wrong_barcode_rto` claim counts as RTO) versus customer returns, and an unverified type stops for operator review. It navigates to the Returns/RTO category at `/support/1`, clicks the matching subcategory tab, and opens the issue by alternating a visible-label click with a DOM click (following the link's href if needed) for up to six attempts. Raise a Ticket is opened the same way, and success is detected by the sub-order input appearing. Every dead end returns a specific reason telling the operator what to do in the open browser.

sections.title: execute: form fields and eligibility
sections.explanation: The bot types the sub-order ID and, when the fields exist, the AWB and packet ID, then clicks a Check, Verify or Search button so Meesho validates the order. Two eligibility checks follow: `readIneligibleMessage` looks for an error-styled 'not eligible' message under a field, and `readEarlyBlockerMessage` scans for the broader skip messages. Either one returns `not_eligible` with a screenshot, so the order is kept for review and never claimed. The 'State of the packet' listbox is set by an in-page script that opens the dropdown and clicks the exact option, with three attempts. The callback number is filled only from an optional bundle value, using the native value setter followed by `input` and `change` events so the form notices the programmatic value; the bot never invents a number. A flyer or barcode field, if present, gets the packet ID or AWB.

sections.title: execute: evidence uploads, description
sections.explanation: If no evidence was downloaded the run stops without filing. For each file input on the form, the code picks that box's files from the evidence map by field (falling back to filename keywords, or one unused image for unknown boxes), and only the optional attachments box may be skipped when empty. Video boxes go through the .mp4/23 MB gate first, every file then gets the local pre-flight, and there is a single attach attempt with no blind retries when the outcome is uncertain. Acknowledgement is read near the input: a file count, a file name, a thumbnail or a success word, with no error text. Any unverified box, or a form with no upload boxes, returns `manual_intervention_required` naming each failed field and leaves the browser open for recovery. The description goes into the last visible textarea, which the code tags with a temporary id so `humanType` can target it.

sections.title: execute: prepare, submit, ticket capture
sections.explanation: A screenshot of the filled form is always taken. A `prepare` run on an account that requires approval stops here with `prepared`; only a `submit` run, or a run on an auto-submit account, continues. The code waits up to 20 seconds for Submit to become enabled, and if it stays disabled it reports the field errors or empty fields, as `not_eligible` when the text contains a blocker message. After clicking Submit, a ticket counts only if Meesho shows a new 9- to 15-digit number that was not listed before and is not one of the claim's own reference numbers. If none appears on the page the Support table is read again, and if there is still no new ticket the run returns `manual_intervention_required` instead of guessing.

sections.title: Page readers and ticket status check
sections.explanation: `readIneligibleMessage` polls for up to 5 seconds for a 'not eligible' message styled as an error by class name or by a red computed text colour, and `readEarlyBlockerMessage` takes one sample of short visible leaf texts. `checkClaimStatus`, the override that turns on Meesho ticket tracking, first opens the per-ticket deep link `.../support/ticket/{id}` and classifies the page text; for rejections and approvals it adds the reason or amount from `extractMeeshoResolution` to the status text and note. If the page gives no clear status it falls back to the Support table, clicking 'My tickets' if needed and opening the row's detail drawer to capture a rejection reason. Any exception still returns `supported: true` with an error note and empty status text, which the engine reports as `not_found`. `readTicketTableRows` and `readRecentTicketIds` read the table cells and the numeric ticket IDs that `execute` relies on.

desktop-agent/src/browser-runner.ts.overview: `BrowserRunner` is the engine's low-level Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) driver for a system Chromium browser (Edge, Chrome or Chromium). It finds a browser binary for each OS, spawns it with its own user-data profile and a remote-debugging port, speaks raw CDP JSON-RPC over a WebSocket, and provides human-like typing, clicking and file-upload helpers that the marketplace automation classes from tour step 13 build on. Its `close()` method stops the whole browser process tree (`taskkill /T /F` on Windows, a process-group kill on POSIX), which is how the project follows the AGENTS.md rule that no supplier browser child may outlive a claim. Its launch error message shows this is the external-browser path: the desktop app uses its bundled browser unless `BROWSER_ADAPTER` forces the external one, and headless Linux servers use it with the distro's Chromium.

sections.title: PATH lookup helper
sections.explanation: The imports bring in the sandbox-flag helpers from `browser-flags.ts` and the shared logger. `whichBinaries()` runs `where` on Windows or `command -v` on POSIX for each candidate name, takes the first line of output, and returns it if the file exists, or if it is a bare command name with no path separator. Errors are swallowed on purpose: a missing binary just falls through to the next name, so browser discovery never throws.

sections.title: System browser discovery
sections.explanation: `findSystemBrowser()` looks for the executable in a fixed order. An explicit `BROWSER_PATH` override always wins if the file exists; the comment mentions warehouse PCs with custom install paths, and the Linux engine image sets it too. On Windows, Edge is tried before Chrome because every modern Windows install ships with it. macOS checks the standard `.app` bundles, and every other POSIX system walks the common `/usr/bin`, `/snap` and `/opt` locations. Each branch ends with a PATH lookup through `whichBinaries()`, and `null` means no compatible browser was found.

sections.title: Session type and runner state
sections.explanation: `BrowserSession` is what `launch()` returns: the child process, the DevTools WebSocket URL, the resolved profile directory and the debug port. The class holds one page-level WebSocket, the spawned process, the port and the profile path, plus an ever-increasing message `id` and a `pendingCallbacks` map keyed by that id. That map is the entire mechanism `send()` uses to match each CDP response to its request.

sections.title: Launching Chromium with a profile
sections.explanation: `launch()` resolves the browser, creates the per-panel profile directory if needed, and builds the command line. That includes remote debugging on the chosen port (default 9222), a separate `--user-data-dir` so each supplier panel keeps its own cookies, anti-automation and low-resource flags, and a 256 MB V8 heap cap in line with the hardware rule. Sandbox handling goes through `browserSandboxArgs()`, which adds `--no-sandbox` only when `BROWSER_NO_SANDBOX=1` is set or when running as root on Linux, because supplier pages are untrusted. On POSIX the process is spawned `detached`, which gives it its own process group for `close()` to kill. The method then polls `/json/version` every 500 ms for up to 15 seconds to get the `webSocketDebuggerUrl`. If the endpoint never appears, it kills the process and throws.

sections.title: CDP connection and JSON-RPC
sections.explanation: `connectToPage()` lists the targets on the debug port, prefers the first `page` target, opens a WebSocket to it and waits for the open event. One message handler matches each response's `id` against `pendingCallbacks` and resolves or rejects the stored promise; unparseable frames and CDP events are ignored. It then enables the `Page`, `Runtime` and `DOM` domains. `send()` takes the next id, registers the callbacks and writes the JSON frame. It has no timeout of its own, so if a reply never arrives the promise stays pending. The engine's per-cycle watchdog (tour step 12) is what puts a limit on a hung call.

sections.title: Navigation, evaluation, challenge detection
sections.explanation: `navigate()` sends `Page.navigate` and then sleeps a fixed 3 seconds instead of waiting for a load event. This is simple, but it depends on pages loading within that time. `evaluate()` wraps `Runtime.evaluate` with `returnByValue` and `awaitPromise`, so injected scripts can return plain JSON or await a promise. `captureScreenshot()` decodes the base64 PNG and writes it to disk as evidence. `detectCaptchaOrOtp()` checks the page text and DOM for CAPTCHA iframes or OTP inputs, so the automation can stop and hand over to a human instead of trying to get past the challenge.

sections.title: Human-like typing
sections.explanation: `humanType()` focuses and selects the target element. It then clears it through the native `value` setter taken from the `HTMLInputElement` or `HTMLTextAreaElement` prototype and dispatches `input` and `change` events, the usual way to make a React-controlled input register a programmatic change. Next it types one character at a time with CDP `Input.dispatchKeyEvent`. After every keystroke it sets the intended text so far through the native setter again, so the field ends up correct even if a key event was dropped. Random 40-90 ms gaps between keys and a 1-second pause at the end imitate human typing speed. Selectors and text are inserted into the script with `JSON.stringify`, which keeps them safely quoted.

sections.title: Click helpers
sections.explanation: Five click strategies handle different portal markup. `clickByTextIncludes()` and `clickByExactText()` walk the whole DOM, including open shadow roots, prefer leaf nodes whose text matches, and click the nearest `a`, `button` or `[role=button]` ancestor. `clickVisibleLabel()` picks the smallest visible element whose text matches exactly and sends real CDP mouse events at its centre. `clickLabelInDom()` climbs up to eight ancestors, crossing shadow-root hosts, to find a link or a pointer-styled target, then dispatches a full pointer and mouse event sequence and returns any `href`. `humanClick()` moves the mouse to the element's centre in two `mouseMoved` steps from a random offset, calls `el.click()`, and waits 1 second for the page to settle.

sections.title: File upload helpers
sections.explanation: `uploadViaChooser()` opens a separate browser-level CDP WebSocket, attaches to the page target with `flatten: true` to get a `sessionId`, and turns on `Page.setInterceptFileChooserDialog`. It clicks the button with the given label using real mouse events, waits up to 8 seconds for `Page.fileChooserOpened` to report a `backendNodeId`, and fills that input with `DOM.setFileInputFiles`, so no native file dialog ever opens. The socket is always closed in `finally`. `setFileInputFiles()` handles plain file inputs. It first installs a one-time patch on `HTMLInputElement.prototype.dispatchEvent` that passes `change` events to the element's React `onChange` prop, then finds the element with `DOM.querySelector` and sets the files directly. Both helpers return `false` instead of throwing, so the caller can try another approach.

sections.title: Process-tree teardown
sections.explanation: `close()` first asks the browser to exit with `Browser.close`, swallowing any error. Because `send()` has no timeout, this step depends on the browser replying. It then closes the socket and waits 1.5 seconds so the profile can write its cookies to disk. Finally it kills the whole process tree. On Windows it runs `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F` and falls back to `SIGKILL`. On POSIX it sends `SIGTERM` to the negative pid (the process group created by the detached spawn), then `SIGKILL` after 1.5 seconds, with `pkill -P` as a last resort. This is the code behind the AGENTS.md rule that every supplier browser must be stopped with full process-tree signals so nothing is left running on 4 GB terminals.

desktop-agent/src/submit-guard.ts.overview: A small, pure module that decides at the last moment, just before the engine clicks Submit on a supplier portal, whether a claim job is still safe to file. Minutes can pass between leasing a job and submitting it, so the engine fetches the job bundle again and runs `isSafeToSubmitBundle()`. Anything that is not actively fileable stops the run before the portal is touched. The module is fail-closed by design and mirrors the checks the server repeats atomically in `completeJobSubmission` (tour step 11). It is how tour step 13 makes sure a stale or already-resolved claim is never filed.

sections.title: Design rationale header
sections.explanation: The doc comment describes the race the guard closes: while evidence downloads and the browser works, an operator may retry the job, another agent may file it, or the claim may get an outcome. It states two principles. The guard is fail-closed: an unknown stage or status aborts. It is also a second layer of defence: the server checks the same conditions again, but this gate stops a real portal ticket from being filed only for the server to reject it with 409. The M9 note records the authorization fix: a saved supplier login or local cookie state never counts as approval to submit.
