sections.title: Stage and status sets
sections.explanation: Three `ReadonlySet` constants hold the policy as data. `SUBMIT_BLOCKED_JOB_STAGES` lists job stages that mean this run has lost its lease or the job is finished: `queued` after a retry, `completed`, `failed`, `not_eligible` and `manual_intervention_required`. `SUBMIT_BLOCKED_CLAIM_STATUSES` lists claim states that already record an outcome, where filing again would create a duplicate ticket. `SUBMITTABLE_CLAIM_STATUSES` is an explicit allowlist that mirrors the server's lease allowlist. Having an allowlist as well as a denylist is what makes a new or unknown status fail closed. Because the sets are exported, tests and other modules use the same names.

sections.title: isSafeToSubmitBundle gate
sections.explanation:
The function trims the stage and claim status to plain strings and returns a discriminated union: `{ ok: true }`, or `{ ok: false, reason }` with a reason an operator can read. The checks run in this order:

- A missing stage means the job no longer exists.
- When `approvalRequired` is true (the default), only the backend-issued `submitting` stage authorizes the click.
- A blocked stage stops the run.
- An empty claim status stops the run.
- A recorded outcome stops the run.
- Anything outside the submittable allowlist stops the run.

For auto-submit accounts `approvalRequired` is false: the credential flag is the standing authorization, and the gate checks only that the job is current and has no recorded outcome. The function is pure, with no I/O, so it is easy to unit-test (`desktop-agent/submit-guard.test.ts` is in the `npm test` list).

desktop/main.ts.overview: The Electron main process for the Windows desktop claim bot. It tunes Chromium for 4 GB / 2-core PCs, serves the bundled React renderer over the privileged `returnapp://desktop` scheme, and either starts the automation engine in-process or connects to a remote engine set by `RETURN_ENGINE_URL`. It also hosts the supplier browser views in the main window or in hardened detached windows, and runs the tray, the IPC handlers behind `preload.cjs`, the update downloads, and the self-healing logic (renderer reloads, engine start retries) that a 24/7 bot needs. It is the centre of tour step 14 and the client of the engine from step 12: it never runs a worker loop of its own.

sections.title: Imports and low-spec switches
sections.explanation: The first import loads the engine's environment settings before anything else runs. The engine functions (start, pause, run once, status) and the native browser-view host API are imported directly from `desktop-agent`, because a local engine runs inside this process. The command-line switches cap the V8 heap at 256 MB, limit renderer processes to two, disable native window occlusion, and turn off the `AutomationControlled` blink feature so supplier anti-bot systems do not flag the embedded browser. `userAgentFallback` is set to a standard Chrome user agent for the same reason. Module-level state holds the window, the tray, the `isQuitting` flag that tells a real quit apart from close-to-tray, and the `--hidden` flag that autostart uses.

sections.title: Renderer scheme and protocol handler
sections.explanation:
`registerSchemesAsPrivileged()` must run before the app is ready. It makes Chromium treat `returnapp://desktop` as a standard, secure origin with fetch support, while page CSP is still enforced (`bypassCSP: false`). `rendererUrl()` returns the scheme URL in a packaged build and the Vite dev server otherwise (`localhost:5180`, or `DESKTOP_RENDERER_URL`). `registerRendererProtocol()` serves files only from `desktop/renderer/dist`:

- Requests for other hosts are rejected.
- The path is normalized, and anything that escapes the dist folder (path traversal) is refused.
- Extensionless SPA routes fall back to `index.html`, and missing assets get a 404.
- If the renderer was never built, every request gets a readable 503 page.

`isRendererNavigation()` is the origin check used later to block navigation and to filter load failures.

sections.title: Engine target resolution
sections.explanation: `EngineTarget` is a discriminated union: a local engine with its bind settings, or a remote engine with a URL and a token. `readRemoteEngineTarget()` checks `RETURN_ENGINE_URL` strictly. The value must parse as a URL, use http or https, and have no path, and it must not send the token over plain http to a non-loopback host (`isInsecureRemoteUrl`). `ENGINE_TOKEN` must also be set. Each failure throws with a message that says how to fix it, instead of leaving a half-working dashboard. `startLocalEngine()` calls `startDesktopAppServer()` with `resolveEngineBind()` and resumes the claim bot if an operator is already signed in. `engineOrigin()` returns the origin that the header injection uses later.

sections.title: Shell status, toggle, status push
sections.explanation: `shellStatus()` gives the tray and the bridge one status shape. For a local engine it reads `engineStatus()`. For a remote engine it calls `GET /api/status` with the bearer header and a 5-second `AbortSignal.timeout`, and returns an 'unreachable' label on failure, so a stalled server cannot hang the tray refresh. `toggleWorker()` reads the status again just before acting on a local engine. For a remote engine it sends an explicit `pause` or `start` action instead of a blind toggle, so an out-of-date menu label cannot do the opposite of what the operator meant. `startBotStatusPush()` polls every 5 seconds and sends `desktop:bot-status-changed` to the renderer, skipping a destroyed window, so the renderer does not need to poll for this itself.

sections.title: Supplier and detached view hosts
sections.explanation: `registerSupplierViewHost()` gives the engine's native browser-view module callbacks to add and remove `WebContentsView`s on the main window, read its content bounds, and show or focus it. That is how supplier sign-in, OTP and CAPTCHA happen inside the app with no system browser. The detached-window host lets the Detach button move a live view, with its cookies, DOM state and worker lease, into a separate `BrowserWindow`. That window is built from `DETACHED_WINDOW_WEB_PREFERENCES`, with no Node and the sandbox on, because supplier pages run untrusted script. OTP and CAPTCHA popups move with the detached view and are resized with it, and control characters are stripped from window titles. Closing a detached window docks the tab back through `handleDetachedWindowClosed()`, unless the app is quitting.

sections.title: Update download and installer launch
sections.explanation: `resolveUpdateDownloadTarget()` accepts only URLs whose file name ends in `.exe`, and maps them into the Downloads folder with a `.part` file beside the target. The older popup path, `downloadUpdateAsset()`, reads the whole response into memory. The renderer-driven `downloadUpdateForRenderer()` instead streams it through a `Transform` that reports `desktop:download-progress` and writes to the `.part` file. The file is renamed only when the download succeeds, and leftovers are deleted in `finally`. Streaming keeps a large installer within the 256 MB heap rule and never leaves a truncated installer behind. `runUpdateInstallerForRenderer()` launches only a `.exe` inside Downloads. The doc comment says 'directly inside', but the prefix check also accepts subfolders. It replies at once, then after 1.5 seconds starts the installer detached with `cmd /c start` and quits with `isQuitting` set, so close-to-tray does not stop the quit.

sections.title: Window bounds and reload tuning
sections.explanation:
The shell saves the window's normal position and size in `window-bounds.json` under `userData`. Reading is defensive: the JSON is treated as untrusted and validated by `parseSavedBounds()`. Saving skips the minimized and maximized states, because those report misleading bounds, and `persistWindowBoundsSoon()` limits writes to one per second while the window is dragged. The constants below set limits on self-healing reloads:

- When the window is shown, reload only if the last page load finished more than 30 minutes ago, and at most once a minute.
- Force a reload of an unresponsive renderer only after 15 seconds, and at most twice in 10 minutes.

sections.title: createMainWindow
sections.explanation:
The window uses a persistent session partition, so operator and supplier cookies survive restarts, and registers the `returnapp` protocol on it. When the engine has a token (any remote engine, or a local engine bound to a non-loopback host), `webRequest.onBeforeSendHeaders` adds the `Authorization` header only to requests for the engine origin. That is how the renderer reaches a protected engine without ever seeing the token. The `BrowserWindow` runs with `contextIsolation`, no `nodeIntegration`, and `preload.cjs`. Geometry and lifecycle events go to the browser-view module so the embedded supplier view keeps fitting the dashboard. Several guards keep a 24/7 window alive:

- `will-navigate` blocks leaving the renderer origin.
- `setWindowOpenHandler` denies popups and sends `.exe` links to the downloader.
- A failed renderer load is retried after 3, 6 and 12 seconds.
- A crashed renderer reloads after 2 seconds, and an unresponsive one reloads within the limits above.
- Closing the window hides it to the tray instead of quitting.

sections.title: Tray menu and IPC handlers
sections.explanation:
`createTray()` rebuilds a context menu from `shellStatus()` on every refresh: the engine label, running or paused state, the active job, pause/resume, a one-shot 'Check for Claims Now', and Quit, which sets `isQuitting`. `checkForClaimsNow()` deliberately calls `engineRunOnceNow()` or `POST /api/scheduler/poll-now`, so it never resumes a paused worker. The `ipcMain` handlers are the main-process side of the preload bridge:

- app info
- a system-stats snapshot computed on demand from `app.getAppMetrics()`, with no timers, to keep idle CPU low
- the engine target URL, without the token
- bot status and toggle
- update download and install
- the browser-rect and fullscreen messages, where the rect is checked again here for finite, non-negative numbers

sections.title: App lifecycle, retries, autostart
sections.explanation: A single-instance lock makes a second launch focus the existing window. If the engine fails to start, `scheduleLocalEngineRetry()` tries again every 30 seconds, up to 20 times. It stops early on a configuration error in `RETURN_ENGINE_URL`, which it reads through `readRemoteTargetSafely()` so the error cannot become an unhandled rejection. When a retry succeeds, it rebuilds the window so the bearer injection matches the real engine origin. `registerAutoStart()` adds a hidden start-at-login entry only for packaged Windows builds, and skips it in remote mode: the entry carries no environment, so it would quietly start a local engine instead. `whenReady()` connects all of this. It shows the window even without an engine, using a loopback placeholder target, so the renderer can show its connecting state. `before-quit` saves the window bounds and disposes detached views, and `window-all-closed` quits only when `isQuitting` is set.

desktop/preload.cjs.overview: The preload script is the only bridge between the isolated React renderer and the Electron main process. It runs with `contextIsolation` and uses `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld` to publish a small, explicit `window.desktopApp` object: request methods, a bot toggle, notifications, update download and install, and supplier-browser layout messages. It deliberately exposes no raw `ipcRenderer`, no Node APIs and no secrets; the engine token stays in `main.ts`. AGENTS.md rule 19 treats this file and `desktop/renderer/src/types/global.d.ts` as one contract that must change together. It is the bridge described in tour step 14.

sections.title: Bridge contract header
sections.explanation: Only `contextBridge` and `ipcRenderer` are taken from Electron, and `ipcRenderer` is used inside this file without ever being handed to the page. The comment sets the security contract: no `nodeIntegration`, no raw `ipcRenderer`, nothing from process, env or secrets, and the remote `ENGINE_TOKEN` never crosses the bridge, because the main process adds the bearer header through `webRequest`. The file is CommonJS (`.cjs`) because it starts with `require`.

sections.title: Request/response methods
sections.explanation: `isDesktop` and `platform` let renderer code check that it is running inside the shell. Each getter wraps `ipcRenderer.invoke()` on a fixed, namespaced channel (`desktop:get-app-info`, `desktop:get-system-stats`, `desktop:get-engine-target`, `desktop:get-bot-status`, `desktop:toggle-bot`) and returns the promise from the matching `ipcMain.handle` in `main.ts`. Because the channel names are hard-coded, the page cannot call any other channel. That is the safety gained by not exposing `ipcRenderer` itself.

sections.title: Subscriptions, notifications, updates
sections.explanation: `onBotStatusChange()` and `onDownloadProgress()` register a wrapper listener that drops the IPC event object, so the renderer receives only the payload. Each returns an unsubscribe function that removes exactly that listener. Rule 19 requires this pattern so that a renderer reload or an effect cleanup never leaves duplicate listeners behind. A callback that is not a function gets a no-op unsubscribe instead of an error. `sendNotification` uses one-way `send()`. `downloadUpdate` and `runUpdateInstaller` use `invoke`, and their results report success, the saved path or an error.

sections.title: Supplier browser layout messages
sections.explanation: `setBrowserWorkspaceRect()` tells the main process where the dashboard's browser area is, so the native supplier view can be placed inside it. Sending `null` hides the view but keeps its session. The payload is checked before it crosses the bridge, so only finite numbers and non-negative sizes are sent. `main.ts` checks it again when it arrives, as a second layer of defence. `setBrowserFullscreen()` forwards the operator's Expand or Exit Fullscreen request.

desktop/renderer/src/App.tsx.overview: The root component of the bundled desktop renderer (`desktop/renderer`). It does its own hash routing across seven sidebar tabs and chooses between three top-level states: a connecting page when the engine is unreachable, the operator login gate, and the signed-in app shell. It keeps the operator session alive with a polling check that never signs the operator out because of a network blip. It also hosts the update banner, a follow-up watcher that raises OS notifications through `window.desktopApp`, and an error boundary around each page. This is part of tour step 14: every engine call goes through `services/config`, a re-export of `engineApi.ts`, without an `Authorization` header.

sections.title: Imports and tab registry
sections.explanation: `App` imports every page component plus the session, theme and engine-status hooks, and gets its API helpers from `./services/config`, a thin re-export of `engineApi.ts`. `TABS` is the one table of sidebar entries. It maps each tab id to its URL hash, label and component, and `TAB_BY_HASH` and `TAB_BY_ID` are lookup maps built from it, so adding a page means adding one row. `asApiError()` turns anything thrown into an `EngineApiError`, with status 0 for failures that are not HTTP errors, so later error handling can rely on one shape.

sections.title: Hash routing hook
sections.explanation: The renderer follows the repo's no-router convention with a small `useHashRoute()` hook. The first tab is taken from a valid `location.hash`, otherwise from a tab saved in `localStorage`, otherwise the dashboard. A `hashchange` listener, removed on cleanup, keeps state in step with back and forward navigation. `navigate()` sets the hash, or just updates state if the hash is already current. Every `localStorage` call is wrapped in try/catch because storage can be unavailable, so saving the tab is best-effort.

sections.title: Connecting page
sections.explanation: `ConnectingPage` is shown when the engine API is unreachable, and it needs no API data of its own. It shows the engine URL being tried, and tells a network failure (status 0, retried every few seconds) apart from a real HTTP error message. It offers a Retry button that is disabled while a retry is running. This is the offline state, drawn by the renderer itself, that AGENTS.md rule 17 requires instead of loading the engine's own dashboard.

sections.title: Operator login gate
sections.explanation: `LoginGate` posts the email and password to `/api/operator/login` with `apiPost`. On success it clears the password field before saving the user in the session context, so the password does not stay in component state. On failure it shows the engine's own `{ error }` body, such as a backend role refusal, or the client error message. The form uses proper `label`/`htmlFor` pairs, `autoComplete` hints and an error with `role=alert`, and it shows which engine the operator is signing in to.

sections.title: Update banner
sections.explanation: `UpdateBanner` calls `/api/updates/check` once a user is signed in and then every 30 minutes, but only when the auto-update preference from the Updates page is turned on. Errors are swallowed so an update check can never disrupt the shell. The banner is hidden when no update is available, or when the operator chose 'Later' for that release tag, which is saved in `localStorage`. The download button is handled by the `UpdateDownloadFlow` component.

sections.title: Follow-up ticket notifications
sections.explanation: `useFollowUpNotifications()` polls `/api/follow-ups` every 60 seconds while signed in. It compares the previous and current rows with `detectFollowUpNotifications()` and raises OS notifications through `window.desktopApp.sendNotification`. A module-level Set of keys already notified, saved to `localStorage` and limited to the last 200, stops the same ticket change from being announced again after a restart. The next poll is scheduled with `setTimeout` only after the current one finishes, so slow responses never overlap. Errors go to `handleAuthError`, so a 401 ends the session.

sections.title: Page error boundary
sections.explanation: `PageErrorBoundary` is a class component because React error boundaries still need `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`. It catches render errors from a page, logs details to the console, and shows a readable message with a Reload button instead of a white screen. AGENTS.md lists this as the white-screen fix from desktop 1.3.1. The shell gives each boundary the tab id as its `key`, so switching tabs resets a boundary that has caught an error.

sections.title: App state and session keep-alive
sections.explanation: `App` combines the session, theme, hash route, engine status (polled every 5 seconds) and the follow-up watcher, and looks up the engine base URL once for display. The session effect calls `/api/operator/session`. A clear answer sets or clears the user. A thrown error records a connection error and retries after 5 seconds, so a network blip never signs the operator out. The `sessionEpoch` comparison avoids clearing a session that a sign-in created while the check was still in flight. The `offline` flag combines the session error with a network-type status error. The worker pill is memoized from the status snapshot, and `onSidebarKeyDown` moves focus between the tab buttons with ArrowUp and ArrowDown.

sections.title: Shell layout and render
sections.explanation: Rendering has three outcomes: `ConnectingPage` when offline, `LoginGate` when there is no user, and the shell otherwise. The shell has a fixed 200 px sidebar, which the comment says the supplier browser view never covers, using a roving `tabIndex` and `aria-current`. The top bar shows the active tab, the worker pill, the operator's name and role, the CPU/RAM `SystemStatsPill` and a theme toggle. Below it come the update banner and the active page inside its error boundary. `TabId` and `TAB_BY_ID` are re-exported so pages can reuse the tab ids without keeping a second copy.

desktop/renderer/src/services/engineApi..overview: A small typed fetch client that every renderer page uses to call the claim engine's HTTP API. It gets the engine base URL once from the preload bridge, falling back to the local engine at `127.0.0.1:3005`. It turns failures into a typed `EngineApiError` and provides `apiGet`, `apiPost` and `apiDelete` helpers. Its most important rule is something it does not do: it never sets an `Authorization` header. For a protected engine the Electron shell adds the bearer token itself (tour step 14), so the token never reaches renderer code.

sections.title: Auth contract header
sections.explanation: The only import is the `EngineErrorBody` type. The doc comment is the module's contract. The base URL comes from `window.desktopApp.getEngineTarget()` and is cached, a plain browser in development falls back to the local engine, and remote auth is handled by the shell's `webRequest` hook. It forbids adding an `Authorization` header or accepting a token from anything the renderer can see, which keeps the AGENTS.md rule that the token never crosses the preload bridge.

sections.title: Cached base URL resolution
sections.explanation: `resolveEngineBase()` caches a promise rather than a string, so callers that arrive at the same time on first use share one bridge call instead of racing. It asks the bridge for the engine target and trims trailing slashes. It falls back to `LOCAL_ENGINE_BASE` when the bridge is missing, throws, or returns an empty URL, which `main.ts` uses to mean 'engine still starting'. `invalidateEngineBase()` clears the cache for when the shell switches to a different engine.

sections.title: Typed errors and predicates
sections.explanation: `EngineApiError` carries the HTTP `status` and the parsed error `body` along with the message. Status 0 is reserved for 'the engine could not be reached at all'. The type-guard functions `isNetworkError()` (status 0) and `isSessionError()` (status 401) let UI code tell an offline engine, which shows the connecting page, apart from an expired session, which goes back to login.

sections.title: Core request function
sections.explanation: `request()` adds a leading slash to the path if needed and waits for the cached base URL. It sends a JSON `Content-Type` and body only when a body is given. A rejected fetch, such as a refused connection or a DNS failure, becomes an `EngineApiError` with status 0 and a message naming the base URL. For a non-2xx response it tries to parse the engine's JSON error body, and uses its `error` field as the message when there is one. A 204 returns `undefined`. Any other response is parsed as JSON and cast to the caller's generic type. That cast is not checked at runtime, so the types in `types/engine.ts` must match what the engine actually returns.

sections.title: Verb helpers
sections.explanation: `apiGet`, `apiPost` and `apiDelete` are thin wrappers that fix the HTTP method. `apiPost` always sends a JSON body, defaulting to `{}`, so engine routes that parse JSON never receive an empty body. Pages import these helpers, directly or through `services/config.ts`, instead of calling `fetch` themselves.

desktop/renderer/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx.overview: The renderer's landing page, a live overview of the claim engine for the operator. It polls engine status, jobs, supplier panels and ticket follow-ups at different rates. Pure functions in `dashboard/dashboard-logic.ts` derive the overall headline ('All panels green' or 'Action required') and the per-panel chips. The page shows job-stage KPIs, a worker card with pause/resume and poll-now actions, a live engine log, and a supplier panel strip with a 'Rejoin rotation' action. It is the page tour step 14 describes, and it calls the engine only through `engineApi.ts`.

sections.title: Imports and polling intervals
sections.explanation: The page combines the shared hooks (`useEngineStatus`, `useEnginePolling`), the typed engine client and response types, small UI components, the pure helpers from `dashboard/dashboard-logic.ts`, and the `useLogStream` hook. Keeping that logic in a separate module means it can be unit-tested outside React. The poll intervals follow how quickly each source changes: panels every 5 seconds, jobs every 10 seconds, follow-ups every 60 seconds. `actionErrorMessage()` uses the engine's own error body when the failure is an `EngineApiError`.

sections.title: Worker pill and tone tables
sections.explanation: `WorkerPill` turns a status snapshot into one badge, checked in this order: processing (with the active job summary), running, paused if signed in, otherwise idle. The three `Record` lookup tables map a chip tone or a log level to Tailwind classes. Because they are typed as `Record<PanelChipTone, string>` and `Record<LogLevel, string>`, the compiler reports any tone or level that has no style.

sections.title: Polling and derived state
sections.explanation: Status is polled every 2 seconds here, faster than the shell's 5 seconds, and the three `useEnginePolling` calls each return a `{ data, error }` pair. The panels value has three states: `undefined` while loading, `null` on error, or an array. The render code shows a spinner, an error card or the strip for each. `panelsOverride` shows the fresh panel list returned by a successful action until the next poll replaces it. `deriveOverallStatus`, `derivePanelChips` and `countJobStages` are memoized. The next-poll countdown starts from each status snapshot and counts down locally once per second, so the number moves without extra network calls.

sections.title: Worker and panel actions
sections.explanation: `toggleWorker()` sends an explicit `?action=pause` or `?action=start` to `/api/scheduler/toggle`, chosen from the current status, instead of a blind toggle, and then refreshes the status. `pollNow()` triggers a single poll. `rejoinRotation()` clears a held panel (manual action, cooldown or prepared) through `/api/panels/:key/clear`, with the key URL-encoded, and only one panel action can run at a time. Each action has its own busy flag and error message. `useLogStream(5)` keeps the five most recent engine log entries, and the colour of the headline dot follows the overall state.

sections.title: Status headline and KPI grid
sections.explanation: The first card shows the overall title and detail, such as 'All panels green' or 'Action required', with a coloured dot and the per-panel chips. This matches the dashboard headline described in AGENTS.md. The KPI grid shows a spinner before the first jobs response and an error state if that response never arrives. Once data exists, a later failed refresh keeps the old numbers and shows an amber 'Showing last snapshot' notice above them. The five `StatCard`s (total, completed, queued, in progress, action required) come from `countJobStages()`.

sections.title: Worker card and live activity
sections.explanation: The worker card shows the next-poll countdown, the last heartbeat, the last poll and, when the engine reports it, the nightly-window state for follow-up checks. Its buttons are disabled, with a title explaining why, while the status is unknown. This follows AGENTS.md rule 10: every control works or is disabled with a reason. The activity panel shows the engine log stream newest first, with live, connecting and reconnecting badges and a colour for each log level. Its Clear button is disabled when the list is empty.

sections.title: Supplier panel strip
sections.explanation: Each supplier panel card shows its state dot, its marketplace badge, an Automated or Assisted label, a cookies badge if a session was saved, and the last result. The list handles the loading, error and empty states explicitly. Held panels (`manual_action`, `cooldown`, `prepared`) get a Rejoin rotation button. While another panel's action is running, that button is disabled with a title saying why.

Dockerfile.overview: The production image for the Express API and the React web console that runs on the Hostinger VPS. It is a two-stage `node:22-alpine` build. The builder installs every dependency, runs the full four-project typecheck and the Vite + esbuild build. The runner keeps only production dependencies, the built `dist/` client, the single `server/dist.js` bundle and the SQL schema files. The container runs as the non-root `node` user on port 3001, with a heap cap and an HTTP health check. Tour step 15 uses it as its example of a multi-stage build.

sections.title: Builder stage base
sections.explanation: The `syntax` line pins the Dockerfile frontend version. The builder stage starts from `node:22-alpine` and adds `libc6-compat`, which helps npm packages whose native binaries were built for glibc run on Alpine's musl libc.

sections.title: Dependency layer and sources
sections.explanation: `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are copied, and `npm ci` runs before any source is copied, so Docker reuses the cached dependency layer when only the code changes. `npm ci` installs dev dependencies too, because the build and the typecheck need them. The `desktop/` and `desktop-agent/` sources are copied even though they are not shipped: the typecheck includes the desktop projects, so building the image checks them as well.

sections.title: Typecheck and build
sections.explanation: `npm run typecheck` runs `tsc` on the web, server, desktop and desktop-renderer projects, so a type error fails the image build. `npm run build` then runs `vite build` to put the web client in `dist/`, and esbuild to bundle `server/index.ts` into `server/dist.js`. esbuild runs with `--packages=external`, which leaves npm packages out of the bundle, so the runner still needs `node_modules`.

sections.title: Runner stage and environment
sections.explanation: The runner starts again from a clean `node:22-alpine` and adds only `curl` (for the health check) and CA certificates. `NODE_ENV=production`, `PORT=3001` and a `NODE_OPTIONS` old-space limit of 384 MB are set as defaults in the image. The production compose file sets the same values again.

sections.title: Production deps and artifacts
sections.explanation: `npm ci --omit=dev` installs only runtime dependencies, and the npm cache is cleaned to make the layer smaller. Only the `dist/` web bundle and `server/dist.js` are copied from the builder. The `.sql` schema files are copied from the build context because `server/db.ts` applies them at startup (tour step 3), and `public/` is copied for static assets. `/app/data` and `/app/certs` are created and given to the `node` user; these are the paths `docker-compose.production.yml` mounts as volumes.

sections.title: Non-root user, health, start
sections.explanation: `USER node` runs the server without root privileges. The `HEALTHCHECK` curls `/api/health` every 30 seconds after a 15-second start period, so Docker can see when the container is unhealthy. `CMD` runs `node server/dist.js` directly; the comment notes that this avoids the overhead of tsx and keeps memory use low.

docker-compose.production.yml.overview: Defines how the API container from the root Dockerfile runs in production on the Hostinger VPS. It builds and runs one `return-app` service with a restart policy, environment loaded from a `.env` file on the server, a port bound only to loopback, persistent data and certificate volumes, a health check, log rotation, and CPU and memory limits. Traefik, reached through the external `shared_infra` network, serves the public domain and a fallback hostname over HTTPS with Let's Encrypt certificates, with HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects and HSTS headers. It is the deployment target described in tour step 15.

sections.title: Service, build and ports
sections.explanation: The compose project and the service are both named `return-app`. The container is named `Return-App`, and its image is built from the root Dockerfile. `restart: unless-stopped` brings the container back after a crash or a reboot. Port 3001 is published only on `127.0.0.1` on the host, so the API is not reachable directly from the internet; public traffic comes in through Traefik on the shared network.

sections.title: Environment and host aliases
sections.explanation: Runtime configuration comes from a `.env` file on the server through `env_file`, which keeps secrets such as the database connection string out of the compose file and the image. The project rules say never to open that file. The inline variables repeat the production defaults and set `TZ` to Asia/Kolkata for date handling. They also give `SENTRY_DSN` a default through `${SENTRY_DSN:-...}` substitution; that default value is hard-coded in the committed file. `extra_hosts` maps `host.docker.internal` and the VPS hostname to the host gateway, so the container can reach services running on the host.

sections.title: Traefik routers and redirects
sections.explanation: The service joins the `shared_infra` network and opts in to Traefik with `traefik.enable`. Two HTTPS routers on the `websecure` entrypoint serve the custom domain and a Hostinger fallback hostname. Each uses TLS from the `letsencrypt` certificate resolver and the shared headers middleware. Two matching routers on the plain `web` entrypoint use a `redirectscheme` middleware that sends a permanent redirect to HTTPS.

sections.title: Security headers and backend port
sections.explanation: The `return-app-headers` middleware forces an SSL redirect and sets HSTS for one year (31536000 seconds), including subdomains and with the preload flag, so a browser refuses plain HTTP after its first visit. The load-balancer label tells Traefik that the container listens on port 3001. The last two labels are metadata for Hostinger's hPanel Docker Manager.

sections.title: Volumes, health, logs, limits
sections.explanation: `./data` is mounted read-write at `/app/data`, and `./certs` is mounted read-only at `/app/certs`, matching the directories the Dockerfile creates. The health check repeats the image's curl to `/api/health`, with a longer timeout and start period. `json-file` logging rotates at 20 MB and keeps three files, so logs cannot fill the disk. The resource limits cap the container at one CPU and 512 MB, which leaves headroom above the 384 MB heap cap. `shared_infra` is declared `external` because the Traefik stack creates and owns it.

.github/workflows/ci.yml.overview: The main GitHub Actions workflow that checks the web console and the API. On every push and pull request to `main`, and on manual dispatch, it installs dependencies, runs the four-project typecheck, and builds the Vite client and the esbuild server bundle. It then runs the full `node:test` suite against a throwaway `postgres:16` service, so the database tests run instead of being skipped, and finally checks that the production Docker image still builds. It is the CI check described in tour step 15.

sections.title: Triggers and permissions
sections.explanation: The workflow runs on pushes and pull requests that target `main`, plus `workflow_dispatch` for manual runs. `permissions: contents: read` gives the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` the least access it needs, because this job only reads the repository.

sections.title: Throwaway PostgreSQL service
sections.explanation: The single `verify` job runs on `ubuntu-latest` with a `postgres:16` service container on `localhost:5432`. The user and password are throwaway values written inline, and the database is named `return_test`. The comment explains the choice: the name contains 'test', as the project requires of a test database, and the host is localhost, so the connection rule in `server/db.ts` uses no TLS for it. Production data is never touched. The health-check options make the job wait until `pg_isready` succeeds before the steps start.

sections.title: Checkout and Node setup
sections.explanation: The steps check out the code, install Node 20 with npm caching keyed on the lockfile, and run `npm ci` for a clean install that matches the lockfile exactly. CI uses Node 20, while the Docker images and the desktop release workflow use Node 22.

sections.title: Typecheck, build, test, Docker
sections.explanation: `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` fail the job early on any type or bundling error. The test step sets `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to the service database, so the database-backed tests run here. Locally they are skipped without that variable, and a skipped test has not passed. The last step runs `docker build` on the root Dockerfile, so a broken image is caught before deployment, although nothing is pushed.

.github/workflows/desktop-release.yml.overview: Builds and publishes the Windows desktop claim bot. It runs on `windows-latest` whenever desktop, engine, claim-related server or packaging files change. It fails a pull request that changes them without bumping the version in `package.json`, then runs the typecheck, build and tests and produces the NSIS installer. On pushes to `main`, or a manual dispatch with publish turned on, it creates a `desktop-v<version>.<run>` GitHub release that is not marked latest. It then deletes all but the newest two desktop releases and never touches the Android ones. This is the release part of tour step 15, and it enforces AGENTS.md rule 20.

sections.title: Path-filtered triggers
sections.explanation:
The push and pull_request triggers use the same path list:

- `desktop/` and `desktop-agent/`
- the server claim files, claim schemas and their tests
- the web Claims page and shared types
- `build/`, the package files and this workflow file

Only changes that can affect the desktop build start the workflow. The `desktop/renderer/**` entry adds nothing, because `desktop/**` already covers it. `workflow_dispatch` adds a boolean `publish` input, true by default, for manual releases.

sections.title: Permissions and concurrency
sections.explanation: Permissions are read-only at workflow level; only the publish job later raises them to `contents: write`. The concurrency group is per ref with `cancel-in-progress: false`, so a second release run on the same branch waits in line instead of cancelling the first partway through publishing.

sections.title: Version-bump check
sections.explanation: The build job checks out the full history (`fetch-depth: 0`) and sets up Node 22. On pull requests, a bash step reads the version from `package.json` at the PR's base commit with `git show` and compares it with the head version. If the two are the same, it writes a GitHub `::error::` annotation and fails. The comment explains why: the in-app updater ignores tags that differ only in run number, and NSIS skips an upgrade to the same version, so a desktop fix without a version bump would never reach installed apps.

sections.title: Build, test, installer artifact
sections.explanation: The job runs the full set of checks again on Windows: `npm ci`, the typecheck, the build and `npm test`. `npm run desktop:dist` then builds the renderer, bundles `main.ts`, and packages the NSIS installer with electron-builder. `upload-artifact` stores `dist-electron/Return.App.Setup.*.exe`, and `if-no-files-found: error` fails the run if no installer was produced.

sections.title: Publish job setup
sections.explanation: `publish-release` runs after `build-desktop` and only for pushes to `main` or a manual dispatch with `publish` turned on, so pull requests build but never publish. It is the only job with `contents: write`, and it downloads the installer artifacts into `release-input`.

sections.title: Create or update the release
sections.explanation: The bash script collects the `.exe` files and fails if there are none. It reads the version from `package.json` and builds the tag `desktop-v<version>.<run number>`. `gh release create` publishes the installer against the exact commit, with release notes about the panels and the low-spec optimizations. It passes `--latest=false` so the Android APK releases keep GitHub's Latest badge. If the release cannot be created because the tag already exists, the `||` branch uploads the files again with `--clobber`.

sections.title: Pruning old desktop releases
sections.explanation: `gh release list` with a jq filter selects only tags that start with `desktop-v` and sorts them newest first by publish date. Everything after the first two (the current release plus one for rollback) is deleted along with its tag. Filtering on that prefix is what keeps this workflow away from the Android `v1.0.*` releases, which belong to the APK workflow. Each delete ends with `|| true`, so one failed deletion does not fail an otherwise successful release.

deploy/engine/Dockerfile.overview: Packages the automation engine from tour step 12 for a headless Linux server, the second deployment mode next to the Windows desktop app. It uses `node:22-slim` with the distro's Chromium and its runtime libraries, installs production dependencies, and copies only `desktop-agent/`. It runs the engine straight from TypeScript through tsx, with a 256 MB heap cap, as an unprivileged user under tini. The environment defaults bind the engine to all interfaces on port 3005, which the engine allows only when an `ENGINE_TOKEN` is set (AGENTS.md rule 15). A health check calls the one route that needs no token.

sections.title: Purpose header
sections.explanation: The header says what the image is for: queue polling, CDP browser automation of supplier portals, panel state, the health probe and the bearer-token control API, all without a graphical desktop. Chromium is installed from the distro rather than bundled, and is driven headless over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. According to the comment, this is the same code path the Windows build uses against the system browser.

sections.title: Base image and engine env
sections.explanation: The image uses `node:22-slim` (Debian) rather than Alpine because Chromium and its libraries come from apt. The environment sets the data directory for profiles and evidence (`AGENT_DATA_DIR`), binds the engine to `0.0.0.0:3005`, selects headless browser mode, and points `BROWSER_PATH` at `/usr/bin/chromium`, which `findSystemBrowser()` checks first. Binding to all interfaces triggers the engine's fail-closed rule: it will not start without an `ENGINE_TOKEN` of at least 24 characters. The token is supplied at deploy time and is not part of the image. The comment explains the sandbox: running as the non-root `node` user lets Chromium keep its sandbox, and `BROWSER_NO_SANDBOX=1` is only a last resort for container runtimes that block the user namespaces the sandbox needs.

sections.title: Chromium and system libraries
sections.explanation: One `RUN` layer installs Chromium, CA certificates, `curl` for the health check, the Liberation fonts so pages can render text, the GTK, NSS, X11 and DRM libraries that headless Chromium depends on, and `tini`. `--no-install-recommends` and deleting the apt lists afterwards keep the image smaller.

sections.title: Dependencies and engine source
sections.explanation: The lockfile is copied and `npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund` runs before any source is copied, so the dependency layer stays cached. `tsx` is a regular dependency in `package.json`, so it is kept by `--omit=dev` and can run the TypeScript sources at runtime. Only `desktop-agent/` is copied; the web client, the Android app and the Electron shell are not part of this image.

sections.title: Data directory, user, health
sections.explanation: The engine's data directory is created and owned by `node`. The comment says to mount a volume there because it holds browser profiles, the evidence cache and logs, which AGENTS.md treats as secret. `USER node` drops root, `EXPOSE` documents port 3005, and the `HEALTHCHECK` curls `/api/health`, the only engine route that does not need the bearer token.

sections.title: tini entrypoint and engine command
sections.explanation: `tini` runs as PID 1 and reaps the Chromium child processes the engine starts, so no zombie browsers pile up after a claim. The `CMD` runs `node` with `--max-old-space-size=256` to match the desktop shell and AGENTS.md rule 13; without it Node would size its heap from the host's total RAM. It loads tsx through `--import` and starts `desktop-app-server.ts` with `--no-window` for headless operation.

src/date-field.tsx.overview: Shared DateField input that always displays DD/MM/YYYY regardless of the OS locale while keeping ISO yyyy-mm-dd values for the API, layered over a hidden native date picker.

src/pages/Admin.tsx.overview: Admin settings page with tabs for users and sessions, issue categories and options, logistics partners and aliases, the product SKU master (staged batched import, unmapped SKU review, auto-link), marketplace accounts and automation credentials, claim templates, and system, report and payment settings.

src/pages/Claims.tsx.overview: Claims page with overview, claim queue and desktop automation tabs: aggregated rupee claim totals with CSV export, a filterable claim queue, a detail modal with copy buttons, evidence gallery, lightbox and video player, unified claim creation from a return lookup, and automation agent, job and credential monitoring.

src/pages/Dashboard.tsx.overview: Overview page that loads /api/dashboard and renders stat cards, hourly scanning throughput, operator and marketplace processing, return volume with a marketplace donut, top reasons, issues by marketplace, high-risk SKUs and recent scans.

src/pages/IronBatches.tsx.overview: Iron Send batch management: lists numbered daily batches (IRN-YYMMDD-NNN) with state and handover filters, a batch dialog with the Return Team handover workflow, receive and download actions, Excel/CSV/slip downloads and printing, and a dialog to create a batch from pending records.

src/pages/IronTracking.tsx.overview: Iron tracking page: lists Iron Send records by state with account and date filters and summaries, embeds the batches section, and provides dialogs to receive ironed units, create batches, clear pending records and set the overdue threshold, gated by role.

src/pages/Login.tsx.overview: Sign-in page that posts credentials to /api/auth/login with a remember-device option and maps 401, 403, 429 and 503 responses to operator-friendly messages; the session lives in an HttpOnly cookie.

src/pages/Reports.tsx.overview: Return register page (/register): server-side filtered, sorted and paginated register table with approved and operational CSV exports, record detail and ticket editor modals, live refresh, and code-split analysis tabs for Analytics, Shopify and OMSGuru.

src/pages/ReturnTracking.tsx.overview: Return tracking page: monthly return-creation tracking from /api/returns/tracking with account and date filters, return report CSV upload, scan reconciliation, SPF claim eligibility badges and 1-click claim filing, plus CSV export.

src/pages/Uploads.tsx.overview: Data uploads page: previews and imports marketplace return files and scanner lists per account, shows validation exceptions, unmapped SKUs and batch progress, downloads templates and exception CSVs, and lists upload history.

src/partners.ts.overview: Maps logistics partner names (Delhivery, Shadowfax, Xpress Bees, Flipkart Logistics, Valmo) to logo image paths for partner badges.

src/register-view.test.ts.overview: node:test characterization tests pinning register-view behaviour: query building, pagination and sort mapping, issue, sub-issue and ticket labels, ticket status tones, flyer and matched-field text, and the four register tabs, using SYN- synthetic fixtures.

src/register-view.ts.overview: Pure, DOM-free view helpers for the return register: filter, sort and pagination query building with server sort-key mapping, issue and ticket label derivation, status tones, display label maps, and the register tab definitions and parser.

src/returns-table.tsx.overview: Shared returns table used by the Overview (compact) and Reports (full) pages, built on DataTable with marketplace badges, issue and ticket-status columns, and an inline editable ticket cell that saves on blur or Enter.

src/shell.tsx.overview: Workspace shell components: Loading and PageError states, the collapsible Sidebar with role-filtered navigation and claims badge, and the page Header with titles, live-sync badge, server date and scan shortcut.

src/ui.tsx.overview: Shared UI primitives: an inline SVG Icon set, brand marks (YouthnicMark, ReturnLogo), Badge, MarketplaceBadge and PartnerBadge with logo fallback, Modal, StatCard, and a generic column-driven DataTable used across all pages.

android/app/src/main/java/shop/youthnic/.overview: WorkManager CoroutineWorker that retries uploading a single claim evidence file (photo or video) in the background when the in-app upload fails, deleting the local file on success.

OkHttp-based REST client for the Android scanner covering auth, marketplace accounts, scan session/lookup/complete, register history, sync cursor, claims (search, Meesho drafts, unified create, evidence multipart upload) and the latest-release manifest, returning Kotlin Result values.

Barcode rules for the scanner: normalises raw scans, extracts AWBs or Amazon order IDs from barcode/QR content, filters allowed 1D/2D formats, generates server-valid SYN-MOBILE client scan keys, and provides a DuplicateGuard that throttles repeated camera detections.

Two-level catalog image cache (LRU memory cache sized to 1/8 of heap plus an MD5-keyed disk cache) that downloads product images over OkHttp and decodes down-sampled bitmaps for thumbnails and the full-screen viewer.

Live update client that keeps a WebSocket to /api/live open and falls back to polling /api/sync/state every 4 seconds, tracking the audit sync cursor and notifying the scanner when data changed so today's figures reload.

Defines the per-line verification state and submit data models and builds/validates the POST /api/scan/complete body exactly as server/register-rules.ts expects, including missing-unit, affected-unit, sub-issue, ticket and notes rules.

Persists the scanner session in EncryptedSharedPreferences (falling back to private prefs): server URL, bearer token, user identity and role, last selected marketplace account, last scanned return snapshot, permission prompts and sound/vibration/flash preferences.

Single-shot CameraX + ML Kit barcode capture screen with torch toggle that returns the first valid scanned AWB/order code to the caller via an activity result; used by the claim capture flow for AWB and flyer fields.

Home screen listing the user's marketplace accounts as coloured channel cards; opens the scanner for a channel, the claim capture screen (prefilled from the last scan) or settings, asks camera and notification permissions once, and shows an in-app update card.

Two-step marketplace claim filing wizard: step 1 looks up the return by scanned or typed AWB/sub-order and captures issue type and parcel condition; step 2 collects photo, gallery and unboxing-video evidence per template, submits via the unified-create claim API, uploads evidence with a progress dialog and queues failures to WorkManager.
Full-screen product image viewer that loads a catalog image through ImageCache and supports pinch-to-zoom and panning with a transformation matrix.
Sign-in screen that lets the operator set the server URL, log in with email/password and remember-device, then explains and requests camera permission before opening the channel list.
Dialog for typing an AWB or order ID when the camera cannot read the barcode; cleans the entry with BarcodeRules and hands it to the scanner's lookup callback.
Dialog listing the most recent scans newest-first with IST timestamps and colour-coded outcome badges.

Bottom sheet where the operator verifies a looked-up return line by line: received quantity, physical check, server issue category and sub-issue chips, ticket and notes, plus Meesho flyer capture, validated with ScanPayload before handing VerificationSubmitData back to the scanner.
Settings screen with toggles for beep, vibration and screen flash, showing server URL and app version, a manual check-for-updates action and logout.
Launch screen that validates a stored session with /api/auth/me, keeps the session when offline, clears it when revoked, and routes to the channel list or login.
Camera permission helpers covering the three states (granted, can still ask, blocked) plus a plain-words rationale dialog and a deep link to the app's system settings.
Camera and performance tuning constants for warehouse scanning: 720p preview, 1080p analysis for 1D barcodes, ~10 fps analysis throttle, 2-minute idle pause and FPS range selection helpers.
Pure signal table for scan verdict cues (OK, DUPLICATE, NOT_FOUND, CHECK, STOP): photo-safe screen blink timings, vibration patterns, synthesised tone sequences and PCM generation.
Low-latency audio and haptics manager that pre-builds AudioTracks from ScanSignals PCM per cue, falls back to ToneGenerator, and honours the sound and vibration preferences in SessionManager.
Small UI helper object: view tinting and pill styling, safe colour parsing, dp conversion, number and megabyte formatting, and server-time parsing with IST date/time and relative-age labels.

android/app/src/test/java/shop/youthnic/.overview: JUnit tests for BarcodeRules and DuplicateGuard covering QR/URL rejection, length bounds, format filtering, duplicate suppression and cooldown, client scan key server-rule conformance and Amazon order ID extraction.
JUnit tests for CameraTuning resolution constants, FPS range selection (including no matching upper bound) and the describe string.

JUnit tests for ScanPayload verifying the scan-complete body and validation messages: clear lines send no issue, missing units, affected-unit counts, ticket-only-when-required, Iron Send without mandatory notes and plain-word problems.
JUnit tests for ScanSignals ensuring blinks match beeps, no more than three flashes per second, flashes start on and end dark, cues are distinct and PCM is audible but unclipped.

desktop-agent/agent-cleanup.test.ts.overview: node:test suite proving AgentBackendClient.cleanClaimEvidenceFiles deletes downloaded claim evidence but keeps the referenced submission screenshot, and removes everything when nothing is referenced.

desktop-agent/browser-adapter.test.ts.overview: Tests supplier browser adapter selection (native bundled Chromium vs external system browser), the Electron-only guard for the native adapter, BrowserRunner's structural fit to SupplierBrowserApi, the marketplace support pre-check, and the Chrome user-agent and Sec-CH-UA client hints set on supplier sessions.

desktop-agent/browser-flags.test.ts.overview: Tests the Chromium sandbox policy: the sandbox stays on by default and is disabled only for a truthy BROWSER_NO_SANDBOX or when running as root on Linux.

desktop-agent/cors.test.ts.overview: Tests the engine CORS allowlist: returnapp://desktop is always allowed, Vite dev origins only in development, ENGINE_CORS_ORIGINS extras are parsed leniently but exactly, wildcards and arbitrary origins are denied, and corsHeadersFor never emits '*'.

desktop-agent/cycle-watchdog.test.ts.overview: Tests withCycleTimeout with mocked timers: the body result wins inside the budget, the CYCLE_TIMEOUT sentinel and a single onTimeout fire when the timer wins, late settlements are ignored, onTimeout errors are swallowed, and the engine cycle budgets ship as expected.

desktop-agent/engine-config.test.ts.overview: Tests the engine bind and remote-access policy: loopback defaults without a token, refusal to bind a reachable host without a 24+ character token, port validation, constant-time token comparison, bearer header parsing, IPv6 and wildcard client URLs, insecure plain-http remote detection and exact same-origin checks.

desktop-agent/evidence-files.test.ts.overview: Tests the local evidence-file helpers against a temp directory: strict claim id validation, path-traversal-safe file resolution, sorted listing that skips .part files and directories, content-type/disposition mapping and stream headers.

desktop-agent/follow-up-bundle.test.ts.overview: Tests that followUpExecutionBundle carries only the claim and panel (no evidence, no credentials, follow_up stage) and enforces the ticket-status reader contract: only Meesho overrides checkClaimStatus among the registered marketplace engines.

desktop-agent/local-secrets-bundle.test..overview: Bundles local-secrets with esbuild into the packaged CJS shape next to a stubbed electron module to prove Electron safeStorage (DPAPI) is reachable in the installed app, with a negative control showing the pre-fix createRequire(import.meta.url) logic fails.

desktop-agent/local-secrets.test.ts.overview: Tests the local secret protection fallback: tokens round-trip without OS encryption, legacy plaintext and empty values are read safely, and an undecryptable DPAPI value is reported unusable instead of throwing.

desktop-agent/meesho-issues.test.ts.overview: Broad Meesho automation test suite covering issue-code and parcel-condition label mapping, ticket-row parsing, already-filed ticket detection, upload-field mapping and local evidence checks, resolution/rejection extraction, the 23 MB unpacking-video gate, early blocker detection and MeeshoAutomation constructor defaults.
